items.title: EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache last-block drop causes a 1,648-token recompute per hit on one hybrid Qwen3.8 GDN layout — ~30-40% batch throughput loss on prefix-reusing workloads with speculative decoding
items.author: Suppressor72
items.body_excerpt:
EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache last-block drop causes a 1,648-token recompute per
hit on one hybrid Qwen3.8 GDN layout — ~30-40% batch throughput loss on
prefix-reusing workloads with speculative decoding enabled

## Environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0`, V1/V2 model runner, async scheduling
- Dual RTX 5090 TP=2, FP8 weights + FP8 KV, prefix caching on
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid: GDN/Mamba layers + full attention → 15
  MambaSpec KV groups + full-attention group; scheduler/hash block = 1648
  tokens); other hybrid layouts should be evaluated by their own scheduler
  alignment
- Speculative: dflash (DFlash2, K=7) and mtp — both reproduce; also
  reproduces with an always-K=0 tiered config `[[1,16,0]]` +
  `skip_draft_when_k0: true` (drafter provably never runs at c ≥ 3; without
  `skip_draft_when_k0`, K=0 draft-state sync may still run)

## Summary

With any EAGLE-family `speculative_config` set, multi-round / repeated-prompt
workloads lose ~6-10 points of prefix-cache hit rate versus an identical
no-spec boot (97.5% → 86.9-91.7% in our harness). The cause is the EAGLE
last-block drop (`drop_eagle_block`) in the prefix-cache hit path:

1. `kv_cache_coordinator.py` flags **all** KV groups as eagle when the model
   has no `is_eagle_group` annotation (conservative fallback).
2. The EAGLE-marked dense/full-attention group drops one alignment unit from
   its hit (protecting against (a) draft-layer KV for the last block depending
   on the writer's continuation and (b) prefill-lookahead pollution at chunk
   boundaries); hybrid reconciliation then limits the combined hit to that
   shorter boundary, so the request recomputes one 1,648-token scheduler-
   aligned unit.
3. On dense-attention models that alignment unit is a 16-token block. On this
   hybrid GDN/Mamba layout it is **1,648 tokens**. The same protection
   therefore costs ~100× more cache hit here; other hybrid layouts should be
   evaluated by their own scheduler alignment.

Measured per-request-per-round (32k identical prompt re-sent, cache trace of
`get_computed_blocks`):

| Config | warm lookup hit | tail recompute | c=8 tok/s (vs no-spec 327) |
|---|---|---|---|
| no speculative_config | 31360 (20×1568) | 640 tok | 327 |
| dflash K=7 + tiers | 29664 (18×1648) | 2336 tok | 206 (−37%) |
| dflash + drop disabled (ablation) | 31312 (19×1648) | 688 tok | 322 (−1.6%) |

Disabling the drop recovers essentially the entire warm prefix-reuse gap
(+56% at c=8) on this workload — the last-block rule, not spec-decode step
machinery, accounts for it (a separate cold-prefill drafter cost exists on
unique-prompt traffic; see below) (we profiled the
engine loop: per-step decode time is within 0.6% of no-spec at resolved K=0).

The regression is easy to miss: single-request benchmarks with unique prompts
don't reuse prefixes, and aggregate token/s hides where the time goes. Watch
`vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` and the re-prefill chunk census instead.

## Why the drop is still needed (and why "just disable it" is not the answer)

The drop is load-bearing for consumers that draft: draft-layer KV in the last
matched block depends on tokens past the matched prefix (the writer's
continuation), and chunked prefill with drafting combines a lookahead token
into boundary KV. Serving such a block to a request that will draft from that
boundary gives it stale/foreign draft KV. Speculative decoding stays
lossless (the target verifies every token), so the damage is acceptance
degradation rather than wrong outputs — but for K>0 consumers the recompute
the drop forces is the correct behavior.

The asymmetry is that a consumer running at **resolved K=0** (dynamic
speculation tiers with `skip_draft_when_k0`, or any K=0 tier) never executes
the drafter at all, so it never reads draft-layer KV: the drop protects a
consumer that does not exist. Our proposed fix makes the drop conditional on
exactly that (reference implementation on our fork — over our open-PR limit
on main right now, will open the PR when a slot frees:
https://github.com/Suppressor72/vllm/tree/feat/eagle-k0-consumer-drop @
dfb6eeae79): skip it when the admission's projected
resolved K is 0 under `skip_draft_when_k0`. Result on the same harness:
c=8 206 → 304 tok/s (no-spec 327, hard-disable ceiling 322), prefix-cache hit
rate 91.7% → 95.4%, zero change at c=1/c=2 where K>0 still drafts.

## Repro

Measured on nightly `0.26.1rc1.dev926+gb05ae5dc0` + local patches (DFlash2
backport #52816, `skip_draft_when_k0` #53420/#53426 lineage, dflash tier
validation) — the cache-path code under discussion is upstream code; config:

```json
{"method": "dflash",
 "model": "<DFlash2 drafter for the target>",
 "num_speculative_tokens": 7,
 "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size": [[1, 2, 7], [3, 16, 0]],
 "skip_draft_when_k0": true}
```

The causal comparison stays within one 1,648-token geometry: stock hit
29,664 (18 blocks) → drop-disabled 31,312 (19 blocks), same boot layout. The
no-spec arm (31,360 at a different 1,568-token layout) is context, not the
proof.


1. Any hybrid-GDN target with dflash/mtp/eagle `speculative_config`,
   `enable_prefix_caching=true`.
2. Client: re-send the same ~32k prompt (chat completions), 4 rounds × 8
   concurrent sessions, 256 tokens each.
3. Compare against the same boot without `speculative_config`:
   aggregate tok/s, `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total`, and (instrumented)
   `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` hit lengths — hits land exactly on
   block-size multiples and are one block shorter under spec.

## Additional observation (separate, not addressed by the PR)

With fully unique prompts (`--salt auto`: no reuse possible) the spec boot
still runs at ~0.59× no-spec on this target (150.7 vs 255.8 tok/s at c=8,
prefill-dominated legs) — a cold-prefill drafter-context cost that is
inherent to running the drafter, distinct from the cache issue above. We have
not yet decomposed it; happy to file separately if maintainers prefer.

items.title: [Bug]: FlashInfer TensorRT-LLM NVFP4 KV cache produces invalid Qwen3.5-397B output on Blackwell
items.author: mikekg
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

## Environment

- GPU: NVIDIA B200
- vLLM: `0.28.1rc1.dev199+g7c5dc571c`
- FlashInfer: `0.6.18`
- CUDA: `13.0`
- CUDA graphs: enabled
- Attention backend: FlashInfer TensorRT-LLM

### 🐛 Describe the bug

# FlashInfer TensorRT-LLM NVFP4 KV cache produces invalid Qwen3.5-397B output on Blackwell

## Summary

On B200, `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` produces mostly empty or immediately terminated responses when FlashInfer's TensorRT-LLM attention backend uses an NVFP4 KV cache. The matched FP8 KV-cache configuration produces normal answers.

All measurements retain the compiled CUDA-graph path.

## Evaluation protocol

The comparison uses all 1,319 GSM8K test questions, five solved examples per prompt, temperature 0, and at most 1,024 generated tokens per answer. “Invalid” means that a response contains no parseable final numeric answer.

| KV cache and maximum concurrent sequences | Flexible exact match | Invalid responses |
|---|---:|---:|
| FP8, 512 | 96.664% | 0.682% |
| NVFP4, 64 | 6.520% | 93.177% |
| NVFP4, 512 | 4.549% | 94.920% |

The failure at both limits rules out a high-concurrency-only artifact. Comparisons using the same prompts and scorer rule out chat-template and answer-parsing differences. The FP8 control uses the same FlashInfer backend, narrowing the failure to behavior specific to the NVFP4 KV path or its interaction with this model.

## Reproduction

The following launches one tensor-parallel vLLM server across four B200 GPUs:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 \
  --max-num-seqs 64 \
  --max-model-len 32768 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --block-size 128 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --linear-backend marlin \
  --moe-backend marlin \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_capture_sizes":[1,2,4,8,16,32,64],"inductor_compile_config":{"enable_auto_functionalized_v2":true}}'
```

`--max-num-seqs 64` means that this server may process at most 64 requests concurrently.

## Expected behavior

NVFP4 KV quantization may cause a small accuracy change relative to FP8, but it should continue producing coherent, parseable answers.

## Actual behavior

More than 93% of responses contain no parseable final answer. Typical failures are empty output or a short fragment such as `Assistant`.

## Investigation so far

PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55670 fixes a real low-level scale-conversion defect: the TensorRT-LLM NVFP4 KV kernel returns an FP8 scratch output when BF16 model output is required, and the fallback conversion must restore its output scale. A focused synthetic high-range regression passes with that patch.

However, a matched compiled full-model run with the patch remained at 4.776% exact match and 94.845% invalid responses. The output-scale defect is therefore not sufficient to explain this Qwen failure, and the root cause remains unresolved.

The next focused check reproduces the TP-local attention geometry used here—eight query heads, one KV head, head dimension 256, kernel page size 128—and covers long prefill plus first decode through the production NVFP4 cache-update/layout path.

Low-level scaling contract:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/7c5dc571cbd1064ecc8a9b1045637ff647aa22cb/tests/kernels/attention/test_flashinfer_trtllm_attention.py#L298-L338

Original NVFP4 KV support:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40177

Possibly related issue:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41651

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug] enable_blending with LMCacheConnectorV1 crashes at startup: VLLMModelTracker.register_model is never called
items.author: matu79go
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Enabling CacheBlend (`enable_blending: true`) with the vLLM V1 connector (`LMCacheConnectorV1`) crashes the engine at startup:

```
ValueError: vllm model for vllm-instance not found.
```

Root cause: `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create()` calls `VLLMModelTracker.get_model(ENGINE_NAME)`, but **nothing in the current tree ever calls `VLLMModelTracker.register_model()`** — grepping the repo shows the only references are in `lmcache/v1/compute/models/utils.py` (definition) and `lmcache/v1/compute/blend/utils.py` (the `get_model` call). The registration call appears to be a leftover from the old `lmcache_vllm` fork era.

## Environment

- LMCache: main @ `668a1fd`, built from source
- vLLM: 0.19.1 (official `vllm/vllm-openai:latest-cu130-ubuntu2404` image, aarch64 / GB10)
- Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, `--enforce-eager --no-enable-prefix-caching`

## Reproduction

```yaml
# lmcache config
chunk_size: 256
local_cpu: true
max_local_cpu_size: 32
enable_blending: true
use_layerwise: true
blend_special_str: " # #"
blend_check_layers: [1]
blend_recompute_ratios: [0.15]
```

```
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_both"}' ...
```

EngineCore dies during `_initialize_kv_caches` → `LMCacheConnectorV1Impl.__init__` → `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create` → `VLLMModelTracker.get_model` raises.

## Workaround that made blending work for us

A tiny vLLM general plugin that wraps `GPUModelRunner.load_model` and registers the model right after load:

```python
# entry point group "vllm.general_plugins"
def register():
    import importlib
    for mod in ("vllm.v1.worker.gpu_model_runner", "vllm.v1.worker.gpu.model_runner"):
        try:
            cls = importlib.import_module(mod).GPUModelRunner
        except Exception:
            continue
        orig = cls.load_model
        def load_model(self, *a, _orig=orig, **kw):
            out = _orig(self, *a, **kw)
            from lmcache.v1.compute.models.utils import VLLMModelTracker
            VLLMModelTracker.register_model("vllm-instance", self.model)
            return out
        cls.load_model = load_model
```

(Note vLLM 0.19 has two runner modules — the default flat `gpu_model_runner.py` and the V2 `gpu/model_runner.py` — so both need the hook.)

## Additional friction points hit on the same path (worth doc fixes at least)

1. `blend_check_layers` / `blend_recompute_ratios` default to `None`; with blending enabled, `process_qkv` crashes with `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`. Either give working defaults or validate at config load.
2. The default `blend_special_str: " # # "` (trailing space) never matches in-stream tokens for Llama-3 BPE: `encode(" # # ")[1:]` = `[' #', ' #', ' ']`, but in a real prompt the trailing space merges into the next word (`' all'` etc.), so `SegmentTokenDatabase._fast_split_by_subtensor` finds **zero separators** and every lookup misses. Using `" # #"` (no trailing space, `[674, 674]`) works. Also, the *first* document of a prompt tokenizes without a leading space, so its segment hash differs from the same document appearing mid-prompt — prepending a fixed dummy segment (`"docs:" + SEP`) restores position-invariant reuse.
3. Setting `blend_special_str` via env var strips the meaningful leading/trailing whitespace — it only works via `LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE` yaml.

Happy to turn the workaround into a PR if you can advise where the registration should live properly (connector init? runner wrapper?).

items.title: [RFC][MP] Lossless KV Compression with GPU Decompression
items.author: rob-9
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

In line with discussion in #4025, this RFC proposes a stored format and load path for losslessly compressed KV cache blocks in LMCache's multiprocess (MP) architecture. 

The target path keeps each block compressed while it is read from L2 storage and transferred toward the GPU, then uses the selected GPU backend (nvCOMP on NVIDIA or hipCOMP on AMD) to decompress it in GPU memory:

```text
Store: KV block → lossless compression → L2 storage
Load:  L2 storage → compressed GPU buffer → GPU decompression → GPU KV cache
```

The initial implementation targets NVIDIA and AMD GPUs in LMCache's vLLM MP path through concrete `NvcompBackend` and `HipcompBackend` implementations. Both implement the shared `GpuDecompressBackend` contract proposed in #4149, while vendor-specific capabilities and execution details remain inside each backend. Other GPU decompression engines are follow-up work through the same backend and abstractions.

On the store path, asynchronous CPU compression is the initial default because it avoids GPU compute contention with inference. GPU compression will be compared using the same codec and workloads and should replace the CPU default only if it improves end-to-end performance.

Combined with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS), AMD Infinity Storage (AIS), or a suitable RDMA path, compression could reduce the bytes read from L2 and transferred to the GPU. Whether that improves latency is an end-to-end benchmark question.

## Motivation

Large KV caches can take significant time to load from local NVMe or remote L2 storage. The model cannot resume inference until the required KV blocks reach its GPU cache, so this transfer can directly increase latency.

Technologies such as GDS, AIS and RDMA can make the transfer more efficient, including by moving data directly into GPU memory. They do not, however, reduce the number of bytes that must be transferred. Lossless compression addresses that separate problem by storing each KV block in a smaller representation.

Compression helps only if the block remains compressed for a useful part of the transfer. With CPU decompression, LMCache loads the compressed bytes into host memory, expands them there, and then copies the full-size block into GPU memory:

```text
Storage
    → compressed host buffer
    → CPU decompression
    → full-size copy to VRAM
    → usable GPU KV block
```

This reduces the storage read, but the final host-to-GPU copy still carries the full uncompressed block. GPU decompression could instead keep the block compressed while it travels to GPU memory and expand it there:

```text
Storage
    → compressed GPU buffer
    → GPU decompression
    → usable GPU KV block
```

This is not automatically faster. GPU decompression consumes compute and memory bandwidth, requires temporary buffers and workspace, and introduces synchronization and buffer-management costs. It is beneficial only when the saved transfer time exceeds those costs and any interference with model inference. End-to-end benchmarks, rather than decompression throughput alone, must determine whether the design improves latency.

### Existing LMCache Boundary

In LMCache's existing MP path, `StorageManager` may wrap an L2 storage adapter with `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`. The wrapper adds serialization around the adapter while preserving the same interface for callers:

```text
Store: KV object → serialize → L2 adapter → storage
Load:  storage → L2 adapter → deserialize → KV object
```

This boundary is useful because individual storage adapters do not need to understand the stored representation. The serde wrapper can add compression without duplicating compression logic in every adapter.

In the normal DRAM-backed MP path, serde loads byte-addressable L1 temporary buffers, while GPU onboarding later places data into the model's paged KV cache. Direct GPU decompression therefore either gives serde GPU execution state or keeps the record compressed until onboarding. 

cuFile and hipFile handle L1-to-GPU transfer during onboarding, not generic L2-to-device loads. The current L2 interface also lacks exact-size discovery and device-destination capabilities.

## Proposed Design

The feature is selected through an L2 adapter's serde configuration. `StorageManager` continues to construct the adapter and wrapper. The initial CPU-compression store path uses existing logical L2 operations; a future GPU-compression path must integrate before the existing GPU-to-host KV copy. GPU onboarding may require the deferred-load contract described below.

```text
StorageManager
    ↓ constructs
SerdeL2AdapterWrapper
    ├── stored-format serde processor
    └── underlying L2 adapter
            ↓
         storage
```

### Architecture Boundary

GPU decompression crosses two existing responsibilities: serde understands the stored representation, while GPU onboarding owns the device context and final KV cache placement. The component that invokes the selected `GpuDecompressBackend` must have access to both the compressed GPU input and the destination GPU KV buffer, as well as the device, stream, block mapping, and buffer lifetimes.

Two placements are possible:

1. **Inside `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`.** This keeps compression and decompression encapsulated in serde, but the wrapper would need GPU-resident buffers and worker-owned GPU state that it does not have today.
2. **During GPU onboarding.** Onboarding already knows the target device, stream, and paged KV cache layout. Serde would continue to define the format, codec metadata, and store-side compression; onboarding would transfer the compressed bytes, invoke the decoder, and place the output. However, LMCache has no common device-staging and placement interface across its transfer paths.

The current ownership boundaries therefore make onboarding the more natural placement, but this changes the meaning of load completion. An L2 load can finish while the object is still compressed, so the design must distinguish `record_lo

items.title: [Bug] fs_native L2: files left by a previous process are never counted toward max_capacity_gb or evicted (disk grows unbounded across restarts)
items.author: OscarSavNS
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter, chunk files persist across a server restart and are still served (lookup is a `stat` on the file), but the new process never registers them. They don't count toward `max_capacity_gb`, and the eviction policy never sees them, so **they are never evicted**. Each restart can strand up to a full cap of untracked files, and disk usage grows without bound until the filesystem fills.

## Observed

`lmcache/vllm-openai` image, LMCache `0.5.6rc1` (commit `9a7b6050`), MP server with:

```
--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/lmcache/l2","num_workers":32,"use_odirect":true,
  "max_capacity_gb":1000,"eviction":{"eviction_policy":"LRU","trigger_watermark":0.9,"eviction_ratio":0.1}}'
```

1. Wrote ~1.2 TB of KV. LRU eviction worked as documented: usage hit the 0.9 watermark three times and dropped to 871 GB each time (`L2 usage 0.90 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction`).
2. Restarted the server with the same `base_path`: 298,340 files, 911.7 GB on disk.
3. After the restart, `GET /status` reported `l2_eviction_controller.adapters[0].total_bytes_used = 0`.
4. Requests over the pre-restart prefixes were served from those files: 16.76M tokens, every full chunk, `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` +16,760,832. After that, tracked usage was 0.49 GB, i.e. only the new writes, while 911.7 GB of served files stayed untracked.

## Root cause (on `dev` at dc68527c)

- Byte accounting and eviction order are fed only by stores that the current process completes: `_notify_keys_stored` in `l2_adapters/base.py`, called from the native adapter's store completions. Neither `fs_native_l2_adapter.py` nor `native_connector_l2_adapter.py` scans `base_path` at startup.
- Reads of pre-existing files fire `on_l2_keys_accessed`, and `LRUEvictionPolicy.on_keys_touched` ignores keys it doesn't track (`if key in self._order`).
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` decrements usage on delete only for keys in `_key_sizes`, i.e. stored by this process.
- Re-storing an existing key is a no-op on disk (`csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp`: "Skip if already stored on disk").

RFC #4738 mentions this in passing ("Restart recovery: ... Existing files on disk are not automatically registered again"), but as part of a larger multi-disk design, and there is no standalone bug for it.

## Impact

With `max_capacity_gb` sized to the disk (the natural configuration), one restart with a full cache followed by a refill exceeds the disk. Any deployment that restarts routinely (rollouts, crashes) accumulates untracked files. Operators have to choose between wiping `base_path` on every start, which loses the persistence, and eventually running out of space.

## Proposed fix (prototyped, tested)

File names are already reversible: `fs_l2_adapter._filename_to_object_key` inverts the names the C++ connector writes. The prototype:

- adds `L2AdapterInterface.recover_persisted_objects() -> int` (default no-op), delegated by the serde and fault-inject wrappers;
- `StorageManager` calls it for each adapter **after** the L2 eviction states have registered their listeners, at init and in `add_l2_adapter`;
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` takes an optional `persisted_object_scanner`. `recover_persisted_objects` records each object in `_key_sizes` (so eviction deletes decrement usage) and announces it through `_notify_keys_stored`. It goes newest-first, so LRU's reverse insertion puts the oldest file at the eviction head. Keys already tracked are skipped;
- `fs_native` gains `recover_on_start` (default `true`) and a scanner that `os.scandir`s `base_path`. It decodes `.data` names, takes `st_size` and `st_mtime`, and skips `.tmp` files, undecodable names and directories.

Tests: 13 new (scanner, adapter recovery/ordering/delete/double-count, config, and `StorageManager` end-to-end: leftover files are accounted, over-cap leftovers are evicted oldest-first, `recover_on_start: false` keeps today's behaviour). The existing tests in `test_native_connector_l2_adapter`, `test_fs_native_l2_adapter_config`, `test_runtime_adapters`, `test_l2_adapter_base`, `test_fault_inject_l2_adapter`, `test_storage_manager_l2_keys` and `test_l2_adapter_factory` still pass (185 passed). Run on the 0.5.6rc1 commit; the patch also applies cleanly to current `dev`.

**Validated on a real cache:** 0.5.6rc1 plus the patch, restarted over the 911.7 GB directory above, with the cap lowered to 800 GiB:

```
fs_native: found 298492 persisted objects (849.44 GiB) in /lmcache/l2 in 3.0 s (0 entries skipped)
L2 adapter 0: registered 298492 objects recovered from persistent storage (usage 912076931072 bytes)
L2 usage 1.06 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
L2 usage 0.96 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
```

- **Settled usage:** 0.86. The disk went from 912.2 GB to 738.85 GB, with 738.78 GB tracked, within 0.01% of `du`.
- **Oldest first:** the evicted files were the oldest by mtime; the newest were kept.

Open questions for maintainers:

- **Default:** should `recover_on_start` default to `true`? It changes startup behaviour, since eviction can run immediately when leftovers exceed the watermark.
- **Scan cost:** the scan is synchronous at startup. ~300k files took 3.0 s to scan plus 0.5 s to register here; a very large directory might want a background scan.
- **Other adapters:** the same gap likely applies to other persistent adapters, e.g. `fs` and `nixl_store`; the hook is generic.

Happy to open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] LFUCachePolicy state desync causes KeyError crash under memory pressure
items.author: Chocolatine75
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

With `cache_policy: "LFU"`, the local-CPU backend can crash with a `KeyError`
under memory pressure. `LFUCachePolicy.get_evict_candidates()` removes the keys
it returns from its internal frequency bookkeeping (`key_to_freq` /
`freq_to_keys`), treating *selection* as *eviction*. But the caller does not
always evict every returned candidate, so the policy ends up tracking fewer
keys than are actually resident — and a later access to a still-resident but
untracked key raises `KeyError`.

LRU/FIFO/MRU are unaffected because their only state is the cache dict itself.

### Where it goes wrong

`LocalCPUBackend.batched_allocate()` requests up to 64 candidates, then:
- evicts the first fully-evictable one and `break`s, and
- `continue`s (skips) any candidate whose layer is pinned
  (`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_cpu_backend.py`, the `continue` at the
  per-layer check).

Every candidate `get_evict_candidates()` returned was already dropped from LFU
bookkeeping, but only the evicted one is actually removed from `hot_cache`. The
rest stay resident but untracked. The next `update_on_hit()` on one of them
does `self.key_to_freq[key]` → `KeyError`.

### Reproduction (policy level, no GPU needed)

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
from lmcache.v1.storage_backend.cache_policy import get_cache_policy

class Entry:
    def __init__(self, can_evict=True): self.can_evict = can_evict

p = get_cache_policy("LFU")
p.update_on_put("k")
cache = OrderedDict({"k": Entry(can_evict=True)})

assert p.get_evict_candidates(cache, num_candidates=1) == ["k"]
# caller selected "k" but did NOT evict it (e.g. a pinned layer) — "k" is still
# resident, so a later hit must be fine:
p.update_on_hit("k", cache)   # -> KeyError('k')
```

FIFO/MRU/LRU run the same snippet without error.

### Impact

- Only affects deployments configured with `cache_policy: "LFU"`.
- Crash (`KeyError`) in the allocation hot path once the CPU tier is under
  memory pressure and eviction kicks in; worse with layerwise models where
  `batched_allocate` requests many candidates and evicts one.

### Suggested fix

- Make `LFUCachePolicy.get_evict_candidates()` selection-only (no internal
  mutation), consistent with the other policies.
- Notify the policy on every actual removal in `LocalCPUBackend.remove()` (not
  just forced ones). `update_on_force_evict()` is a no-op for LRU/FIFO/MRU, and
  lets LFU drop a key when it is really evicted (including internal
  `force=False` evictions).

I have a PR ready with this fix plus regression tests for all four policies.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: bench: consolidate long-doc-permutator into kv-tier-pressure
items.author: hans-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`kv-tier-pressure` (added in #5489) is a strict generalisation of `long-doc-permutator`: at `pool_size == docs_per_request` the two produce an identical request stream. Once #5489 lands, `long-doc-permutator` is a special case of it, and keeping both means maintaining two code paths for one workload shape.

This issue tracks consolidating them. #5489 deliberately does **not** do this — it leaves `long-doc-permutator` untouched.

### Evidence they are equivalent

Both constructed at `num_contexts = docs_per_request = 16`, `context_length = 40`, `system_prompt_length = 10`, 20 requests, same seed:

| | `long-doc-permutator` | `kv-tier-pressure` |
|---|---|---|
| documents generated | 16 | 16 |
| requests | 20 | 20 |
| tokens per request (measured) | 665 | 665 |
| message roles | `[system, user]` | `[system, user]` |
| document separators in body | 15 | 15 |
| working set (tokens) | 640 | 640 |
| every request a permutation of all 16 | — | yes |

This is pinned by regression tests in `TestPermutatorEquivalence` (`tests/cli/commands/bench/engine_bench/workloads/test_kv_tier_pressure.py`), so the property will not silently drift.

### Two gaps that must close first

**1. Distinctness at small pools.** `long-doc-permutator` enumerates permutations into a `set`, guaranteeing distinct ones. `kv-tier-pressure` draws each request independently, so it can repeat:

| pool = K | K! | requests | distinct | duplicates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 120 | 100 | 67 | **33** |
| 16 | 2.09×10¹³ | 200 | 200 | 0 |
| 16 | 2.09×10¹³ | 750 | 750 | 0 |

Irrelevant at 16 documents; significant at the permutator's **default of 5**. A drop-in replacement needs either a distinctness guarantee or an opt-in flag.

**2. Warm-up differs.** `long-doc-permutator` sends one dummy request. `kv-tier-pressure` sweeps the whole pool so every document is cached exactly once — necessary for a steady-state tier measurement, but it changes what the engine has seen before the measured phase. Anyone comparing historical permutator numbers needs to know this.

### Options

- **(a)** Reimplement `long-doc-permutator` as a thin wrapper that calls `kv-tier-pressure` with `pool_size == num_contexts` and distinctness enabled. Keeps the CLI surface and historical flag names; one implementation.
- **(b)** Add a `--ktp-distinct-requests` flag to `kv-tier-pressure`, then deprecate `long-doc-permutator` with a release-note pointer.
- **(c)** Keep both and document the relationship. Lowest risk, no maintenance saving.

(a) looks cleanest since it preserves every existing invocation, but it is a behaviour change for anyone relying on the dummy warm-up, so it probably wants a deprecation cycle rather than a straight swap.

### Context

Found while adding `kv-tier-pressure`. Relevant background in #5489: `long-doc-permutator` cannot exercise the L2 tier under *any* configuration, because every permutation carries all documents, making `working_set / min_viable_L1 = 1 / num_inflight_requests` regardless of document count, length or permutation count.

items.title: bench: extract the duplicated dispatch loop shared by five engine_bench workloads
items.author: hans-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

Every concurrent workload in `lmcache bench engine` hand-rolls the same semaphore + task-tracking dispatch loop. There is no shared helper, so each new workload copies ~40 lines of scheduling boilerplate that has nothing to do with what it is actually measuring.

### The duplication

`lmcache/cli/commands/bench/engine_bench/workloads/`:

| workload | `_on_task_done` | `_pending_tasks` | `asyncio.Semaphore` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `long_doc_qa.py` | 2 | 5 | 1 |
| `multi_round_chat.py` | 2 | 5 | 0 |
| `random_prefill.py` | 2 | 5 | 0 |
| `long_doc_permutator.py` | 2 | 5 | 1 |
| `kv_tier_pressure.py` | 2 | 5 | 2 |
| `signals_fanout.py` | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| `prefix_suffix_tuner.py` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `rag_qa_quality.py` | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Five of eight carry a byte-identical `_pending_tasks` / `_on_task_done` pair, and `grep` finds no mixin, base-class helper or shared dispatch utility anywhere in the package.

Measuring it concretely: comparing `kv_tier_pressure.py` against `long_doc_permutator.py` after normalising identifiers, **161 of 570 non-comment lines (28%) are identical**. The longest duplicated runs are exactly the generic parts:

```
15 lines   the send/await/release body of _dispatch
10 lines   _pending_tasks.add / add_done_callback / _on_task_done
13 lines   config validation boilerplate
```

### Why it matters

- **Bug fixes do not propagate.** A fix to task cleanup or exception handling in one workload silently leaves the other four wrong.
- **New workloads inherit the copy.** `kv-tier-pressure` (#5489) is the most recent example — it followed house style precisely because there was no alternative.
- **It obscures the interesting code.** The part of a workload worth reviewing is prompt construction and sizing, and it is currently buried in scheduling plumbing.

### Suggested shape

`BaseWorkload` already owns the outer loop (`_run_async`, `_drain_finished_queue`). The natural place for this is alongside it — something like a concrete helper:

```python
async def dispatch_bounded(self, items, send, max_inflight) -> None:
    """Send `items` with at most `max_inflight` in flight, tracking tasks."""
```

so a workload's `step()` reduces to choosing *what* to send. `prefix_suffix_tuner` and `rag_qa_quality` do not use the pattern at all, so the helper should be opt-in rather than forced into the ABC.

### Scope

Touches five existing workloads plus `base.py`, so it wants its own PR with the existing workload tests as the regression net. Deliberately out of scope for #5489 — flagged there rather than bundled.

items.title: MP observability: `event_bus.queue_depth` / `event_bus.drain_lag_seconds` gauges always export 0
items.author: asaulys
items.body_excerpt:
The EventBus self-monitoring gauges `lmcache_mp.event_bus.queue_depth` and `lmcache_mp.event_bus.drain_lag_seconds` always export 0 in MP mode, even while the bus is queueing events.

**Cause**

- `EventBus.__init__` registers both gauges (`mp_observability/event_bus.py:122-141`), with callbacks bound to that instance.
- At import time the module builds a disabled bus, `_global_bus = EventBus(EventBusConfig(enabled=False))` (`event_bus.py:368`), so the first registration belongs to that disabled bus.
- `init_event_bus()` (`event_bus.py:386-394`) later builds the real bus. Its constructor registers the same instrument names again. The OTel SDK keeps the existing instrument and drops the new callback.
- So both gauges keep reading the disabled import-time bus, which is always 0.

`lmcache_mp.event_bus.dropped_events_total` is not affected: `EventBusSelfMetricsSubscriber` registers it with the live bus.

**Versions**

- Reproduced on v0.5.5 (`05a013b2`) and v0.5.6rc2 (`e73629e2`) with `--otlp-endpoint`. Against the real OTel SDK, an internal queue depth of 5 and a lag of 0.31 s were exported as 0 and 0.0.
- Still present on `dev` at `bffb77a7` (2026-10-05): neither `event_bus.py` nor `otel_init.py` has changed since v0.5.6rc2.

The existing tests in `tests/v1/mp_observability/test_event_bus.py` patch `register_gauge`, so they don't exercise the SDK's duplicate-instrument behaviour.

**Proposed fix**

- Register the two self-gauges once, at module level.
- Have their callbacks read `get_event_bus()` when they are called, instead of capturing `self`. Remove the registration from `EventBus.__init__`.

This stays correct however many times `init_event_bus()` runs. It also stops OTel from keeping a particular bus instance alive, and removes the duplicate registration (and its SDK warning) on every `EventBus` construction. The hot path is untouched; each collection costs one extra global lookup.

I'll follow up with a PR that includes a regression test against a real `MeterProvider` / `InMemoryMetricReader`.

items.title: CUDA: sm_70 (V100) builds with toolkit 12.9.x fail weight-buffer allocation on an empty 32GB GPU; identical source built with 12.8.x loads fine
items.author: SabaTech-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama.cpp at commit `1863ac033` (0.4.0-dev line). Two builds were made from the **identical source tree**, differing **only in the CUDA toolkit** used to compile them:

- Build A: CUDA toolkit **12.9.86** (`nvcc --version` = release 12.9, V12.9.86)
- Build B: CUDA toolkit **12.8.93** (`nvcc --version` = release 12.8, V12.8.93)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

- NVIDIA Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB (compute capability 7.0 / sm_70), PCIe SXM2
- Driver: 580.173.02
- The GPU was otherwise **empty** (< 1 GiB in use) when the failing allocation was attempted, with the model pinned to it via `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`

### Models

A ~27B Qwen-family GGUF quantized to Q4_K_P, 17.9 GB file (~16.4 GiB weights buffer). The exact same model file was used for both builds.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

**Symptom**: builds compiled with CUDA toolkit 12.9.x deterministically fail to allocate the model weights buffer on a sm_70 (Volta) GPU with `cudaMalloc failed: out of memory`, even though the GPU has ~31 GiB free and the buffer is only 16.4 GiB. The identical source compiled with toolkit 12.8.x allocates fine, loads, and serves normally.

The failure is 100% reproducible across repeated launches and happens at the first large weight-buffer allocation, with `--ctx-size 8192` (so it is not a KV-cache sizing issue) and `-ngl 999`.

**Steps**:

1. `cmake -B build-129 -DGGML_CUDA=ON` with toolkit 12.9.86, `cmake --build build-129 --config Release -j`
2. `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<id> ./build-129/bin/llama-server -m <model-path>.Q4_K_P.gguf -ngl 999 --ctx-size 8192 --port <port>` on an otherwise-empty V100-32GB
3. Observe the `cudaMalloc failed: out of memory` error below
4. Repeat with a build from the same commit using toolkit 12.8.93: the model loads and serves correctly

**Context that may help narrow it down**:

- An **older commit** of llama.cpp, built with toolkit 12.9.2 with the same flags, runs fine on the same hardware (in daily production use). So the failing combination appears to be a specific interaction between this tip's code and toolkit 12.9.x on sm_70, not a blanket "12.9 is broken on Volta".
- The toolkit A/B (one variable changed) isolates the toolkit as the cause at this commit.
- Volta has been dropped from the vLLM ecosystem recently, so llama.cpp remaining healthy on sm_70 with current toolkits matters to a shrinking but real user base.

### First Bad Commit

_Not identified_ — the variable isolated by the A/B is the CUDA toolkit version, not a code commit. Older commits built with 12.9.x work, and this commit built with 12.8.x works.

### Relevant log output

```text
W common_fit_params: failed to fit params to free device memory: n_gpu_layers already set by user to 999, abort
E ggml_backend_cuda_buffer_type_alloc_buffer: allocating 16400.57 MiB on device 0: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory
E alloc_tensor_range: failed to allocate CUDA0 buffer of size 17197242368
E llama_model_load: error loading model: unable to allocate CUDA0 buffer
```

items.title: [Bug]: Fake completed replica injection and key spoofing via NotifyOffloadSuccess in Mooncake Store Master
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

Mooncake Store Master's `NotifyOffloadSuccess` RPC (unauthenticated, default 0.0.0.0:50051) accepts caller-supplied offload results with no validation. An unauthenticated peer first forges `MountLocalDiskSegment` with its own UUID (satisfying the mounted-segment precondition) and then injects a COMPLETE disk-tier replica pointing at an attacker-chosen endpoint into any existing object, or fabricates metadata for keys that never existed — the master then reports those keys as existing with a completed replica at the attacker's endpoint. Runtime-confirmed on the master binary shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.2.

### Details

`MasterService::NotifyOffloadSuccess` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp) processes each caller-supplied (key, StorageObjectMetadata) pair: it clears any in-flight offloading task for the key, then calls `AddReplica(client_id, key, LOCAL_DISK replica{metadata.data_size, metadata.transport_endpoint, ReplicaStatus::COMPLETE})`. Nothing verifies that the caller owns the key, that an offload was ever scheduled, or that the endpoint belongs to the caller.

`AddReplica` widens the effect: when the object has no LOCAL_DISK replica yet (the normal case for a memory-resident object) the forged replica is appended; when the object does not exist at all, the call creates fresh metadata owned by the attacker — so the master's existence oracle and replica lists now answer for keys that were never written.

In 0.3.13 the handler requires `HasMountedLocalDiskSegment(client_id)` when offload is enabled; this is satisfied by first sending one forged `MountLocalDiskSegment(attacker_uuid, enable_offloading=true)`, which is itself unauthenticated. The `client_id` in these RPCs is a self-declared UUID with no binding to the connection.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-96763: that issue forges a segment at mount time to redirect transfers, while this one forges completed object replicas through the offload-completion path — a different method with a different missing check, operating on the object layer rather than the segment layer.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, the 0.3.13.post1 wheel's `mooncake_master` (offload enabled) and a victim client holding a memory-resident object `victim_inject_ky`. The attacker forges coro_rpc frames (20-byte header, magic=21; struct_pack bodies; observed function_ids: MountLocalDiskSegment=673169545, NotifyOffloadSuccess=771250242, GetReplicaList=528413044, ExistKey=2302172937). The 0.3.13 `NotifyOffloadSuccess` body is (UUID, vector<OffloadTaskItem{tenant,key,size}>, vector<StorageObjectMetadata{bucket_id,offset,key_size,data_size,transport_endpoint}>):

```python
call(MountLocalDiskSegment, uuid=ATTACKER_UUID, enable=True)          # ok

call(NotifyOffloadSuccess, uuid=ATTACKER_UUID,
     items=[OffloadTaskItem(tenant="default", key="victim_inject_ky", size=16)],
     metas=[StorageObjectMetadata(bucket_id=1, data_size=16,
                                  endpoint="192.168.105.123:39999")]) # ok
# GetReplicaList("victim_inject_ky") now shows a COMPLETE LOCAL_DISK
# replica owned by the attacker UUID with transport_endpoint
# "192.168.105.123:39999" alongside the victim's memory replica

# key spoof on a key that never existed:
call(GetReplicaList, key="spoofed_key_xyz0")   # OBJECT_NOT_FOUND (-704)
call(NotifyOffloadSuccess, ... key="spoofed_key_xyz0" ...)            # ok
call(ExistKey,     key="spoofed_key_xyz0")     # expected<bool> = true
call(GetReplicaList, key="spoofed_key_xyz0")   # attacker's UUID +
                                               # attacker endpoint, COMPLETE
```

All steps observed verbatim in the captured request/response hex on 0.3.13.post1; the before/after `GetReplicaList` pair for `spoofed_key_xyz0` (-704 → completed replica at the attacker endpoint) is the complete spoof demonstration. Expected secure behavior: offload completion must be bound to an authenticated client and to a task the master scheduled, with the endpoint taken from the registered segment rather than the request.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the master RPC port, without credentials, corrupts the persistence-tier metadata plane in two ways. Replica forgery: the master believes an attacker-controlled endpoint holds completed disk replicas of arbitrary victims' keys; any later promotion or disk-tier read that trusts this record can be served from the attacker's endpoint (attacker-supplied cache contents — an integrity attack on the read path; the end-to-end promotion fetch was not demonstrated in this report). Key spoofing: keys that never existed become "existing" with attacker-owned metadata, poisoning the existence oracle that clients and eviction rely on. The call also clears in-flight offloading tasks for arbitrary keys (the disruption variant was not claimed). Integrity of the metadata and read path; availability is not directly affected. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L (8.2), CWE-862. Affected: mooncake-store master <= 0.3.13.post1 (latest release), no patched version yet.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

items.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

items.title: [RFC] Orchestrator-facing Elastic EP lifecycle contract
items.author: julienmancuso
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Dynamo is designing Kubernetes-managed Elastic EP in [Dynamo DEP #13121](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13121). SGLang's merged scale-up path is already close to what an external reconciler needs: it accepts an absolute EP target, distinguishes effective and pending size, lets joining cohorts wait for admission, and exposes asynchronous status.

To turn that into a reliable Kubernetes lifecycle, the orchestrator must be able to recover after a controller restart or request timeout, identify the joining or retiring cohort for one operation, and know when capacity is safe to delete. The goal is not to standardize SGLang's internal topology; it is to make the boundary used by an external process orchestrator explicit and queryable.

## Proposed orchestrator-facing contract

### Resize identity and status

- Accept an absolute target and associate it with an operation ID or generation.
- Treat a repeated request for the active or in-progress target as the same operation.
- Report a stable runtime instance ID, operation ID, effective size, pending target, documented phase, and operation-scoped error.
- Make it possible to distinguish an engine restart from an operation that is still progressing.

A conceptual status shape is:

```json
{
  "instance_id": "server-7",
  "operation_id": "resize-42",
  "effective_ep_size": 4,
  "pending_ep_size": 6,
  "phase": "waiting_for_cohort",
  "last_error": null
}
```

### Control-authority loss

The process that exposes Elastic EP status or coordinates a resize may fail independently of the workers. The external contract should document what happens when the tokenizer manager, primary, or other control authority restarts or disappears:

- whether the committed members can continue serving;
- whether an in-flight operation remains observable, can be resumed by a new authority, or becomes terminally `Unknown` or `NeedsRecreate`;
- whether the last committed topology remains authoritatively queryable;
- how the runtime instance ID changes and stale retries against the previous instance are rejected; and
- when the external orchestrator must recreate the complete engine group.

Transparent continuation is not required. A correlated, fail-closed terminal result that identifies the last authoritative topology—or states that topology is unknown—is sufficient for the orchestrator to retain capacity, fence traffic, and choose recreation safely.

### Joining-cohort identity

For scale-up, expose enough information to associate externally launched joiners with one operation:

- cohort or operation ID;
- expected rank range and ready-rank count;
- a topology/configuration fingerprint;
- explicit mismatch and timeout errors.

This prevents a stale joiner from a failed operation from being admitted into a later resize that happens to reuse the same rank offset.

### Template-invariant initial formation and automatic append bootstrap

An orchestrator should be able to start every allocation of a new engine world from one immutable workload template. Initial formation should not be represented as a sequence of synthetic grow operations.

For the current TP1 automatic-bootstrap profile, let `W` be the number of accelerators visible to one allocation. SGLang should:

- require the initial and maximum EP sizes to be positive multiples of `W`;
- derive TP, DP, EP, node count, and node rank instead of accepting a second, conflicting geometry source;
- form the complete initial world from allocation indexes `[0, initial_ep_size / W)` in one distributed rendezvous;
- treat later indexes as append candidates whose rank offset is `allocation_index * W`; and
- report the observed allocation width so an orchestrator can compare it with its deployment profile and fail closed on a mismatch.

Once the world forms, its control authority should publish a runtime-scoped topology record containing at least the runtime instance ID, initial EP size, allocation width, current effective EP size, and maximum EP size ever committed. The last field is the monotonic `max_committed_ep_size`, not a generic high-watermark counter.

An automatic append is valid only when its offset equals both the current effective size and `max_committed_ep_size`. A slot below `max_committed_ep_size` was previously occupied and requires recovery, even if it is currently inactive. Automatic mode should fail immediately with an explicit recovery-required result rather than waiting for the normal scale timeout.

The topology record is a contract, not a required storage implementation. #39834 currently keeps it in the primary-owned coordination store so it disappears with that runtime and cannot outlive the control authority. Replacing allocation index 0 creates a new control authority and runtime instance; until authority failover exists, an external orchestrator must treat that event as complete engine-group recreation.

Automatic mode is append-only in #39834 and does not infer `recover`. Recovery remains explicit until SGLang has a stable member-identity handshake that can select and validate it safely.

### Health-aware retirement, failure recovery, and replacement bootstrap

An absolute physical EP target expresses how many ranks should remain, but not which ranks. Kubernetes, GPU, or fabric health may identify a specific degraded native member. Requests and status should therefore use stable, operation-scoped native-member identities and distinguish active, unavailable, retired, and safe-to-terminate members.

Planned selected-member retirement and unexpected member loss are separate capabilities:

- During planned retirement, selected members can participate in drain and topology commit. Capability reporting should state whether only a high-rank suffix or arbitrary selected or non-suffix members may be retired.
- After unexpected loss, the missing member cannot participate in the normal retirement barrier. Graceful degradation requires survivors to commit a valid topology and report the

items.title: [Bug] Interrupted Mooncake trace download is reused as a complete cache
items.author: unravel1020
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When SGLang downloads a Mooncake JSONL trace and the streamed HTTP response raises an exception after one or more chunks have been written, the partially written destination file is left in place. On the next `MooncakeDataset.load()`, the file-existence check treats that path as an available dataset and skips the download. The benchmark then reads only the records present in the partial file (or fails while parsing a truncated final line) instead of retrying the download.

This report concerns a path written by a failed download. It does not ask SGLang to remove arbitrary pre-existing user-provided dataset files.

### Reproduction

The following CPU-only reproduction uses a temporary destination that does not exist before the first load. The mocked response yields one complete JSONL record and then raises a connection error while the body is being streamed:

```python
import os
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch

import requests
from sglang.benchmark.datasets.mooncake import MooncakeDataset


class InterruptedResponse:
    headers = {"content-length": "200"}

    def raise_for_status(self):
        pass

    def iter_content(self, chunk_size):
        yield b'{"timestamp": 1, "hash_ids": []}\n'
        raise requests.exceptions.ConnectionError("simulated interrupted transfer")


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    path = os.path.join(temp_dir, "trace.jsonl")
    dataset = MooncakeDataset(path, "conversation", 10)

    with patch(
        "sglang.benchmark.utils.requests.get",
        return_value=InterruptedResponse(),
    ):
        try:
            dataset.load()
        except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
            pass
        else:
            raise AssertionError("the first load should raise ConnectionError")

    print("final path exists:", os.path.exists(path))
    print("rows returned by the next load:", len(dataset.load()))
```

Observed on the commit below:

```text
first load: raises ConnectionError
final path exists: True
rows returned by the next load: 1
```

The second load does not issue another HTTP request because the destination path exists.

### Expected behavior

After a streamed download fails, SGLang should not leave a final path that a later load treats as a complete downloaded dataset. A subsequent load should retry the failed download or report that the downloaded dataset is unavailable; it should not silently benchmark from the partial trace.

### Environment

- SGLang source: `main` at `41812afe432a54308be1c361a4d587952356f958`
- OS: Ubuntu on WSL2, Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64
- Python: 3.12.14
- PyTorch: 2.13.0+cpu; `torch.cuda.is_available() == False`
- No model, server, or GPU is needed for this reproduction.
- `PYTHONPATH=python python -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on this CPU-only environment with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined`; this is unrelated to the reproduction above.

items.title: [Feature]: Support fast weight updates from disk
items.author: SumanthRH
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

vLLM currently uses layerwise reloading while updating weights during RL training without recompilation:  
https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#what-is-layerwise-reloading

This currently assumes that weights for a given layer are loaded in order because the layerwise reloading logic allocates buffers per layer:

https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/training/layerwise/#troubleshooting-excessive-memory-usage

There can be excessive memory usage when weights are received out of order. 

In some use-cases like disaggregated RL, it is desirable to update weights from disk. In this case, it would be good to leverage GPU Direct Storage to directly load weights into GPU memory. 

Users would like to do something like:

```
# in gpu_worker.py
from vllm.model_executor.model_loader.weight_utils import fastsafetensors_weights_iterator

self.model.load_weights(fastsafetensors_weights_iterator(files, use_tqdm_on_load=False))
```

However, the current `fastsafetensors` iterator will lead to large temporary memory allocation due to out of order loading. 

For Qwen 3.5 35B, I saw temporary memory grow to > 40 GB due to the out of order loading issue, with warnings like:

items.title: [Feature]: Request observer hook for the Rust frontend
items.author: questcollector
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

We run vLLM behind an API gateway and collect per-tenant usage records (prompt / cached / generated tokens) in an L7 proxy in front of it today. With the Rust frontend we would rather do this in process, as an out-of-tree module (a small crate that plugs into the frontend and writes usage records to our own store): the frontend knows the exact token counts without parsing responses, including for streams the client aborts before the final usage chunk is sent, which a proxy never sees. We don't want to patch vLLM for this, so upstream would only need a narrow, generic hook.

In the Python frontend this is possible out of tree: a stat logger plugin (`vllm.stat_logger_plugins`) receives per-request `FinishedRequestStats`, and `--middleware` can map the tenant by request id. The Rust frontend has no equivalent hook. (One gap on the Python side: requests aborted by the frontend, e.g. on client disconnect, are removed in `OutputProcessor.abort_requests` without finished stats, so they never reach stat loggers although they consumed tokens. The Rust frontend already records these aborts in Prometheus from `Drop`, so the hook below covers them.)

Today the terminal request data is computed in `RequestMetricsTracker::record_finished` and written straight to Prometheus, so nothing else can consume it. Prometheus is aggregated (no per-request or per-tenant data), and traces are sampled; the tracing plan in RFC #44757 also leaves client-initiated aborts out of the `llm_request` span, which is reasonable for tracing but means aborted streams, which still consume tokens, can't be metered from spans.

Proposal: two small, independent pieces.

**1. `vllm-llm`: a request-completion seam.** Both terminal points of `GenerateOutputStream` (`poll_next` on engine finish, `Drop` on frontend abort or stop-string match) produce one `FinishedRequest` (external / engine request id, model, LoRA, engine index, finish reason, token counts, lifecycle timestamps). The built-in Prometheus recording derives its latency breakdown from the same `FinishedRequestStats`, so metrics and other consumers cannot drift, which is the property RFC #44757 wants between metrics and the `llm_request` span. Registered observers are called synchronously, in registration order, at most once per request; panics are isolated. With no observer registered there is no extra allocation.

```rust
pub trait RequestObserver: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// Called on the request path (possibly inside `Drop`); must not block.
    fn on_finished(&self, request: &Arc<FinishedRequest>);
    /// Called once after the engine client has shut down, e.g. to drain a queue.
    fn shutdown(&self) -> BoxFuture<'_, ()> { /* no-op */ }
}

impl Llm {
    pub fn with_request_observers(self, observers: RequestObservers) -> Self;
}
```

**2. `vllm-server`: register observers the same way as the router extension (#43774).** `ServeExtensions` (router extension + request observers) and `serve_with_extensions`; `serve` and `serve_with_router_extension` keep their behavior and delegate to it. Like
#43774, this is a composition hook for custom binaries, not a stable plugin API.

**Non-goals:** no engine protocol change, no new Prometheus metrics, no queueing or async adapter upstream (I/O-bound observers hand requests to their own task; the OTel SDK already batches spans), and no per-request attribute plumbing through the request types.

### Alternatives

- OTLP spans or logs as the metering source: spans are sampled and client aborts are left out (as planned in #44757), so they are not billing-grade. With this hook, a span emitter is just another observer.
- Scraping Prometheus: aggregated, no per-request or per-tenant data.
- Patching the frontend downstream: works, but every deployment re-patches `request_metrics.rs` / `output.rs`.

### Additional context

- Prototype: an out-of-tree crate on top of the two changes writes per-tenant usage records to a Redis Stream (the tenant is attached by a router-extension middleware keyed by request id, so no upstream change is needed for that). Verified with `vllm-mock-engine`: normal finish, client abort, Redis outage, and flush on SIGTERM.
- Both changes are small and additive: one new module plus wiring at the two terminal points in `vllm-llm`, and one new module plus entry-point wiring in `vllm-server`. Existing APIs keep their behavior; I have a working branch and would split it into two PRs.
- Related: RFC #44757 (this could serve as the base for the Phase 2 `llm_request` span; happy to coordinate with @tahsintunan), #47810, #43641 / #43774.
- #54144 and #57582 touch the same files; I would rebase onto them rather than race them.
- Disclosure: the prototype was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). If this direction sounds reasonable, I'll open the PRs myself, having reviewed every change, and follow up on review feedback.

cc @BugenZhao

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: NIXL DCP config checks don't apply to NixlPullConnector
items.author: lucamotz
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM main `6ad2e06c4a`. Config validation only; reproduces on CPU.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`NixlConnector` is the backward-compatible alias of `NixlPullConnector`, but the NIXL checks in `vllm/config/vllm.py` match only the name `"NixlConnector"`. With `kv_connector="NixlPullConnector"` and `decode_context_parallel_size > 1`:

- the NIXL DCP check in `VllmConfig.__post_init__` doesn't run, so non-MLA models and DCP sizes other than the NIXL transfer parallel size are accepted;
- `adjust_dcp_kv_cache_interleave_size` leaves an unset `--cp-kv-cache-interleave-size` at 1 instead of setting it to the block size, which NIXL P/D requires (`kv_transfer_state.py`). The NIXL worker doesn't check it.

```python
from vllm.engine.arg_utils import EngineArgs

for name in ("NixlConnector", "NixlPullConnector"):
    args = EngineArgs(
        model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct",  # GQA, not MLA
        tensor_parallel_size=4,
        decode_context_parallel_size=2,
        distributed_executor_backend="mp",
        kv_transfer_config={"kv_connector": name, "kv_role": "kv_both"},
    )
    try:
        args.create_engine_config()
        print(f"{name}: accepted")
    except Exception:
        print(f"{name}: rejected")
```

```
NixlConnector: rejected
NixlPullConnector: accepted
```

`NixlConnector` fails the assert "decode_context_parallel_size=2 must be 1 or equal to the NIXL transfer parallel size=4".

`validate_block_size` and the HiSparse connector warning also match only `"NixlConnector"`. The `validate_block_size` skip assumes the interleave size is pinned to the block size, which since #55531 holds only when `--cp-kv-cache-interleave-size` is unset, so adding `NixlPullConnector` there would also stop checking an explicit interleave size for it.

`KVTransferConfig.has_connector` compares names literally, so a fix can go there or at each site. #60168 has a minimal per-site patch with test rows for the two bulleted sites.

Would it make sense to move these shared types into a neutral module, for example:

```text
mem_cache/pool_transfer.py
```

This should only be a code organization change, with no behavior change.

Startup succeeds: KV cache 81272 tokens, draft decode/extend + target verify CUDA graphs captured. A short request completes (200 OK). #33549 (100% util / low power decode hang)

items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Potential hybrid GDN Radix-cache selected-logprob drift on repeated branch scoring
items.author: furedericca-lab
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues and did not find an existing report that fully covers this request shape.
- [ ] I have not re-run this on today's latest main; the reproduction was observed on pinned main commit `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a` (2026-09-25).
- [x] Environment details and a standalone `/generate` reproducer are included below.
- [x] This is a possible correctness issue rather than a general usage question.
- [x] Report is in English.

## Describe the bug

With a hybrid GDN Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, repeated selected-token logprob scoring is stable when Radix Cache is disabled, but the first Radix-enabled branch scoring pass differs substantially from subsequent identical passes.

The observation is:

| Cache configuration | Max repeated selected-logprob delta | Pattern |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Unified Radix Cache enabled | `2.551527976989746` | run 1 differs; runs 2 and 3 match exactly |
| Radix Cache disabled | `0.0` | runs 1, 2 and 3 match exactly |

The prefix is explicitly warmed before the repeated branch batches. With Radix enabled, the server log reports `#cached-token: 0` for the first branch batch and `#cached-token: 128` for later identical branch batches. With Radix disabled, the three repeated branch batches are bit-stable.

This strongly correlates the drift with the cache-hit execution path, but I do **not** want to over-attribute the root cause: the current evidence does not prove that a specific GDN recurrent-state checkpoint, restore, split, or other hybrid-cache internal operation is responsible.

This was found while gating a decision workload that consumes candidate-token logprobs directly, so cache-hit equivalence matters even when the top-1 decision itself does not change.

Related work:

- #22935 — Mamba Radix cache prefix/split behavior
- #34899 — bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
- #38625 — interior/no-buffer checkpoint work

I am not assuming that #22935 or #38625 has the same root cause or fully covers this request shape. In particular, I would like to know whether a shared prefix followed by divergent option branches is expected to preserve selected-token logprobs under deterministic inference when the later identical branch requests hit the hybrid cache.

## Environment

Tested environment:

- SGLang source: `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a`
- SGLang package: `0.5.21.dev612+g2f5c9ac43`
- Model: `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4`
- Model revision: `332d277a083ca395aa2f822842b82f5f2f3913a2`
- Architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN / full attention
- Quantization: ModelOpt mixed FP8/NVFP4
- GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- NVIDIA driver: `610.57.04`
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`
- Python: `3.13.11`
- PyTorch: `2.14.0a0.post20260925` (CUDA 13.4)
- Triton: `3.7.0`
- `sglang-kernel==0.4.7`
- `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19`
- Attention backend: Triton
- Deterministic inference: enabled
- Prefill CUDA Graph: disabled
- Decode CUDA Graph: retained
- Unified Radix Cache: enabled for the failing case
- Observed Mamba strategy: `extra_buffer`
- Comparison case: identical server settings plus only `--disable-radix-cache`

A literal `python3 -m sglang.check_env` dump was not retained for this run; the exact pinned runtime versions above are from the same project environment used for the reproduction.

## Reproduction

Launch the candidate server with Radix Cache enabled:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30001 \
  --trust-remote-code --tp-size 2 \
  --attention-backend triton \
```

Then run this standalone script. It does **not** import Reflex. It warms the exact shared prefix using native `/generate`, then submits the same two divergent branch items three times and compares the selected A/B/C token logprobs.
