items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.

items.title: [Bug][KV Cache] nvfp4 KV silently reuses the checkpoint's fp8-calibrated k/v_scale as NVFP4 global scale → deterministic long-context corruption (single-variable proof, sm_120)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

Serving an NVFP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) on a checkpoint whose `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme` says `num_bits: 8` (e.g. unsloth's NVFP4 quants, which ship fp8-calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale`) silently corrupts the KV cache: 32 tiny `[1]` bf16 scalars are loaded verbatim and consumed as the NVFP4 **global scale**. Removing exactly those 64 **bytes** flips long-context needle from 1/4 to 4/4 on an otherwise bit-identical 22.5 GB checkpoint. No log line ever mentions scales. Related but distinct: [#36121](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36121) (fp4 scales not traveling through HiCache host transfers; footnote has our hybrid-path measurement), [#39942](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39942) (fp8 KV scales silently *dropped* — opposite failure, same blind spot: nothing validates KV scale provenance).

## Setup

SGLang 0.5.21 (official PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (sm_120, TP2), driver 595.91.07. Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid 16 full-attention + 48 GDN layers, head_dim 256, compressed-tensors). Flags: `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --context-length 195000 --page-size 64`, greedy, chat format. (Same rig as my [#36010 evidence post](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36010#issuecomment-5788493111); this bug is **independent of spec decode** — it hits the plain no-spec nvfp4 path.)

## Symptom

With scales as shipped, long-context retrieval collapses: needle **1/4 (d50) / 0/4 (d500)**; answers degenerate into question-echoing after a short thinking block. Everything else looks healthy — boot logs clean, short prompts / tool calls / vision normal. Deterministic: completion tokens reproduce byte-for-byte across boots and repeats.

## Root cause (source walk; mechanism marked as inference)

1. The checkpoint carries 32 per-layer `*.self_attn.{k,v}_scale` tensors — `[1]` bf16 scalars calibrated for **fp8** KV (`config.json → kv_cache_scheme: {num_bits: 8, static_minmax, symmetric}`).
2. *(inference, from source)* At load, `weight_utils.maybe_remap_kv_scale_name()` attaches them to the attention modules unconditionally; the fp4 path (`layers/attention/kvfp4_tensor.py`, comment: *"The KV cache path passes preloaded per-layer scales already on device"*) consumes them as the NVFP4 `global_scale` in `x_fp4 * block_scale * global_scale`.
3. *(inference)* Nothing validates the checkpoint's KV scheme against the runtime `--kv-cache-dtype`. An fp8-geometry scalar (amax/448 family) applied under NVFP4 geometry (amax/6 family) is off by ~75× → every stored K/V is systematically mis-scaled.

## Single-variable proof (same box, same day, same prompts)

| config (one variable per row) | needle d50 | needle d500 |
|---|---|---|
| unsloth + nvfp4, scales as shipped | 1/4 | 0/4 |
| **unsloth + nvfp4, 32 scale tensors stripped (64 bytes total), `kv_cache_scheme=null`** | **4/4** | **4/4** |
| unsloth + fp8_e4m3 (scale geometry matches dtype) | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| `sakamakismile/Qwen3.8-27B-MTP-NVFP4` + nvfp4 (checkpoint ships no scales) | 4/4 | 1/4 |

The stripped copy is a hardlink farm with only `model.safetensors` rewritten (header offsets recomputed; post-check: 0 leftover scale tensors) — the rest of the ~22.5 GB is byte-identical. Same-checkpoint before/after is the control: 64 bytes of metadata move the score by three needle questions.

## Why this is not an edge case

The filename pairing (`…-NVFP4` weights + `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) is the natural reading, and unsloth's NVFP4 releases ship fp8-calibrated KV scales as a matter of their recipe. Everyone doing that pairing gets silently wrong KV with zero log evidence; needle-style evals are the only thing that notices, and most people don't run those. Checkpoints without shipped scales (dynamic path, row 4) are unaffected — which is presumably why this hasn't surfaced loudly.

## Asks

1. **Validate at load**: if the checkpoint carries `k_scale`/`v_scale` and `kv_cache_scheme.num_bits` disagrees with `server_args.kv_cache_dtype`, warn loudly and skip them (fall back to dynamic scales) instead of reinterpreting an fp8 scalar as an fp4 global scale.
2. Checkpoints whose scheme says `num_bits: 4` (e.g. NVIDIA/ModelOpt NVFP4-KV exports) *should* consume their scales — the bug is specifically the mismatched pair, not scale loading per se.
3. Optional `--load-kv-scales {auto,never}` for quick A/B without safetensors surgery (our workaround rewrites a 22 GB file's header — works in 3 minutes, but terrifying to recommend).

## Verified workaround & production numbers

Drop the 32 `*.self_attn.[kv]_scale` tensors from `model.safetensors`, rewrite header offsets, set `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme = null`. The healthy config now serves our production: 185K-token cold prefill ~176 s, decode ~25 tok/s; with HiCache L2 (20 GB host, `write_through`, `page_first`, slru) a post-eviction 185K re-ask lands in **2.4–5.5 s** (vs 178 s cold) with the secret code word intact across the L2 round-trip (2/2 rounds, backup counters confirm real transfers); needle 4/4+4/4; tool-calls live. sm_120 hybrid-attention reference points are thin here — happy to post logs/transcripts.

Footnote re #36121: its fail-fast covers paths our hybrid assembly doesn't traverse (UnifiedRadixCache picks host pools in `hybrid_pool_assembler`), and in our exact combo (nvfp4 + HiCache + page_first + write_through) the fp4 block scales evidently *do* survive L2 as measured above — so the guard as drafted wouldn't cover this configuration either way. Full hybrid-path measurements posted as a review note on that PR.

items.title: [Bug] Scheduler aborts with `double free or corruption` inside the idle-loop invariant check (`session_held_tokens` walk); server hangs permanently afterwards
items.author: LUOSENGWA
items.body_excerpt:
# [Bug] Scheduler aborts with `double free or corruption` inside the idle-loop invariant check (`session_held_tokens` walk); server hangs permanently afterwards

### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version. (occurred on `nightly-dev-20261003-65f75914`)
- [x] I included environment info and logs. (full crash dump + `server_args` below; a py-spy capture will be added if it recurs)
- [x] This is a bug report.

### Describe the bug

On a single-GPU production deployment (Qwen3.5-27B-FP8, hybrid Mamba/GDN, MTP/EAGLE, context 262144, fp8 KV), after ~22h of normal serving the **scheduler process aborted with a heap-corruption fatal** while running the idle-loop invariant check:

```
[2026-10-04 10:32:27] Decode batch, #running-req: 1, #full token: 102547, ... #queue-req: 0   <- last normal line
double free or corruption (out)
Fatal Python error: Aborted

Current thread (most recent call first):
  File ".../sglang/srt/session/streaming_session.py", line 424 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py", line 3543 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/pool_stats_observer.py", line 184 in session_held_tokens
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/invariant_checker.py", line 113 in _check_full_pool
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler_components/invariant_checker.py", line 507 in _check_all_pools
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 4969 in on_idle
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 2003 in event_loop_overlap
  ... run_scheduler_process ...
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

The abort happened between two normal decode batches, with no preceding error/warning (no OOM, no CUDA error, no assertion). Immediately afterwards the whole pipeline goes permanently silent:

- `/health` reports: `Health check failed. Server couldn't get a response from detokenizer for last 20 seconds. ... last_heartbeat time: 10:32:27` — i.e. the tokenizer manager never receives another downstream message from the exact crash moment on.
- `/v1/models` and `/metrics` keep answering 200 — with **frozen counters** (`num_running_reqs` 0, `num_requests_total` no longer increments).
- Every generation request (`/generate`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`) accepts the connection, receives the request body, and then **never returns a single byte**.
- ~2 hours later the container still lists `sglang::scheduler` / `sglang::detokenizer` processes (the scheduler's cumulative CPU time stops growing, i.e. it is wedged in/after the abort path; nothing detects the dead engine and restarts it).
- Manual `docker restart` recovers in 1-2 min; normal serving resumes.

The crash stack is inside the idle housekeeping walk: `on_idle()` → `invariant_checker._check_all_pools()` → `_check_full_pool()` → `pool_stats_observer.session_held_tokens()` → `unified_radix_cache.session_held_tokens()` → `streaming_session.session_held_tokens()` (`session/streaming_session.py:424`, iterating session slots). `double free or corruption (out)` = glibc detected heap corruption, most plausibly from a free/ownership bug in the session/mamba/KV release paths that the idle walk happens to detect (the walk itself performs only reads plus allocations).

### Environment

- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20261003-65f75914` (digest `sha256:035f29e91cfdf3b7d031c28be43ef7bddc93bb1f025e35c02c62ac732b8ba59b`)
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 72GB (SM120), driver/CUDA per image; model: Qwen3.5-27B FP8 (`config model_type=qwen3_5`), hybrid GDN-Mamba + builtin MTP draft (EAGLE).
- Key `server_args`: `context_length=262144`, `kv_cache_dtype=fp8_e4m3`, `mem_fraction_static=0.9`, `chunked_prefill_size=2048`, `max_running_requests=32` (capped to 10 by `max_mamba_cache_size=32`), `speculative_algorithm=EAGLE` (steps=3, topk=1, draft=4), `max_mamba_cache_size=32`, `mamba_ssm_dtype=bfloat16`, `mamba_radix_cache_strategy=extra_buffer_lazy`, `radix_eviction_policy=lru`, `enable_streaming_session=False`, `disable_overlap_schedule=False`, `attention_backend=flashinfer`, `mamba_backend=flashinfer`, `cuda_graph_config`: decode full ≤bs256 + prefill breakable, `page_size=1`, `tp=dp=ep=1`.
- Env vars: `SGLANG_OPT_MAMBA_SKIP_DECODE_LOCK=1`, `SGLANG_IMAGE_MAX_PIXELS=2007040`.
- Serving profile: 24 small agents, mixed short chats + longer (~100-140K token) sessions, sparse multimodal; uptime before crash ~22h24m.
- `SGLANG_ENABLE_STRICT_MEM_CHECK_DURING_IDLE` left at its default (True) — we WANT the idle checks; the problem is what they caught.

### Related issues (checked, not duplicates)

- #26482 / #22511 / #10856 / #11925 — the *post-crash symptom* (`couldn't get a response from detokenizer` + all requests hang). #26482 was auto-closed (stale) without a crash dump; #22511 is the open tracking thread (still reported reproducible under load as of 2026-09). **None of them contain the actual crash stack, which is what this report adds.**
- #36205 — gated the *tree-cache* sanity check (perf/livelock); our crash is in the *pool* check path (`_check_all_pools`), which still runs.
- #40250 / #40252 (merged ~2026-09-25) — session/mamba free-path fixes ("mamba -1 sentinel free", session reap); our build is AFTER them, so if this is the same family the fix looks incomplete.
- #41617 (open) — radix-cache free/ownership bug (`release_kv_cache` frees slots the radix still owns) — same "free ownership" family, different trigger (`--strip-thinking-cache`, which we do not use).
- #34676 (open) — hybrid-Mamba prefill allocation failure that *kills* the scheduler; ours is a *heap-corruption abort during idle check*, not an allocation failure, so it looks distinct.

### Questions

1. Does the crash stack (idle `_check_full_pool` → `session_held_tokens` walk hitting `double free`) suggest a known free/ownership bug in the session slot / unified radix cache paths?
2. Should a scheduler abort be detected and the engine

items.title: [Performance]: On RDNA, hybrid-Mamba models fall back to Triton paged attention and decode collapses at long context
items.author: cadamcat
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

_No response_

### Report of performance regression

## Summary

*Update 2026-08-28. The cause is identified and the fix exists upstream as #45916's split-KV decode kernel, which now admits gfx11 as it stands: the `on_gfx12x()` gate this report asked to widen was widened inside the PR itself on 2026-08-10, so nothing local is needed any more. Verified on gfx1100 here on both 0.23.1 and 0.27, and independently on gfx1151 and gfx1201; details under "Verified: PR #45916 fixes this on gfx1100" and "Re-measured on 0.27 as a controlled A/B" below. Everything else in this report is stock vLLM, which is still what ships.*

On gfx1100, `Qwen3.6-27B` decode time per token grows from 82.5 ms at 518 tokens of context to 235.3 ms at 32K, which is 12.1 → 4.2 tok/s. A kernel-level profile puts effectively all of that growth in one place: `kernel_paged_attention_2d`, the Triton fallback used by the model's 16 full-attention layers.

The 48 gated-delta-net layers are not involved. Their decode kernels cost the same at 1K and at 32K context, which is what the architecture promises and what the implementation delivers.

The reason those 16 layers take the Triton path is `use_rocm_custom_paged_attention` in `vllm/platforms/rocm.py`. Its RDNA branch requires `head_size == 128` and `block_size == 16`. This model has `head_dim=256` and a measured KV block size of 784, so the custom kernel is never eligible.

## The profile: it is not the linear-attention layers

Torch profiler, CUDA graphs left on, kernel calls attributed to the engine step whose window they fall in so that chunked-prefill calls are not mixed into the decode figures. Per-call GPU time, rank 0:

| kernel | layers it serves | ctx=1024 | ctx=32768 | ratio |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode` | 48 linear | 8.466 µs | 8.038 µs | 0.95× |
| `_causal_conv1d_update_kernel` | 48 linear | 2.260 µs | 2.139 µs | 0.95× |
| `triton_w4a16_gemm_kernel` | all | 275.792 µs | 251.447 µs | 0.91× |
| **`kernel_paged_attention_2d`** | **16 full** | **356.664 µs** | **10 095.188 µs** | **28.3×** |

Call counts are identical across the two contexts (528 for the linear-attention kernels, 176 for paged attention), so these are per-call costs, not more work being issued.

At 16 calls per step, paged attention goes from 5.71 ms/step to 161.5 ms/step, an increase of 155.8 ms. Measured end to end, the decode step itself goes from 85.85 ms to 236.9 ms, an increase of 151 ms. **The paged-attention growth accounts for the entire decode slowdown**; every other kernel is flat or slightly faster at the longer context.

## Why the custom kernel is skipped

`vllm/platforms/rocm.py`, `use_rocm_custom_paged_attention`, RDNA branch:

```python
return (
    _ON_GFX1X
    and (sliding_window == 0 or sliding_window == (-1, -1))
    and (qtype == torch.half or qtype == torch.bfloat16)
    and head_size == 128
    and block_size == 16
    and (gqa_ratio >= 3 and gqa_ratio <= 16)
    ...
)
```

For `Qwen3.6-27B`: `head_size` is 256, so the fourth condition fails. `cache_config.block_size` measures **784** on this model — 16 × 49, the shape hybrid Mamba/GDN models produce — so the fifth fails too. `gqa_ratio` is 6 and does pass.

**No single condition is the blocker.** Calling `use_rocm_custom_paged_attention` directly with counterfactuals: `head_size` forced to 128 still returns `False`, `block_size` forced to 16 still returns `False`. There is also a third, independent disqualifier — `is_pow2(784)` is `False`, and `chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py` sets `use_custom = False` on that check by itself. The custom HIP kernel is unreachable here three times over.

The fallback warning at `chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:420` fires.

**The `head_size` condition is not conservative gating, it is the kernel's actual limit.** `CALL_CUSTOM_LAUNCHER_BLK_HEAD` in `csrc/rocm/attention.cu` dispatches only `case 64` and `case 128` and `TORCH_CHECK`s on anything else, so relaxing the check would just move the failure. Worth stating because it is the first fix anyone would reach for. `block_size` dispatch covers 16 and 32, so that condition has the same character.

This also means the fallback is not specific to hybrid models. `head_dim=256` alone is enough, and `gemma-4-31B` on this machine has it too. That model takes the Triton path as well and shows an elevated slope, 0.339 against 0.118 for the `head_dim=128` Qwen3-8B, though with 16 KV heads it has far more parallelism to work with and never collapses.

## Why the Triton fallback is slow on this model in particular

Dense models on the same machine also take the Triton path, and they do not degrade like this. The difference is how much parallelism the kernel has to work with at decode, where the batch is 1:

| model | KV heads | query heads | GQA | decode µs per context token |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3-8B, BF16 dense | 8 | 32 | 4:1 | 0.118 |
| gemma-4-31B, w4a16 dense | 16 | 32 | 2:1 | 0.339 |
| **Qwen3.6-27B, hybrid** | **4** | 24 | 6:1 | **4.840** |

With 4 KV heads and a batch of 1, there is very little for the kernel to spread across the 84 CUs on this card.

Two independent measurements agree with that reading. First, per-card power *falls* as context grows, from 265 W + 265 W at 518 tokens to 232 W + 227 W at 24K, while every dense model in the same sweep holds 265 W flat. That is an idle GPU, not a busy one. Second, normalising by how much KV each model actually reads makes the gap wider rather than narrower: this model has the *smallest* KV footprint of the three at 64 KiB per token, against 144 KiB for Qwen3-8B and 160 KiB for gemma-4-31B, because only 16 of its 64 layers carry a KV cache at all. Per KiB of KV read, it is 92× the cost of Qwen3-8B and 36× that of gemma-4-31B.

## The same model does not degrade under llama.cpp

Same machine, same day, same model, only the inference engine changed. `llama-bench -p 0 -n 128 -d <depth> -r 2`, Q4_K_M GGUF, both c

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash (glm5_next): no SM120 sparse-MLA path for rope-free MLA (qk_rope_head_dim=0) — three failure modes on RTX PRO 6000
items.author: tmttodd
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

GLM-5.3-Flash (`glm5_next`) cannot start on **SM120** (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, compute 12.0) with the dedicated `glm53-flash` image: the architecture's **rope-free sparse MLA** (`qk_rope_head_dim: 0`) has no working attention/KV path on this capability. Three distinct failure modes below, ending at an explicit kernel shape guard. Weight loading itself is clean (including a quantized checkpoint — Marlin NvFp4 auto-selected), so this is purely the sparse-MLA attention/KV-cache lane.

### Environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:glm53-flash-x86_64-cu130@sha256:2e771fa615452282cc331eb418b3ef21636fce355bea0491fca89e6d362ab703` (engine banner: `0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187`; per-model image published for #53906)
- GPUs: 4× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition (96 GB, **SM120 / compute 12.0**), driver 595.71.05, host CUDA 13.2, TP=4
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` — text config `kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_nope_head_dim=256`, **`qk_rope_head_dim=0`**, `index_topk=2048` (34 linear-attention + 11 DSA layers)
- Checkpoint under test: local weight-only NVFP4 (compressed-tensors, routed experts only; attention/vision/MTP in BF16). The failures below are independent of weight quantization — they occur in backend selection / KV-cache paths before or regardless of quantized GEMMs.
- Args: `--tensor-parallel-size 4 --max-model-len 131072 --max-num-seqs 256 --reasoning-parser glm45 --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-prefix-caching --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90` (no speculative config)

### Failure mode 1 — default (`kv_cache_dtype=auto`, also explicit `fp8_e4m3`)

Engine init reaches CUDA-graph memory profiling, then the MLA cache write asserts:

```
RuntimeError: Worker failed with error 'concat_and_cache_mla,
/workspace/csrc/libtorch_stable/cache_kernels.cu:866, pe_dim must be 64 for fp8_ds_mla'
```

`FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120` requires the packed `fp8_ds_mla` layout (explicit `fp8_e4m3` is normalized into it), whose cache-write kernel hardcodes the DeepSeek entry shape (512 NoPE + 64 RoPE). Rope-free MLA (pe_dim 0) violates it.

### Failure mode 2 — `--kv-cache-dtype bfloat16`

```
ValueError: No valid attention backend found for cuda with AttentionSelectorConfig(
  head_size=512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, kv_cache_dtype=bfloat16, use_mla=True, use_sparse=True, ...)
Reasons: {TRITON_MLA: [sparse not supported],
          FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120: [kv_cache_dtype not supported, kv_cache_dtype not supported]}
```

Note the bf16-capable no-rope lane (`FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE`, which explicitly whitelists `qk_nope_head_dim=256 / kv_lora_rank=512` per its `supports_combination`) is never considered: `platforms/cuda.py::_get_backend_priorities` hardcodes the `major == 12` MLA candidates to `[TRITON_MLA, FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120]`.

### Failure mode 3 — experimentally widening the SM100 no-rope lane to SM120

To test whether the gap is routing-only, we injected a runtime patch (sitecustomize) that (a) appends `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE` to the SM120 candidate list and (b) widens `FlashInferMLASparseTRTLLMBackend.supports_compute_capability` to `{10, 12}`. The lane is then selected, all 120 shards load cleanly, and init stops at a precise shape guard:

```
ValueError: SM120 sparse MLA v32/GLM expects kv_lora_rank=512, qk_rope_head_dim=64,
and query head dim 576; got kv_lora_rank=512, qk_rope_head_dim=0, query dim=512
```

i.e. the SM120 sparse-MLA kernel path exists only for the DeepSeek-shaped (rope-64 / query-576) case; the rope-free GLM shape (query 512) has no SM120 kernel.

### Ask

Either extend the no-rope (`qk_nope=256 / kv_lora=512`) sparse-MLA support that ships for SM100 to SM120 (kernel + `supported_kv_cache_dtypes` + the hardcoded candidate list in `platforms/cuda.py`), or document `glm5_next` as unsupported on SM120 in the model's serving notes so consumer/workstation Blackwell users don't chase configuration fixes for a kernel gap.

Happy to test candidate images/patches quickly — we have a 4× RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) TP4 environment with the model staged and can boot-verify within minutes. Full boot logs for all three modes available on request.

items.title: [RFC]: Scheduler-Aware Multi-Tier KV Caching for vLLM with MORI-UMBP
items.author: charxwu
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

vLLM's GPU prefix cache is bounded by accelerator memory. CPU offloading can extend capacity within an engine, while an external KV store can preserve and reuse prefixes across engines, DP ranks, nodes, and engine restarts. The open [vLLM UMBP feature request](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48191) tracks this need for AMD deployments.

MORI-UMBP provides an AMD-focused storage path with HIP-visible GPU-buffer registration, NUMA-aware host DRAM, MORI-IO RDMA, SSD backends, tier-placement policy, and scheduler-visible KV location and hit metadata. Integrating it into vLLM provides several concrete benefits:

- **Shareable capacity:** standalone UMBP places the node-local KV pool in a separate process so DP ranks and model instances can share DRAM. This also allows round-robin traffic to reuse KV across DP ranks.
- **Direct GPU-to-store movement:** grouped ranged operations move between registered vLLM KV buffers and UMBP without requiring a connector-owned contiguous host staging copy.
- **Cache lifetime independent of the engine:** standalone storage survives worker restart or rolling upgrade, avoiding a complete host-cache warm-up.
- **Global placement and routing:** distributed UMBP can use cluster-wide capacity and location information instead of making every placement or eviction decision from one rank's local view.
- **Replication-aware storage:** byte-identical TP replicas can share one object identity in shared storage, while rank-sharded data retains distinct shard identity. Writer election can additionally reduce duplicate traffic when every reader can reach the elected writer's object.
- **Layer-wise overlap:** grouped ranged I/O, batched offload, and per-layer completion allow later-layer KV loading to overlap earlier-layer compute.
- **Tiered capacity:** UMBP can extend the same object namespace from DRAM to SSD and optional UMBP-owned HBM without adding medium-specific branches to the vLLM connector.

The initial integration should not require a redesign of vLLM's connector API. `MooncakeStoreConnector` provides a useful structural precedent: one `KVConnectorBase_V1` implementation dispatches to scheduler-side lookup/planning and worker-side registration/transfer logic.

`UMBPStoreConnector` follows that vLLM-facing structure while keeping UMBP semantics behind `IUMBPRuntime`. Embedded mode is worker-private and masterless; standalone mode shares a node-local service; distributed mode uses Master routing, peer-owned slots, MORI-IO, and heartbeat-acknowledged publication. Identity, layout, metadata, completion, preemption, and failure-to-recompute remain common across all three modes.

## Proposed Change

### Summary

This RFC proposes adding one vLLM V1 `UMBPStoreConnector` backed by MORI-UMBP. It follows the proven scheduler/worker organization of `MooncakeStoreConnector` while keeping UMBP-specific lookup, transfer, and publication semantics behind `IUMBPRuntime`.

The connector supports embedded, standalone, and distributed UMBP modes without duplicating vLLM-facing code. All modes share replication-aware object identity, KV layout, grouped/layer-wise transfer planning, metadata, job lifecycle, pinning, completion, and failure-to-recompute behavior; only runtime topology and data movement differ.

Implementation proceeds through small PRs, beginning with the shared connector framework and embedded mode, then adding standalone and distributed runtimes. A broader backend-neutral connector for UMBP, Mooncake, and other stores is recorded as an open architectural discussion and does not block UMBP delivery.

### Goals

- Add one vLLM V1 `UMBPStoreConnector` following the existing `KVConnectorBase_V1` scheduler/worker lifecycle.
- Support embedded, standalone, and distributed UMBP modes through one shared connector framework.
- Select the UMBP runtime mode at connector initialization without changing scheduler/worker connector code.
- Use vLLM content-derived block hashes, never physical GPU block IDs, as the basis of persistent object identity.
- Make object identity replication-aware per KV-cache group:
  - sharded TP data keeps a logical shard/rank component;
  - byte-identical TP replicas use one shared object key when the selected runtime storage is shared by those ranks;
  - private embedded pools retain the physical copy needed by each process, even if their logical key is identical.
- Avoid redundant writes only when the runtime can prove that one writer's object is visible to every rank that will read it. Key deduplication and writer election are separate optimizations.
- Keep KV layout planning, connector metadata, transfer job state, pinning, completion, and recomputation logic common across all modes.
- Use UMBP ranged Put/Get operations for non-contiguous GPU KV regions.
- Support both bulk and layer-wise execution through the shared framework: submit grouped asynchronous range operations, wait only for the layer about to execute, and batch completed-layer offloads.
- Register vLLM GPU KV allocations once and pass registered GPU regions directly to UMBP/MORI-IO without connector-owned contiguous staging.
- Treat missing, evicted, timed-out, stale, or partially transferred objects as cache misses and safely recompute them.
- Keep UMBP transport, routing, and publication details out of vLLM scheduler, model-runner, and attention code.
- Incubate through `kv_connector_module_path` against a pinned vLLM revision before considering upstream registration.

### Architecture

![vLLM and MORI-UMBP architecture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charxwu/vllm/b6827f6b9ad236a7806f1e60fe739494eb81a7ed/docs/assets/vllm-umbp-architecture-v2.svg)

_Figure 1. `UMBPStoreConnector` bridges vLLM's scheduler and worker lifecycle to UMBP's control and data planes._

vLLM owns request scheduling and GPU KV blocks. `UMBPStoreConnector` maps vLLM's scheduler/worker lifecycle onto UMBP control and data operations. UMBP owns routing, transfer, publication, and sto

items.title: [RFC]: Bound frontend drain latency for bulk aborts and long non-streaming completions
items.author: aoshen02
items.body_excerpt:
# Motivation.

Bulk abort is expected to be the fast path for pausing online RL generation,
but its latency can scale with all output retained by the frontend. In a
DP8/EP8/TP1 deployment with eight API server processes, aborting 2,000
non-streaming completion requests at a reported approximately 3,500 generated
tokens per request produced 96-177 seconds of frontend tail latency. Actual
returned means were 4,850-5,445 tokens because generation continued while the
frontend lagged. The engines had already accepted the abort; API processes
were still draining queued outputs,
detokenizing sampled logprobs, constructing response models, materializing
Python dictionaries, and encoding JSON.

The largest amplifier was API-process load imbalance. The parent enabled
`SO_REUSEPORT`, but all workers inherited copies of one socket and therefore
shared one accept queue. In one run, the busiest API process owned 1,492 of
2,000 requests. Balanced DP-engine load did not imply balanced frontend load.

This matters beyond RL pause. The same work appears when long non-streaming
completion requests finish or are aborted together, especially when sampled
logprobs or token IDs are returned. A fast model can produce outputs faster
than one Python frontend process can consume and serialize them.

This RFC follows the completed pause/resume API RFC #32103, whose follow-up
list explicitly called out better abort handling. It does not change pause
mode semantics or DPEP coordination. At RFC creation, searches of issues and open PRs using
pause/abort, frontend serialization, logprobs, API server, and reuseport terms
found no overlapping proposal or implementation. Related work is
complementary:

- #56754 drains in-process requests before sleep.
- #52875 reduces per-frame cost for simple streaming completions.
- #47933 preserves `finish_reason="abort"` for scale-out token streams.

## Reproduction and evidence

The primary setup used two GB200 nodes, DP8/EP8/TP1, eight API servers, 2,000
requests, and sampled `logprobs=0`. A four-layer checkpoint made the frontend
bottleneck easy to reproduce; the final candidate was also validated with the
full 78-layer MXFP8 checkpoint.

On the reduced model, the unmodified frontend took 96.18 and 177.12 seconds
from pause to its last response serialization in two runs. The measured
seven-file candidate took 3.38 seconds at 7.28 million returned tokens, and
5.18 seconds at 10.08 million returned tokens versus 96.18 seconds at 10.89
million unmodified. The six-file patch proposed here differs only by removal
of a null-result lazy-context change and was itself measured as the valid
2.924-second `no_lazy_context` leave-one-out arm.

On the full model, one unmodified baseline was 6.97 seconds frontend and 7.44
seconds through all client results, with a balanced 187-270 requests per
frontend. Four additional unmodified runs using a two-process client that
concentrated connections on fewer workers reached 8.92-21.10-second frontend
tails, with 462-907 requests on the busiest process. Two used the 3,500-token
trigger and two used 3,800. They have no patched counterpart and are baseline
evidence, not an A/B comparison.

Two seven-file-candidate repeats completed frontend serialization in 3.63 and
3.90 seconds and all client parsing in 3.81 and 4.19 seconds; waiting for both
the pause HTTP response and all client results took 3.81 and 7.67 seconds. This
validates parity and absence of regression at full scale. It does not reproduce
the reduced model's 100+ second tail in a matched A/B or isolate the listener
change. GPU response parity was also captured on this measured seven-file
candidate; equivalence to the shipped six-file state rests on hash identity
with the measured `no_lazy_context` arm rather than a separate post-trim GPU
capture.

We then ran an eight-arm, same-allocation leave-one-out experiment. Every arm
aborted and rendered exactly 2,000 responses. The complete candidate was
bracketed at 2.953 and 3.054 seconds, giving a 0.102-second drift bound.

| Removed optimization | Frontend-tail regression |
| --- | ---: |
| Independent `SO_REUSEPORT` listener per API worker | +6.199 s |
| Bounded single-token decode cache | +1.075 s |
| Flat sampled-logprob storage | +1.039 s |
| Direct Pydantic JSON serialization | +1.176 s |
| Explicit event-loop yields | +0.125 s |
| Lazy byte-fallback context lookup | -0.080 s |

The first four effects are 10-61 times the measured run drift. The lazy
context change was removed. Event-loop yields are retained for a deterministic
fairness invariant: without them, a ready output queue can consume 100 batches
before a waiting control task runs. Leave-one-out effects interact and must
not be summed to reconstruct the original 100+ second result.

The listener result is one stochastic draw for a client opening approximately
2,000 connections. Its +6.199-second effect is not a general point estimate;
keep-alive-heavy clients can see a different distribution or no benefit.

## Implementation update — 2026-09-23

Phase 1 is proposed in **#58278: [Frontend] Give API workers independent reuseport listeners** (draft, not merged). The narrowed implementation changes only listener selection and per-worker socket ownership. General CLI startup/shutdown behavior stays identical to the base; lifecycle refactoring is deferred. The following GPU measurements belong to historical head `377818881b`, not the current revision.

A prior **listener-only** GPU/HTTP ABBA experiment completed on node18 using one node with four GB200s, four-layer HY4-preview BF16, DP4/EP4/TP1, four default API processes, 250 requests per replica (1,000 total), non-streaming completions and sampled `logprobs=0`.

| Metric | Shared listener (A, two runs) | Independent listeners (B, two runs) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Last frontend serialization | 8.298 / 10.698 s | 4.551 / 4.746 s |
| Median frontend serialization tail | 9.498 s | 4.649 s (51.1% lower) |
| Last client response body received | 9

items.title: [Bug] DFlash2/DSpark + prefix caching corrupt output after a cache hit on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (compressed-tensors) on 0.30/0.31; 0.29, FP8 target and MTP are fine
items.author: sinmkd
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (also reproduced on 0.30.0). vLLM 0.29.0 passes the same test.
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, flashinfer-python/cubin 0.7.0.post1 (0.6.18.post1 on 0.30.0), CUDA 13.3, driver 610.57.04
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell 48 GB (sm_120), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-34
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` NVFP4 checkpoint, compressed-tensors mixed precision (NVFP4 on the MLP projections, FP8 W8A8 on attention / GDN projections / lm_head, `linear_attn.{in_proj_a,in_proj_b,norm}` and `mtp.*` unquantized via `ignore`)
- Drafter: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (`DFlash2DraftModel`, sliding_window 2048), `num_speculative_tokens: 7`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since 0.30.0, serving Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 with the DFlash2 drafter and prefix caching enabled produces garbage after a prefix-cache hit. The first requests of a conversation are fine. From the third request on, once the prompt resumes from cached blocks, the model emits a single repeated token (`duct`, over and over) with no coherent content, and the drafter accepts nothing (`SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted: 0 tokens`). The same five requests against 0.29.0 come back coherent every time. I have run the comparison twice on each version.

The test is a replay of a real agent conversation: five consecutive chat-completions requests from one session (31,776 / 45,606 / 52,737 / 65,364 / 67,502 prompt tokens, 25 tool schemas, seed 17), sent in order to a fresh engine so each request hits the previous one's prefix. The conversation itself is private, but I can build a synthetic equivalent if that helps.

Serve command (production flags):

```
vllm serve /models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --max-model-len 250000 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 17379961324 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7}' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --override-generation-config '{"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":20,"min_p":0.0}' --scheduling-policy priority
```

env: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0 VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=false`. Prefix caching on (default), `mamba_cache_mode` resolves to `align`.

### What I tried, to narrow it down

All on 0.31.0, same five requests, fresh engine each time:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| nothing (command above) | fails at request 3 |
| PR #57128 applied (the `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` / `drop_eagle_block` fix) | fails |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` instead of FlashInfer | fails |
| `--linear-backend cutlass` (in-tree CUTLASS NVFP4 GEMM) | fails |
| `--linear-backend marlin` (weight-only W4A16, no activation quant) | fails |
| smaller KV pool / 180K window / util 0.94 (copied from my FP8 route) | fails |
| `"disable_eagle_block_drop": true` in the speculative config | worse: garbage from request 1, even cold |
| **no speculative config at all** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` (checkpoint's own MTP head)** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"dspark","model":"RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-speculator.dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7}`** | **fails at request 3** |
| **FP8 target (`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`, `quant_method: fp8`) with the same DFlash2 config** | **passes 5/5, twice** |

A unique `cache_salt` per request on 0.30.0 also makes requests 3–5 pass, so the failure needs an actual cache hit.

So the NVFP4 GEMM kernels are not involved (three different kernels, including weight-only, all fail), the GDN prefill kernel is not involved, and the KV pool size is not involved. What it needs is: a hidden-state drafter (DFlash2 or DSpark; MTP is fine) + a prefix-cache hit + this compressed-tensors NVFP4 target, on 0.30 or later. The FP8 checkpoint with the identical drafter config is fine. Turning off the EAGLE trailing-block drop makes it strictly worse, which reads to me like the drafter is leaving bad Mamba/GDN state in the cached tail block and the drop normally hides it inside a request but not across requests.

The compressed-tensors checkpoint is the obvious difference from the FP8 one: it has an `ignore` list covering `linear_attn` sub-modules (the bf16 `in_proj_a` / `in_proj_b` / `norm`) alongside `config_groups` that target `linear_attn.{in_proj_qkv,in_proj_z,out_proj}` at FP8. If the drafter path resolves those layers differently from the plain `fp8` loader, that would be where I'd look first, but I haven't gone further than the table above.

Related: #53912 and #55766 describe neighbouring hybrid-GDN prefix-cache corruption with speculative decoding.

### What I can provide

Per-request replay output (prompt token counts, finish reasons, draft metrics), engine logs for every ablation above, and a synthetic reproducer on request.

items.title: [Feature] L1/L2/L3 cache hit rate observability — Prometheus metrics, OTel spans & per-request JSONL trace
items.author: grissomsh
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

LMCache's current `PrometheusLogger` provides basic metrics (`time_to_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_requests`), but is missing:

1. **Per-tier cache hit rate** — no way to distinguish whether a hit came from L2 (CPU RAM), L3 (NVMe Disk), or a remote backend.
2. **TTFT decomposition** — `frontend_latency` (API server → engine core) and per-request `kv_lookup_time` / `kv_retrieve_time` are not surfaced.
3. **Per-request tracing** — no way to correlate cache-hit details to an individual request for debugging latency spikes.

These gaps make it hard to answer operational questions like: *"Why did TTFT spike — was it a slow disk read, CPU cache contention, or GPU prefix cache eviction?"*

---

### Design Goals

1. **Three-layer observability model**: throughput → latency → cache hit rate
2. **Minimally invasive**: extend existing `LMCStatsMonitor`, `PrometheusLogger`, and `cache_engine` — no breaking API changes
3. **TP-aware**: cross-process bridge via `/dev/shm` for Worker ↔ EngineCore per-request data relay when TP > 1
4. **Self-verifying**: every trace carries token identity equations for automated correctness validation

---

### Proposed Design

#### Layer 1 — Throughput: Token Source Decomposition

```
Tokens/s = local_compute + L1_hit + L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit
```

**Approach**: Extend `cache_engine.py`'s `retrieve()` / `retrieve_layer()` to classify hit tokens by storage backend. Add a `_BACKEND_NAME_TO_HIT_TIER` mapping:

| Backend | Tier |
|---------|------|
| `LocalCPUBackend` | L2 |
| `LocalDiskBackend` / `GdsBackend` | L3 |
| `RemoteBackend` | Remote |

**New Prometheus metrics** (6 total):

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

#### Layer 2 — Latency: TTFT Decomposition

```
TTFT = frontend_latency + queue_time + prefill_time
prefill_time ⊃ kv_lookup_time + kv_retrieve_time
```

**Approach**: Add `LMCacheKVConnectorStats` (extending vLLM's `KVConnectorStats`) on the vLLM side, and expose per-request timing through `vllm_v1_adapter.py`'s `request_finished()` via `EngineCoreOutput.kv_transfer_params`.

**New Prometheus metrics** (9 bridge metrics + 1 framework metric):

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram | KV lookup latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram | KV retrieve latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: process_tokens phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: CPU→GPU DMA phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L2 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L3 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side remote bridge |
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram | API server → engine core latency |

#### Layer 3 — Cache Hit Rate & Per-Request Trace

One JSONL `[trace]` line emitted per request at completion:

```json
{
  "ts": 1782023561.679,
  "rid": "chatcmpl-xxx",
  "prompt_tokens": 3934,
  "output_tokens": 32,
  "TTFT_ms": 169.2,
  "queue_ms": 0.04,
  "prefill_ms": 130.1,
  "decode_ms": 144.6,
  "e2e_ms": 314.3,
  "frontend_ms": 39.0,
  "input_tokens_cache_hit": 3840,
  "L1_hit": 0,
  "external_kv_hit": 3840,
  "L2_hit": 0,
  "L3_hit": 3840,
  "remote_hit": 0,
  "input_tokens_no_cache_hit": 94,
  "kv_transfer_mode": "non_layerwise",
  "kv_lookup_ms": 1.2,
  "kv_retrieve_ms": 101.5
}
```

**Token identity equations** (verifiable by automated scripts at runtime):

```
prompt_tokens = input_tokens_cache_hit + input_tokens_no_cache_hit
input_tokens_cache_hit = L1_hit + external_kv_hit
external_kv_hit ≈ L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit   (≈ due to chunk_size=256 granularity)
```

#### Cross-Process Bridge (TP > 1)

When TP > 1, `retrieve()` runs on Worker_TP0 while `request_finished()` runs on the EngineCore/scheduler process. Per-request data is relayed via file-based bridge in `/dev/shm/lmcache_bridge/` (tmpfs, memory-backed):

- Per-tier counters: file + `fcntl.flock` for atomic cross-process updates
- Timing data: `write-tmp + os.replace` for atomic JSON
- Cleanup: throttled periodic sweep + retry limit (3) to prevent `/dev/shm` exhaustion

#### OTel Span Attributes

8 attributes on the `"llm_request"` span:

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_frontend` | API → engine |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_lookup` | KV lookup |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_transfer` | KV retrieve |
| `gen_ai.usage.l1_hit_tokens` | L1 (GPU prefix cache) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l2_hit_tokens` | L2 (CPU RAM) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l3_hit_tokens` | L3 (NVMe/SSD) |
| `gen_ai.usage.remote_hit_tokens` | Remote backend |
| `gen_ai.latency.kv_transfer_mode` | layerwise / non_layerwise |

---

### Metrics Summary (16 new Prometheus metrics)

**LMCache side (6):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

**vLLM bridge (9):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_transfer_mode` | Info |

**vLLM framework (1):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram |

---

### Verification

The design has been validated end

items.title: [RFC] Native PD disaggregation in MP mode
items.author: limarkdcunha
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Problem

Current behavior: Today, the user must manually deploy, configure, and maintain an external, unmanaged reference script (examples/disagg_prefill_mp/disagg_proxy_server.py) to handle control-plane orchestration. While LMCache natively handles the data plane handoff (prefill stores to the server; decode reads from it), routing decisions and prefill-completion signaling are bolted onto this loose example script.

This introduces severe problems such as :

- Slow "done" signal. To learn "prefill finished," it runs a separate mini server just for that message, and waits on it. That's an extra network round-trip and a thread hand-off sitting right in the path before the user gets their first token — pure delay, nothing gained.

- Rigid setup that breaks easily. It always pairs prefill #2 with decode #2, in that fixed order, using host/port lists typed in at startup. Want to add or remove a machine? Restart the whole proxy. And it has no way to notice a machine died — it'll happily send requests to a dead one.

- Reinventing what already exists. LMCache already has mp_coordinator, which tracks live instances, checks their health, and holds fleet-wide metadata (quota, blend fingerprints, and so on). The proxy ignores all of that and rebuilds a worse version of instance tracking from scratch — static host/port lists, no health, no roles.

Expected outcome:
Ship PD orchestration as a **separate, native router/proxy service**. It owns routing, request forwarding, and completion signaling. `mp_coordinator` keeps its existing job — tracking fleet state (membership, health, roles) — and just exposes that data for the router to read. Coordinator never handles a request; router never owns fleet state. This retires the standalone example proxy script and makes PD disaggregation native.

## 2. Non-goals

Worth being explicit about what this RFC does not touch:

- No changes required on the vLLM or SGLang side — both already expose the hooks LMCache needs (`kv_transfer_config` connector). This is entirely an LMCache-side orchestration change.
- The KV data-transfer path itself (CUDA IPC / SHM / socket fallback) stays exactly as-is. Only orchestration — routing and completion signaling — changes.
- The prefill/decode scheduling policy inside the serving engine isn't touched. LMCache orchestrates the handoff; the engine still does the compute.
- Coordinator high availability is out of scope here — see Open Question 4.

## 3. Proposal

Router/proxy owns all PD orchestration (routing, forwarding, completion signaling); coordinator only exposes fleet metadata, per §1.

Three changes:

1. **Role-aware membership (coordinator metadata).** Instances declare `prefill` or `decode` at registration, extending the existing register/heartbeat path. Only piece that touches the coordinator.

2. **Native completion signaling.** Replaces the HTTP telemetry hop with an internal "prefill done, decode may proceed" signal. The main open decision — options below.

3. **Fleet-aware routing (in the router service).** The router picks prefill/decode targets from live membership and health, instead of static round-robin pairing. In v1 this means round-robin over live, role-matched, healthy instances — a real improvement over today's static pairing, even though it isn't load-aware yet. True load-aware selection is deferred; see Open Question 2.

   **Fleet discovery**, part of this change: the router caches its own copy of the fleet metadata and routes from that, rather than calling the coordinator per request. Keeps the coordinator out of the request path.

   **How it gets that copy.** No push/subscribe mechanism on the coordinator today — only `GET /instances` (a pull). "Coordinator pushes to router" would be net-new work.

   Cheaper path for v1: router polls `GET /instances` every second or two, refreshes its cache. Reuses what's already there; staleness window is small enough to be covered by the retry-and-resync rule further down.

   True push can come later if polling proves too coarse.

That covers routing and membership — the harder piece is completion signaling, since it's the one place where getting it wrong means decode reading garbage or hanging. Worth walking through where the signal actually comes from today before picking an approach.

## Completion signaling — the options

Where does "request X is fully stored, across every worker" actually get decided today? Not on the LMCache MP server — it's assembled in LMCache's own vLLM adapter (`get_finished`, in `vllm_multi_process_adapter.py`), triggered by vLLM calling that method. That adapter already handles cross-worker aggregation, dedup, and the healthy/unhealthy cases correctly, and once it's satisfied it fires `on_request_store_finished(...)` — today, an HTTP POST to the proxy's telemetry server. Since that adapter is LMCache's own code (it just happens to run inside vLLM's process), we can change how it announces completion without touching vLLM at all. The MP server itself never sees this — it only sees individual store commits, with no concept of "all workers done for this request."

Three ways to build the native signal:

**Option 1 (recommended) — swap the transport.** Keep the adapter's `get_finished` detection exactly as it is, and just replace the HTTP POST with a native notify (ZMQ, straight to the proxy). Reuses cross-worker logic that's already correct and battle-tested, so it's the smallest change we can make. The signal still originates in the adapter rather than the MP server — fine, since the adapter is our code either way.

**Option 2 — move the aggregation server-side.** Rebuild "all workers done" tracking inside the MP server itself: count `COMMIT_STORE`s per request across every rank, and emit the signal from there. Fully decoupled from vLLM's loop, but it re-implements, as new work, something the adapter already does correctly. Not worth the cost for what it buys.

items.title: [Bug][MP] lmcache_mp.l1_read counts released read reservations even when no GPU retrieve occurs
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` is documented as "Number of chunks read from L1"
(`docs/source/mp/observability/metrics.rst`).

However, the counter also increments when L1 read reservations are only
released and no LMCache-driven CPU→GPU retrieve is submitted.

With the vLLM connector, this can happen when the requested prefix is already
available in vLLM's local GPU prefix cache.

LMCache lookup/prefetch finds the matching chunks and retains/read-locks them.
Later, `update_state_after_alloc()` determines that no external retrieve is
needed and calls `free_lookup_locks()`.

That path eventually reaches `L1Manager.finish_read()`, which publishes
`L1_READ_FINISHED`. The `lmcache_mp.l1_read` metric therefore increases even
though no LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

In my repro:

- 5 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused `l1_read` to increase by 5.
- Another 6 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused it to increase by 6.
- After restarting vLLM, the same 6 retained keys were actually retrieved from
  L1, and `l1_read` again increased by 6.

So `lmcache_mp.l1_read` increases by the number of retained/released keys in
both cases and does not distinguish a real retrieve from a lookup reservation
that is later released unused.

---

**To Reproduce**

Environment:

- LMCache dev @ `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
- vLLM `0.30.0`
- MP mode
- ZMQ transport
- `lmcache_driven` transfer
- `--chunk-size 16`
- 1x A100

Steps:

1. Start the LMCache MP server with `--chunk-size 16`.
2. Start one vLLM instance using `LMCacheMPConnector`.
3. Send prompt P (85 tokens) once to populate the cache.
4. Send P plus a short suffix (97 tokens) twice using the same vLLM process.
5. Observe the LMCache logs and `/metrics`.
6. Restart only vLLM, leaving the LMCache server running.
7. Send the same P + suffix request again from the fresh vLLM process.
8. Compare `lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total` with the actual retrieve metrics.

Observed before restarting vLLM:

```text
=== 1: P, cold ===
Stored 80 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 6.0
(no l1_read)
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 2: P + suffix, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 5/6 retained keys (5 L1, 0 L2) in 1.2 ms
Stored 16 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 8.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 5.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 3: same request again, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 0.9 ms
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 9.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)
```

The `l1_read` counter increased:

```text
0 -> 5    (+5)
5 -> 11   (+6)
```

exactly matching the number of retained keys, while no GPU retrieve was
submitted.

The extra `Stored 16 tokens` in step 3 is unrelated to this issue. The two
requests produced different completions, so the final chunk containing
generated tokens differed.

As a control, I then restarted vLLM while keeping the same LMCache server
running. This removes vLLM's local GPU prefix cache, so the cached prefix has
to be retrieved from LMCache.

The same request then produced:

```text
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 1.7 ms
Retrieved 96 tokens in 0.001 seconds

lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 17.0
lmcache_mp_num_submitted_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
lmcache_mp_num_finished_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
```

The previous reading, taken after step 3, was:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
```

No other requests were sent in between, so the real retrieve also increased
`l1_read` by exactly 6:

```text
11 -> 17   (+6)
```

This gives the following A/B comparison:

```text
Case A: 6/6 retained, no retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +0
num_finished_retrieves +0

Case B: 6/6 retained, real CPU->GPU retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +1
num_finished_retrieves +1
```

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` therefore grows by the same amount in both cases. Only the
`num_*_retrieves` metrics distinguish whether a real retrieve occurred.

Relevant code path at `1ca53a8a`:

- `lmcache/v1/mp_observability/subscribers/metrics/l1.py:49`

  `L1MetricsSubscriber` subscribes to `L1_READ_FINISHED`.

- `lmcache/v1/distributed/l1_manager.py:433`

  `finish_read()` publishes one `L1_READ_FINISHED` event containing the keys
  whose read locks were released; the metric subscriber counts those keys.

- `lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_connector.py:1381` →
  `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py:481`

  `free_lookup_locks()` → `finish_read_prefetched()` → `finish_read()`,
  without a data-transfer request on the no-retrieve path.

---

**Expected behavior**

The metric semantics and documentation should be consistent.

If `lmcache_mp.l1_read` is intended to represent chunks actually read from L1,
it should not increase for the `free_lookup_locks()` path when no retrieve was
submitted.

If it is intentionally a read-reservation lifecycle counter, its description
should make that clear and documentation should not use it as proof that a
retrieve occurred.

This is especially relevant because the SGLang quickstart
(`docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst`) currently tells users they can
"confirm the retrieve" by checking:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total
```

The repro above shows that this counter can increase even when no
LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

I reproduced the no-retrieve behavior with the vLLM connector. I have not
tested whether the same no-retrieve path is reachable through SGLang.

---

**Screenshots**

Not required for reproduction. The relevant LMCache server logs and metric
values are included above.

---

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04
- Browser: N/A
- LMCache: `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
-

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Offloaded-MoE prefill leaves the GPU idle waiting on serial expert H2D copies (single-GPU -ncmoe)
items.author: thecodacus
items.body_excerpt: Sharing a performance finding from profiling the offloaded-MoE path (`--n-cpu-moe` / `-ncmoe`) — the setup where a big MoE model runs on a small GPU with the experts kept in system RAM and streamed in per layer. My box: RTX 3060 12GB, Ryzen 5600X, 32GB DDR4, PCIe 4.0, Ubuntu 24.04. Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Q4_K_M), `-ncmoe 26`, prefill at pp2048 / ub2048. Everything below is single-box and gen4-specific, so numbers will move on other hardware. On this setup prefill is bottlenecked by PCIe transfers, not GPU compute. Profiling with Nsight, the GPU sits idle a large fraction of each prefill pass waiting on expert-weight H2D copies, and those copies run serially with the matmul that consumes them — layer N's weights finish uploading, then layer N computes, then N+1's weights start uploading. The upload and the compute don't overlap on the offload path. Two changes helped a lot, both prefill-only and both producing token-identical output at temp 0: 1. Page-locking the mmap-backed CPU expert weights so the H2D transfers DMA directly instead of going through a pageable bounce buffer. ~+21% on its own. 2. Overlapping the expert uploads with compute on a second stream with a few staging slots, so layer N+1's weights upload while layer N is still computing. This is where most of the win is. Together that took prefill from ~1143 to ~1880 tok/s at identical settings — roughly +64%, pure code, no config change. GPU idle during prefill dropped from ~42% to a few percent. I prototyped both behind env flags on a fork so I could A/B them on the same binary and confirm the output stayed identical: https://github.com/thecodacus/llama.cpp/tree/fable5/prefetch-experts (there's a benchmark writeup in the branch with the exact commands and the full before/after log). I'm raising this as a finding rather than a PR — partly because AGENTS.md asks for that, and partly because the right way to expose something like this upstream is probably whoever owns the CUDA scheduler deciding on the shape, not me dropping a patch on you. Two honest caveats: this was measured a few weeks back at around the b6xxx era, and the CUDA backend has moved since, so the exact idle percentage may be stale — I haven't re-run against current master. And I know pipeline copies are already a thing for the multi-device case; the gap I'm describing is specifically the single-GPU offload path, which always gets `n_copies = 1`. Main question for maintainers: is reducing GPU idle on the offload path something you'd want addressed, and if so, is overlap-on-a-second-stream the right approach — or is there a reason the offload copies are serial today that I'm not seeing? Happy to share nsys timelines or run other configs if that's useful. here is nsys trace

items.title: Unit test coverage and hardening for /v1/systemone
items.author: sometimesanotion
items.body_excerpt:
My thesis:  llama.cpp supporting decision APIs and the "semantic if" means that the likely use cases could hammer the API orders of magnitude harder than typical harnesses or LLM teams.  Hardening and clear error codes are a must.

The /v1/systemone endpoint will likely be supporting many more models and use cases.  I found no unit tests for it.  So, I red-teamed its code, I looked for queuing idioms already in the codebase, I brought in the most robust features of another decision fork I'd worked on, and created a PR.  It's at https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30027

It adds robust unit tests, queuing, hardening, and error reporting that matches the Jev 1.13 API, and it detects capacity for labels from the model so that you don't get silent failures on tinyllama or any other low-capacity model. 

By pure line count, this shouldn't be a single PR, but most of the bulk is in unit tests.  I think the case can be made as to why these things necessarily go together, and going from zero to possibly adequate unit tests for this API is an unavoidably large jump.  I also think they'll be a boon to future PRs and maintenance, not a burden.

Of course, this deserves a discussion, and people may have their own ideas about what's needed here in the first place.  Just doing my part so others' review time is well-spent!  Feedback welcome.

items.title: [RFC]: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference（CCF 赛题四）
items.author: Pinoeer-kingxi
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

<!-- GitHub-safe plain Markdown. Copy from the raw .md text, not from Word or a rich-text preview. -->

# RFC: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| RFC | RFC-EPD-Agent-Multimodal-2026 |
| Status | Draft |
| Date | 2026-07-05 |
| Target Project | Mooncake / Mooncake Transfer Engine / MooncakeStore |
| Target Integrations | vLLM, SGLang, Qwen-VL/Qwen3-VL-style multimodal models |
| Scope | Encoder-Prefill-Decode disaggregation, Agent state cloning, cross-step KV reuse, evaluation protocol |
| Primary Audience | Mooncake maintainers, serving-system contributors, vLLM/SGLang integration reviewers |
| Implementation Horizon | One-month prototype milestone, followed by staged hardening |
| Compatibility Target | Preserve existing PD and colocated serving paths; new features must be gated by configuration |

---

## Summary

This RFC proposes an extension to Mooncake for **agentic multimodal inference**. The core idea is to generalize Mooncake's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving capability from a two-stage Prefill-Decode model into a broader **Encoder-Prefill-Decode (EPD)** architecture, while also supporting:

- **Agent state cloning** for multi-branch reasoning;
- **visual feature caching** for repeated image/document contexts;
- **cross-step KV reuse** for repeated workflow prefixes;
- **tool-call offload/restore** to release GPU memory during blocking I/O;
- **A2A handoff** for state transfer among planner, executor, verifier, and domain agents;
- **coordinated scheduling** across Encoder, Prefill, Decode, and storage resources.

The proposal introduces a unified `MultimodalState` abstraction that represents visual feature bundles, textual/multimodal KV pages, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, TTL, and ownership.

The design intentionally avoids a single global strongly-consistent KV registry. Instead, it uses:

1. **KV Directory** for eventually consistent metadata lookup;
2. **Workflow Shards** for per-workflow strong consistency, refcount, CAS, fork, release, and CoW;
3. **Decentralized Scheduler** for admission control, priority scheduling, offload/restore, and A2A-aware routing.

For KV reuse correctness, the RFC uses a conservative default:

> **Exact Prefix Reuse by default; Approximate Reuse only behind validation gates and feature flags.**

Approximate reuse is never required for correctness. If any validation step fails, the system falls back to exact prefix reuse or full Prefill.

---

## Motivation

### Multimodal inference is naturally EPD-shaped

Multimodal inference contains three computationally different stages:

1. **Encoder**: image/video/audio features are produced by a modality encoder.
2. **Prefill**: the language model processes the full multimodal prompt and builds KV cache.
3. **Decode**: autoregressive generation produces output tokens.

Traditional PD disaggregation couples Encoder with Prefill. This becomes inefficient when the same multimodal context appears repeatedly across turns, agent steps, or branch candidates. Separating Encoder from Prefill enables:

- independent scaling of visual encoder workers;
- reuse of visual features across turns and workflows;
- lower repeated prefill cost for multimodal prompts;
- more flexible routing for prefill-heavy versus decode-heavy workloads.

### Agent workflows require persistent state

Agent workloads are not simple one-shot requests. They involve:

- multi-turn conversations;
- external tool calls and long I/O waits;
- multi-branch reasoning such as Tree-of-Thought, beam search, and verifier branches;
- A2A handoff between planner, executor, retriever, tool agent, and verifier;
- repeated prefixes across workflow steps.

These patterns make KV state a first-class runtime object rather than a temporary per-request artifact.

### Mooncake is well positioned for this extension

Mooncake already focuses on disaggregated KVCache management and high-performance transfer. Extending it to EPD and agentic workflows is a natural next step because the same core primitives are needed:

- cross-node tensor transfer;
- distributed KVCache pooling;
- offload and restore;
- memory ownership;
- scheduling across heterogeneous workers;
- efficient movement of large intermediate states.

This RFC defines a practical architecture that can be implemented incrementally and reviewed in stages.

---

## Goals

This RFC has the following goals.

### G1. Support EPD disaggregation

- Separate Vision Encoder, Prefill, and Decode into independently schedulable workers.
- Transfer Encoder outputs to Prefill and Prefill KV pages to Decode through Mooncake Transfer Engine.
- Preserve fallback paths to normal colocated or PD-only execution.

### G2. Introduce a unified multimodal state abstraction

- Represent FeatureBundle, KVPage, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, leases, and TTL.
- Support snapshot-based state reads, page-level refcount, and Copy-on-Write.
- Provide clear lifecycle transitions for active, shared, offloaded, restored, released, and aborted states.

### G3. Support Agent State Cloning

- Enable low-cost fork for multi-branch reasoning.
- Avoid deep-copying full KV state for each branch.
- Make branch writes safe through page-level CoW.
- Make refcount correctness testable and observable.

### G4. Support cross-step KV reuse

- Use exact prefix reuse as the safe default.
- Add approximate or non-contiguous reuse behind validation gates and feature flags.
- Always preserve fallback to full Prefill.

### G5. Reduce control-plane bottlenecks

- Avoid a globally locked GDKR-style metadata service.
- Move refcount and CAS to workflow-local shards.
- Keep cross-workflow metadata eventually consistent with bounded staleness.
- Prevent a single hot workflow or global registry from throttling unrelated workflows.

### G6. Provide a reproducible evaluation protocol

- Define datasets, workload construction, ba

items.title: Deadlock risk between snapshot restore and segment mount (segment_mutex_ / client_mutex_ ordering)
items.author: quantz8a
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`MasterService::ApplySnapshotState()` reverses the lock order used by `MountSegment()` / `UnmountSegment()`, which can deadlock when snapshot restore races with a client mount or unmount.

## Affected path

- `ApplySnapshotState()` obtains an exclusive lock on `SegmentManager::segment_mutex_` via `segment_manager_.getSegmentAccess()` (`mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp:11232`).
- While still holding that lock it calls:
  - `UnmountSegment()` (`:11238`), and
  - `Ping(client_id)` (`:11248`).
- Both of those paths acquire `client_mutex_`:
  - `Ping()` does `std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> lock(client_mutex_)` (`:8405`).
  - `UnmountSegment()` does `std::shared_lock<std::shared_mutex> client_lock(client_mutex_)` (`:3127`) before re-acquiring `segment_mutex_` (`:3133`).

## Reverse order in the other callers

- `MountSegment()` first takes `client_mutex_` exclusively (`:900`) and then, inside its liveness callback, takes `snapshot_mutex_` and `segment_mutex_` via `segment_manager_.getSegmentAccess()` (`:909-:913`).
- `UnmountSegment()` takes `client_mutex_` before `segment_mutex_` as shown above.

So the code has both:

1. `segment_mutex_ (unique) -> client_mutex_ (shared)` in `ApplySnapshotState()`.
2. `client_mutex_ (unique) -> segment_mutex_ (unique)` in `MountSegment()`.

## Deadlock scenario

- Thread A is in `ApplySnapshotState()`: it holds `segment_mutex_` exclusively and blocks trying to take `client_mutex_` (via `Ping`).
- Thread B is in `MountSegment()`: it holds `client_mutex_` exclusively and blocks trying to take `segment_mutex_` (via `getSegmentAccess()`).

A and B wait on each other, forming a classic ABBA deadlock. The same inconsistent ordering exists for the snapshot-restore unmount path.

## Suggested fix

Do not call `UnmountSegment()` or `Ping()` while holding the snapshot-restore `segment_mutex_` hold. Collect the unready/all segment lists under `segment_mutex_`, release the lock, then unmount/ping/metric-update outside the lock. See the accompanying PR.
