items.title: [RFC]: Autoscaler-driven elastic EP: observe-first staging, membership semantics, and failure rules
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix's PodAutoscaler scales replicas, and for MoE serving that unit is coarse: one replica can span dozens of GPUs, and traffic rarely varies in whole-replica quanta. vLLM can now resize DP/EP membership at runtime (`enable_elastic_ep`, `POST /scale_elastic_ep`, `POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep`, plus the DP-coordinator wave protocol), and #2288 asks AIBrix to drive it, starting observe-only. This RFC proposes how that drive should work, staged as observe, act, and graceful draining, and focuses on the platform-side semantics that are missing today: aligning three divergent states (Kubernetes resources, engine-committed membership, routable capacity), treating an engine resize as a transaction inside a reconcile loop, and writing down failure rules before production discovers them. The proposal is deliberately conservative: default off, hold rather than auto-recover, never act on unverified state. The observe stage is already in flight (#2812); we are asking for feedback on the act-side semantics before implementing them.

### Motivation

Whole-replica scaling is coarse and expensive for MoE: one replica may span dozens of GPUs, and traffic variation is rarely a whole-replica quantum. The engine now exposes the levers to resize DP/EP membership at runtime, but nothing in AIBrix drives them. Existing platform attempts in this space are either heavy (new CRDs, gated off) or still exploratory, and the upstream external-orchestration contract is not frozen yet (vllm/vllm#42515, vllm/vllm#43202).

**Benefit hypothesis (to be measured).** Two effects decide whether elastic EP is worth enabling. Sub-replica demand changes can be absorbed inside a footprint instead of moving whole replicas, which makes capacity quantization finer and avoids provisioning for step peaks; and ramps can be served as soon as the engine commits new ranks, without waiting for new pods. The cost side is the commit window (the engine answers 503 while resizing) and the added control complexity this RFC addresses. Enabling is least attractive when demand is stable at whole-replica quanta or when the window is not acceptable for the served workload. We plan to measure the deciding axes on one node first (time to add capacity for a width move versus a replica move, GPU-hours per unit of served traffic under bursty load, and error budget consumed during commit windows); multi-footprint economics need a larger setup and remain future work.

Three properties make this harder than an HPA-style target:

1. **Three states, not one.** Kubernetes knows which pods and processes exist; the engine knows which ranks are committed; the router knows which endpoints can take traffic. These states move at different speeds and in different orders: during a scale-up, capacity exists before the engine accepts it; during scale-down, the engine stops first and capacity is reclaimed after; after a rank failure, the desired state is unchanged while the engine serves degraded. "Replica count" cannot express any of this.

2. **A transaction inside a control loop.** An engine resize is a one-shot operation that takes tens of seconds, has intermediate states, and has no generic rollback. Today's known upstream bugs include a cancel path that corrupts engine state without rollback (vllm/vllm#57691) and a scale-up crash under EAGLE3 + CUDA graphs (vllm/vllm#58479). Kubernetes reconciliation, by contrast, assumes idempotent, replayable steps with eventual convergence; it has no word for "commit or hold". That gap has to be designed rather than coded ad hoc.

3. **No failure vocabulary.** Every step can fail quietly: partial joins, a controller restarting mid-commit, outcomes that cannot be verified after a timeout. Writing down the required behavior for these cases is the core of this RFC.

### Proposed Change

| Stage | What it adds | State |
|---|---|---|
| 0: observe | record engine scaling state in PodAutoscaler status; no decisions | in flight (#2812) |
| 1: act | opt-in width changes with transaction discipline and gates | this RFC |
| 2: draining | gateway policy for the engine's 503 window | this RFC (design) |

**Stage 0: observe (in flight: #2812).** PodAutoscaler records whether a scaling commit is in progress on the target's elastic-EP engines in `status.elasticEPScaling` (`inProgress`, `observedEngines`, `scalingEngines`, `lastTransitionTime`; no width read exists yet). No replica decisions change. This gives operators visibility and gives the controller a trustworthy read path for Stage 1.

**Stage 1: act with guardrails (opt-in, default off).** For deployments that enable elastic EP and opt in:

1. Read the **committed** width from the engine; never trust the last requested value.
2. Use target semantics: ask the engine to *be N* (the engine call takes `new_data_parallel_size` and a `drain_timeout`, default 120s), not to add one, so retries and re-ordering are harmless.
3. Treat each call as a transaction inside reconcile: one bounded operation per attempt (call, wait for commit up to a bound, verify, record the outcome, continue).
4. Gate every operation: never act while the engine reports scaling; never act on degraded or partially committed membership; enforce a settle window and hysteresis so a tens-of-seconds operation cannot oscillate.
5. Re-read state every reconcile; the controller never trusts its own last command (level-triggered).
6. Single writer for width: while act mode is on, the controller is the intended single writer for width; other writers are outside this contract and are surfaced as drift (F7).

**Stage 2: graceful draining.** While a commit is in flight, the engine answers 503 to all requests, including readiness probes. In our single-node test (4 x RTX 4090 48G, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DP 2 to 4) the window lasted 37.2s on scale-up and 15.3s on scale-down; the raw evidence is recorded in #2812. The window affects the data plane of the deployment as a whole, not only the resized ranks. AIBrix holds the autoscal

items.title: [Feature][Gateway] Decode watchdog for SGLang PD requests whose decode pod stops responding
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

With SGLang PD disaggregation, the prefill request only returns once the decode pod has accepted the KV transfer. So when the gateway's prefill leg succeeds, the decode pod owes the client a response.

If the decode pod stops answering at that point, nothing in the gateway notices. This happens when its scheduler dies or wedges, either before the first token or in the middle of a stream.
- The client waits until Envoy's route timeout. For streaming LLM routes that timeout is usually very long or disabled.
- The routing context, and the load it holds on the chosen pods, stays live for the whole wait.
- The decode pod keeps the request's KV pages, because nobody tells it to drop the request.

The PD fail-fast path covers a prefill leg that fails. Nothing covers a decode leg that goes silent after a successful prefill.

### Use Case

SGLang PD deployments behind the aibrix gateway, where a decode pod can hang without its container exiting. Without a bound, such a pod turns every request routed to it into a client-side hang instead of a fast, retryable error.

### Proposed Solution

Add a decode watchdog to the ext_proc stream loop. It is armed only for requests that carry a gateway-owned `rid` (SGLang PD), and it has two phases.

1. **First response.** After the prefill leg succeeds, the decode pod has to send its first message within:
   - `AIBRIX_DECODE_FIRST_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT` for a streaming request (default 60s);
   - `AIBRIX_DECODE_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT` for a non-streaming request (default 0, off). Here the first message is the finished answer, so a safe value depends on `max_tokens`.

   On expiry the client gets a 504 with `x-error-pd-decode: true`, and the ext_proc stream is closed with `DeadlineExceeded`.

2. **Stream idle.** After the decode pod has started answering, `AIBRIX_DECODE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (default 120s) bounds the gap between two of its messages. Every message re-arms it.

   The response is already half-delivered, so no error response can be sent. Instead the ext_proc stream is closed with `DeadlineExceeded`, and Envoy resets the connection.

In both phases:
- the gateway sends one best-effort `/abort_request` for the `rid` to the decode pod;
- the request is counted as failed with `status="pd_decode_watchdog"`;
- a new counter `gateway_pd_decode_watchdog_total{phase}` records the kill;
- every timeout can be overridden per config profile under `routingConfig.pd`, and `0` disables it.

Planned as two PRs:
- first response (504 + abort);
- stream idle (stream reset + abort).

Each PR comes with unit tests, a mock-engine e2e test and docs.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: Runtime and metadata-service nightly images are unexpectedly large (~970 MB)
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

The current ARM64 nightly images for `aibrix/runtime` and `aibrix/metadata-service` are both approximately 970 MB unpacked:

```text
aibrix/runtime:nightly           970MB
aibrix/metadata-service:nightly  970MB
```

This appears unusually large for the runtime and metadata-service processes and is worth investigating.

Both images are built from `build/container/Dockerfile.python`, which installs the dependencies declared by the AIBrix Python wheel. The largest image layer is the `pip install` layer at approximately 814 MB.

## Measurements

| Component | Approximate size |
|---|---:|
| Debian + Python base layers | 156 MB |
| Final `pip install` layer | 814 MB |
| `site-packages` | 844 MiB |

The largest installed distributions are:

| Distribution | Size |
|---|---:|
| scipy | 142 MiB |
| pandas | 74 MiB |
| numpy | 59 MiB |
| plotly | 58 MiB |
| scikit-learn | 55 MiB |
| PuLP | 38 MiB |
| matplotlib | 37 MiB |
| dash | 32 MiB |
| kubernetes | 30 MiB |

Most of the scientific-computing and visualization imports appear under `aibrix.gpu_optimizer`, rather than the runtime or metadata-service entry points. Their installed dependency closure accounts for approximately 584 MiB.

There is also a mismatch between the Dockerfile comment and the package metadata: the Dockerfile says the profiling group is excluded to avoid packages such as pandas and matplotlib, but those packages are currently declared as main dependencies in `python/aibrix/pyproject.toml`. Therefore, `--without profiling` does not exclude them.

The two image names are also built independently from the same Dockerfile. In the inspected nightly builds, their large dependency layers have different digests, so those layers are not shared even though their installed contents and sizes are nearly identical.

## Impact

- Longer image pull and node startup times
- More registry and node storage usage
- Slower scale-out and cold starts for runtime workers
- Longer CI image builds and duplicate uploads
- Larger dependency and vulnerability-scanning surface

## Possible Changes

The exact implementation should be decided after confirming the dependency requirements of every published entry point. Possible changes include:

- Audit direct and transitive dependencies for `aibrix_runtime`, `aibrix_metadata`, `aibrix_batch_worker`, downloader, and GPU Optimizer.
- Adjust Python package metadata and container build targets so each published image installs only the dependencies required by the processes it runs.
- Preserve the storage backends and Kubernetes integrations currently supported by each entry point.
- If two published images remain identical, build the image once and apply both tags so their layers have the same digest.
- Correct the stale Dockerfile comment about excluded dependencies.
- Add image-size reporting or a regression threshold to CI, together with container smoke tests for the affected entry points.

The GPU Optimizer currently runs from `aibrix/metadata-service:nightly`, so any dependency changes must also update or preserve that deployment path.

## Environment

- Architecture: ARM64
- Tags: `nightly`
- Observed image sizes: approximately 970 MB each

items.title: [Bug] ModelAdapter ignores matchExpressions in podSelector
items.author: btxu-db
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The ModelAdapter controller ignores `matchExpressions` in `spec.podSelector`. `getActivePodsForModelAdapter` lists pods with `client.MatchingLabels(instance.Spec.PodSelector.MatchLabels)`, so only `matchLabels` reaches the List call.

What this does in practice:

- A selector with only `matchExpressions` has empty `matchLabels`, so it matches every pod in the namespace. The adapter gets loaded on pods running a different base model.
- A selector that uses both picks up pods the expressions should have excluded.

`ModelClaim` already converts its selector with `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector`, so the two controllers behave differently for the same kind of selector.

### Steps to Reproduce

kind, AIBrix from `main`, `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app` as the engine.

Three Deployments in one namespace, one pod each, labeled:

- `base-stable`: `model=base, tier=stable`
- `base-canary`: `model=base, tier=canary`
- `other-model`: `model=other`

Two adapters:

```yaml
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelAdapter
metadata:
  name: lora-expr-only
spec:
  baseModel: base
  podSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: model, operator: In, values: [base]}
  artifactURL: /models/lora-expr-only
---
apiVersion: model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: ModelAdapter
metadata:
  name: lora-mixed
spec:
  baseModel: base
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: {model: base}
    matchExpressions:
    - {key: tier, operator: NotIn, values: [canary]}
  artifactURL: /models/lora-mixed
```

Result:

```
NAME             PHASE     CANDIDATES   INSTANCES
lora-expr-only   Running   3            [other-model-... base-stable-... base-canary-...]
lora-mixed       Running   2            [base-canary-... base-stable-...]
```

`/v1/models` on the pods confirms the adapters were actually loaded there: `other-model` has `lora-expr-only`, and `base-canary` has `lora-mixed`.

### Expected behavior

The full selector should be used, same as for any other `LabelSelector`. `lora-expr-only` should land on `base-stable` and `base-canary` only, and `lora-mixed` on `base-stable` only.

Fix is to build the selector with `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector` and pass it with `client.MatchingLabelsSelector`. I have a patch for this and will open a PR.

### Environment

- AIBrix: `main` @ `dcc8aa9a`
- Kubernetes: kind v1.30.0, 1 control-plane + 1 worker
- Engine: `aibrix/vllm-mock:nightly` from `development/app`

### Area

ModelAdapter / LoRA

items.title: [Feat] Report unavailable gateway model discovery from /v1/models
items.author: abe-servescale
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description and Motivation

The gateway plugin's `GET /v1/models` reads an informer-derived cache. If Kubernetes discovery stops making progress after initial synchronization, the endpoint can return HTTP 200 with stale model names or an apparently valid empty list. During initial synchronization the HTTP listener is not yet open, so the plugin cannot return a structured unavailable response.

### Use Case

An operator routes the plugin's model list to clients and needs to distinguish a verified empty list from a discovery failure. A missed Pod deletion or readiness update must not remain a successful stale response indefinitely, even in a quiet cluster.

### Proposed Solution

- Add an opt-in maximum verification age for the plugin's model list; the default remains unchanged.
- Keep client-go informers as the normal discovery path. When the last proof expires, a model-list request obtains a bounded, complete Kubernetes snapshot of Pods and enabled ModelAdapters and compares object identities and resource versions with events applied to the gateway cache. Coalesce concurrent checks and avoid background polling when there are no list requests.
- Return HTTP 503 with the gateway's JSON error envelope when the snapshot cannot be verified. A healthy empty installation still returns HTTP 200 with `data: []`. A reported watch error invalidates the previous proof, while the maximum age also bounds stale responses from a silent watch stall.
- Open the plugin HTTP listener before initial discovery completes so requests reaching it receive the same 503 until the cache is usable. Keep inference and gRPC readiness gated on normal initialization.

The change applies to the plugin's model-list endpoint. A front proxy remains responsible when no gateway process or ready Service endpoint is reachable. It does not verify adapter load status or routing availability.

### Acceptance

Cover healthy and empty lists, missed Pod deletion, watch errors, API failures, timeout, recovery, disabled adapter discovery, startup 503, and concurrent requests. Keep the default behavior and non-list cache consumers unchanged.

This is separate from #2912 and PR #2913, which cover optional discovery sources and Ready-Pod listing but explicitly do not add ongoing discovery health.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [PyTorch backend][encoder-decoder] KvCacheConfig(dtype="fp8") overruns the cross-attention KV pool: illegal memory access or silently wrong output unless the pool is 2x the required size
items.author: lminer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With an encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend, setting the KV cache dtype to `fp8` makes
the cross-attention cache access memory beyond its pool. A request only succeeds when the
cross-attention pool holds at least **twice** the blocks the in-flight requests need. Below that
the process either dies with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` or, when the
stray access lands in other mapped memory, returns wrong tokens with no error. The same pool
sizes work with the default cache dtype.

## Environment

- Images: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29` and
  `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.4.0rc0.dev202610040000` (both reproduce)
- GPU: NVIDIA L4 (24 GB), driver 595.91.07; AWS g6.2xlarge
- Model: `google/flan-t5-base`, weights loaded as bf16
- `LLM(backend="pytorch", ...)`, block reuse off, no CUDA graphs

## Reproduction

The prompt is 483 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool. With
`cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5`, `max_tokens=768` gives a 24-block pool and `max_tokens=1024` a
32-block pool (the log line `Max KV cache blocks per sequence: 16 [window size=512], tokens per
block=32, primary blocks=24` confirms the sizes).

```bash
docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host -v $PWD:/w nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29 \
  python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 768     # crashes on the first request
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 1024    # decodes
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py auto 768    # decodes (default cache dtype, same pool)
```

| KV dtype | `max_tokens` | cross pool blocks | blocks needed | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp8 | 768 | 24 | 16 | `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` |
| fp8 | 1024 | 32 | 16 | OK |
| auto | 768 | 24 | 16 | OK |

After the error the process does not exit by itself; it has to be killed.

`fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py`:

```python
"""Encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend: an FP8 KV cache overruns the cross-attention pool.

    python3 fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py <kv dtype: fp8|auto> <kv max_tokens>

The prompt is ~480 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

from tensorrt_llm import LLM, SamplingParams
from tensorrt_llm.llmapi import KvCacheConfig


def main():
    kv_dtype, kv_tokens = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
    # The backend takes the weight dtype from the checkpoint's config.json, so write a bf16 copy.
    src = snapshot_download("google/flan-t5-base", allow_patterns=["*.json", "*.model", "model.safetensors"])
    ckpt = "/tmp/flan-t5-base-bf16"
    os.makedirs(ckpt, exist_ok=True)
    for name in os.listdir(src):
        if name != "config.json" and not os.path.exists(f"{ckpt}/{name}"):
            os.symlink(os.path.realpath(f"{src}/{name}"), f"{ckpt}/{name}")
    config = json.load(open(f"{src}/config.json"))
    config["torch_dtype"] = config["dtype"] = "bfloat16"
    json.dump(config, open(f"{ckpt}/config.json", "w"))

    llm = LLM(
        model=ckpt,
        backend="pytorch",
        max_batch_size=1,
        max_beam_width=1,
        max_input_len=512,
        max_seq_len=2048,
        kv_cache_config=KvCacheConfig(
            enable_block_reuse=False, max_tokens=kv_tokens, cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5, dtype=kv_dtype
        ),
        cuda_graph_config=None,
    )
    prompt = "summarize: " + "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank. " * 30
    print("prompt tokens:", len(llm.tokenizer.encode(prompt)), flush=True)
    params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=32)
    for i in range(3):
        out = llm.generate(prompt, params)
        print(f"request {i}: {list(out.outputs[0].token_ids)[:12]} {out.outputs[0].text[:60]!r}", flush=True)
    print("OK", kv_dtype, kv_tokens)
    llm.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## More than one request in flight

The same rule holds with several requests submitted together. Measured on rc29 with a second,
larger encoder-decoder model, a batch of requests that needs 752 blocks in total:

| cross pool blocks | result |
|---|---|
| 768 | illegal memory access (also on the 1.4.0 nightly) |
| 896 | illegal memory access |
| 1,024 | **no error, wrong output**: every request runs to `max_tokens`, none matches the same request decoded alone |
| 1,280 | illegal memory access |
| 1,536 | OK |

So the threshold is 2 x 752 = 1,504 blocks. With the default cache dtype, 768 blocks are enough.
Admitting the requests one at a time only helps because fewer are then in flight together.

With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` that run reports the failure in the cross-attention context pass:

```
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/cross_attention.py", line 268, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/trtllm.py", line 2330, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/fmha/fallback.py", line 122, in forward
    thop.attention(
RuntimeError: [TensorRT-LLM][ERROR] CUDA runtime error in cudaStreamIsCapturing(stream, &status): an illegal memory access was encountered (../include/tensorrt_llm/common/cudaUtils.h:157)
  tensorrt_llm::common::op::AttentionOp::enqueueContext<__half, tensorrt_llm::kernels::KVBlockArray>(...)
```

## Expected

Either the FP8 cross-attention cache stays inside a pool sized for the requests (as the default
dtype does), or the configuration is rejected for encoder-decoder models. An out-of-range access
should not be able to return wrong tokens silently.

## Guess at the cause

The 2x factor suggests the cross-attention pool is allocated at one byte per element (FP8) while
the cross-attention kernel addresses it with a two-byte element size. Not verified in the source.

## Also seen

With the FP8 cache and a large enough pool, on the larger model the first request after start-up
returns different tokens from the identical request sent again (every run). This does not happen
wit

items.title: [BUG | QST] CPU overhead regression with TVM-FFI
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
In v4.6 update, the following is changed in `python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/cutlass_dsl/cutlass.py`:
```
-                if kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults:
+                # Route through the kwargs-capable compiled class whenever
+                # the signature has kwonly/defaults OR any positional arg
+                # carries a dataclass instance (detected by the spec
+                # converter, including Union[...] over dataclasses). The
+                # kwargs wrapper is the only place tvm-ffi's
+                # ``map_dataclass_to_tuple`` unpack hook fires.
+                if (
+                    kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_names
+                    or map_dataclass_to_tuple
+                ):
```
So basically if a @cute.jit function satisfies one of the following:
- `kwonly_names`: have keyword only arguments (indicated by *)
- `arg_defaults`: have default arguments
- `arg_names`: have any argument that is not a keyword only argument
- `map_dataclass_to_tuple`: have dataclass arguments

With these restrictions (especially `kwonly_names` and `arg_names`), basically only a CuTeDSL function with no arguments can go to the else branch and become a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` which is a subclass of `tvm_ffi.Function` so they get to be called in C++ and bypass python completely. For CuTeDSL functions with arguments, they now have to go through the `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs` path.

This will slightly slow down calling a CuTeDSL function from python due to extra python layers from in `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs`, which isn't a big deal since python is slow anyway. However, if you register the CuTeDSL function via tvm-ffi and call it from C++, the overhead becomes obvious because you will leave C++ and enter python (`TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs.__call__`) and then enter the compiled CuTeDSL function. This makes the CPU overhead regress compared to pre-4.6 version since there wasn't going through python with GIL and argument wrapper stuff.

I also wonder what's the motivation behind this. My guess is this makes a @cute.jit function behave more like a python function where it can use kwargs instead of can only be called using positional args, but meanwhile when we do want to call it with positional args (in C++) this only makes it slower.

Currently there is a hack to fix this, which is instead of registering the compiled CuTeDSL function, we can register its `__tvm_ffi_object__` which would be a `tvm_ffi.Function` object, and we need to guarantee the args order is exactly the same in C++. I feel it's a bit hacky and fragile as cutlass evolves. 

Another proposition of mine is we can tell users (probably in docs) that if they define CuTeDSL functions in this format: `def func(a, b, c, /)` with nothing after / and no default values, then we can optimize this case into a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` because we know nobody will use kwargs in this case. I think if this fix is OK I can open a PR on it.

Not sure what's the opinion of the CUTLASS people?

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
I think my explanation should be clear enough so I don't think I need an example to reproduce.
You can just follow the example in https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3289 and measure the CPU time to notice the difference.

**Expected behavior**
Should be faster?

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
This regressed after v4.6 update

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

But per our benchmark, the overhead it introduces is < 1us, while the overall launch overhead is typically <10 us. We think it is fine to keep this overhead for compatibility of diversed inputs. items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. That line loads the block-sparse count and index tensors: `curr_q_cnt = q_cnt[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block]` and `q_idx[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block, None]`. #3701 found the same kind of small metadata-tensor load for the forward kernel (`cu_seqlens` in the varlen scheduler). Here the IMAD count rises together with the spills (document mask: 653 → 1049). We suspect the address arithmetic of these indexed loads, but have not verified it.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

The attached `nvvm23-sm100-bwd-repro.zip` has the scripts, the nine PTX files and our raw results. Its README has more detail.

*1. No GPU needed.* Assemble the attached PTX pair:

```
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.5.3.nvvm20.ptx -o /dev/null
    16 bytes stack frame, 28 bytes spill stores, 16 bytes spill loads
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.6.0.dev0.nvvm23.ptx -o /dev/null
    152 bytes stack frame, 204 bytes spill stores, 204 bytes spill loads
```

*2. On a B200: time the backward* with the script below (FA4 through `flex_attention`, about 50 lines), once per environment:

```
python3.12 -m venv nvvm20 && . nvvm20/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.3 quack-kernels==0.5.0 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.11
python minimal_repro.py

python3.12 -m venv nvvm23 && . nvvm23/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b20 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0.dev0 quack-kernels==0.5.3 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.12
python minimal_repro.py
```

import torch

items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

items.title: [SM120] sparse MLA MG prefill kernel races on `w_head_sc_all` in released versions (fixed on main by #5197, please backport)
items.author: gavinkvx
items.body_excerpt:
**Affected:** `sparse_mla_prefill_mg_kernel` (SM120 sparse MLA prefill, more than 64 query tokens, models without V rope such as the DSv3.2 path) in v0.6.18 and v0.7.0.post1.

**Cause:** each KV tile's XV MMA reads the per-head V scales in `sm.w_head_sc_all`. Nothing makes the next tile wait for those reads before it zeroes the buffer and rebuilds it.

- In 0.6.18, the SG kernel has the barrier: `if constexpr (!KV::V_HAS_ROPE) bar_sync_t<2, MATH_THREADS>();` at `prefill_kernel.cuh:513`. The MG kernel has no equivalent before its `bar_arrive_alt` (`:1517`).
- On main, after #5197, the reset is preceded by `RoleSync<MATH>::wait()` ("All prior XV readers retired"). That fixes it, but no release includes it.

**Evidence** (RTX 5090, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.13, flashinfer 0.6.18; I also checked the v0.7.0.post1 source, which has the same pattern):

- compute-sanitizer racecheck reports ≥9.9M hazards, with the write at `prefill_kernel.cuh:936` (zeroing) and the read at `:1454` (XV MMA). With the barrier there are 0.
- With `kv_scale_format="pow2_fp32"`, 2000 out of 2000 identical calls give a different result from the first call: about 74 rows × 8–16 heads differ, relative error around 0.1. With the barrier, 0 out of 2000 differ.
- The barrier costs about 1.5% in kernel time.

**Repro**

```python
import torch, flashinfer
from flashinfer.mla import trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla
torch.manual_seed(0); dev = "cuda"; T, CTX, H, K, P = 2048, 24576, 64, 2048, 64
nope = torch.randn(CTX, 4, 128, device=dev) * 0.5
sc = torch.exp2(torch.ceil(torch.log2(nope.abs().amax(-1, keepdim=True).clamp(min=1e-4) / 448)))
kv = torch.cat([(nope / sc).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).view(torch.uint8).reshape(CTX, 512),
                sc.reshape(CTX, 4).contiguous().view(torch.uint8),
                (torch.randn(CTX, 64, device=dev) * 0.5).to(torch.bfloat16).view(torch.uint8)], 1)
kv = kv.view(CTX // P, 1, P, 656)
pos = torch.arange(CTX - T, CTX, device=dev)
key = torch.rand(T, CTX, device=dev); key[torch.arange(CTX, device=dev)[None] > pos[:, None]] = 2
idx = key.topk(K, 1, largest=False).indices.sort(1).values.int()
q = (torch.randn(T, 1, H, 576, device=dev) * 0.5).bfloat16()
ws = torch.zeros(128 << 20, dtype=torch.uint8, device=dev)
run = lambda: trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla(
    query=q, kv_cache=kv, workspace_buffer=ws, qk_nope_head_dim=128, kv_lora_rank=512,
    qk_rope_head_dim=64, block_tables=idx.unsqueeze(1), seq_lens=torch.full((T,), K, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev),
    max_seq_len=K, sparse_mla_top_k=K, bmm1_scale=576 ** -0.5, backend="sparse", kv_scale_format="pow2_fp32")
ref = run().clone()
print(sum(not torch.equal(run().view(torch.int16), ref.view(torch.int16)) for _ in range(200)), "/ 200 runs differ")
```

**Ask:** please backport the `w_head_sc_all` reset ordering from #5197 to the release branch, or cut a patch release that includes it.

items.title: torch.fx.Tracer.record_stack_traces is broken in torch 2.4.0
items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)

items.title: native_aot topk: ARCHS manifest excludes sm_103 (GB300/Blackwell Ultra), AOT routing silently declines
items.author: nWEIdia
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`torch/_native/ops/topk/aot.py`'s `ARCHS` manifest (added in #190899) lists `sm_90`, `sm_90a`, `sm_100`, `sm_100a`, but not `sm_103`/`sm_103a` (GB300 / "Blackwell Ultra"). Per the native-AOT framework's documented contract (`tools/native_aot/decl.py`), codegen emits a runtime device gate from `ARCHS ∩ shipped-arches` that runs *before* any of topk's own coverage logic. Since GB300 isn't in `ARCHS`, that generated gate declines AOT routing unconditionally on GB300, even though topk's own coverage checks (`_kernel_for`, `cpp_covers`, etc.) only key on `major >= 10` and would otherwise treat GB300 (major=10) as covered, same as GB200/B200.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_native/ops/topk/aot.py#L20
```python
ARCHS = ("sm_90", "sm_90a", "sm_100", "sm_100a")
```

## Repro

On a GB300 node (`torch.cuda.get_device_capability()` → `(10, 3)`), with a nightly wheel that embeds the native-AOT topk kernels (`torch._native._native_aot_embedded()` → `True`):

```python
import torch
x = torch.randn(256, 2048, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.profiler.profile(activities=[torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    v, i = torch.topk(x, 64, dim=-1)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
print([e.name for e in prof.events() if e.device_type.name == "CUDA"])
```
Expected (per the grid declared in `aot.py`, N=2048/K=64/fp32 is squarely inside it): a `RadixSelectTopK` kernel launch.
Actual: falls straight through to stock ATen (`sbtopk::gatherTopK`), no DSL kernel attempted, no error.

This is visible in CI as `test/python_native/test_native_aot.py::TestNativeAotTopK` failures on a GB300 runner (`smoke_b200` config), e.g.:
- `test_covered_grid_routes_to_aot`
- `test_deterministic_mode_routes_to_aot_bit_exact`
- `test_dynamic_n_and_work_rungs_route_to_aot`
- `test_register_grid_routing`
- `test_manifest_covers_matches_grid`
- `test_flags_the_stub_declines_are_uncovered`
- `test_out_variant_routes_to_aot`

all with `AssertionError: ... AOT kernel did not fire for {...}`.

## Fix

Add `"sm_103", "sm_103a"` to `ARCHS` in `torch/_native/ops/topk/aot.py`. The per-arch CuTeDSL export loop in `tools/native_aot/toolchains.py` (`cute.compile(..., options=f"--gpu-arch {arch}")`) is already generic per declared arch, so this should just compile and embed the additional target once declared — no other code changes expected.

## Related but distinct

This looks superficially similar to #199514 (NVUniversalGemm defaulting to `sm_100` when no explicit `target_sm` is passed, also surfacing on non-sm_100 Blackwell variants), but the mechanism is different: that one is a missing runtime `target_sm` argument in an inductor backend; this one is a static build-time `ARCHS` allowlist in the native-AOT kernel-export framework that simply hasn't been updated for GB300 yet. Worth fixing independently.

Also confirmed the *JIT* topk override (not AOT) is unaffected — it JIT-compiles against the actual device at runtime and fires correctly on GB300 once `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`/`nvidia-cutlass-operators` are installed, with no `ARCHS` restriction.

## Versions

Initially detected while NVIDIA is enabling GB300 runner CI, via https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/37070045735/job/111063515379?pr=197769 (PR https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/197769). Also reproduced manually with a nightly build of `torch==2.15.0.dev20261004+cu134` (aarch64), CUDA 13.4, on a GB300 node.

cc @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @tinglvv @arjkesh @fbxai @malfet @atalman

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected op` in backward-slice when `tl.gather` feeds `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
A `tl.gather` result used as a `tl.dot` operand inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass at `WSDataPartition.cpp:330` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected op")`) during backward-slice partitioning — `tt.gather` is not in the op whitelist. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        idx = tl.full([M, K], 1, tl.int32)
        a = tl.gather(a, idx, axis=1)          # gather result feeds tl.dot
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:330!
```

## Root cause
`getBackwardSliceToPartition`'s op whitelist does not include `tt.gather`; reaching it hits `llvm_unreachable` rather than a graceful "unsupported" diagnostic. The identical kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()` with `tl.atomic_add` after `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
`tl.atomic_add` on the dot accumulator written **after** `acc += tl.dot` inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts at `WSDataPartition.cpp:775` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()")`) — the atomic carries a task-id count the sliceOp dispatch does not handle. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
        tl.atomic_add(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)   # atomic AFTER dot, on acc
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:775!
```

## Root cause
Inside `WSDataPartition.cpp`'s `sliceOp`, the per-task-id dispatch assumes a fixed set of `asyncTaskIds.size()` values; the atomic-on-accumulator produces a count outside the handled set and hits `llvm_unreachable`. The kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [RFC]: Control-plane orchestration of vLLM sleep mode and kvcached for warm standby and multi-model GPU pooling
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix scales replicas as 0-or-N and only *observes* engine memory state; it never drives it. Two engine-side mechanisms now make GPU memory reclaimable at runtime — vLLM **sleep mode** (park a whole idle model's weights+KV) and **kvcached** (elastically shrink/grow a model's KV so several models share one GPU) — but both are mechanism-only, with no control plane. This RFC proposes AIBrix own the *policy*: a control-plane-driven "warm/asleep" tier between one replica and zero, plus KV-budget arbitration across co-resident models. The result: multi-minute cold starts become second-scale wakes, and one GPU can densely host many long-tail models.

### Motivation

Scaling is binary today. To reclaim a GPU we either keep a replica running (burning HBM while idle) or delete the pod and pay a multi-minute cold start (weight load + CUDA graph capture) when traffic returns. Neither fits bursty or long-tail traffic.

The engine now exposes the levers, but not the policy:

| | vLLM sleep mode | kvcached (github.com/ovg-project/kvcached) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | whole model (weights + KV) | KV cache only (weights allocated outside it) |
| Granularity | all-or-nothing, single process | page-level elastic, cross-process co-residency |
| Target | a fully **idle** model | several **active** models sharing a GPU |
| Mechanism | CUDA VMM; `/sleep` `/wake_up`; level 1 weights→CPU, level 2 discard | CUDA VMM; per-process `cudaMemGetInfo` headroom + `/dev/shm` budget via `kvctl` |
| Control | manual API only; `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`-gated; no autoscaling | decentralized by design; no scheduler/admission/cross-node; `controller/` is a demo |

They are complementary: kvcached handles elastic KV among active co-resident models; sleep parks idle models' weights. Both are VMM actuators that enforce/observe — neither *decides*. The missing piece is a control plane that decides **which** model sleeps/wakes and **when**, **how much** KV budget each co-resident model gets, **admission** when a GPU is oversubscribed, and **routing/readiness** as models move between awake / warm / asleep. AIBrix already scrapes `vllm:engine_sleep_state` but never acts on it, and has no notion of co-resident KV budget — so it is the natural owner.

### Proposed Change

(Sketch only; full design — CRD, state machine, budget algorithm, agent protocol — to follow in a complete doc.)

1. A **warm/asleep lifecycle state** between `minReplicas` and zero: low traffic → `POST /sleep?level=1&mode=wait` (graceful drain); traffic returns → `/wake_up` (seconds). Pod/IP/endpoint persist.
2. A **KV-budget arbiter** across co-resident models, driving `kvctl` limits by policy (per-model min/max/share, priority) with cost-asymmetric reclaim — shrink KV first (cheap), sleep weights only when protected floors don't fit (expensive).
3. A **decide/execute split**: a Go controller (placement, admission, sleep/wake & budget policy, status) over a pod-side agent (kvcached engine, `kvctl`, sleep).
4. **Required couplings:** invalidate the prefix index on sleep (KV is wiped — see the sleep/prefix-index bug), exclude asleep pods from routing/readiness, and document the `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE` requirement.

### Alternatives Considered

- **HPA scale-to-zero** (`minReplicas=0`): already supported, but pays the full cold start and has no warm tier.
- **Leave it to kvcached's decentralized scheme:** works on a single node but has no admission/priority/cross-node policy and no sleep orchestration — precisely the demo `controller/` AIBrix would replace.
- **Token-level time-sharing** (swap at request granularity): higher utilization ceiling but far more complex/intrusive; this RFC targets model-granularity pooling.

items.title: [Bug]: AutoDeploy logger treats verbose and internal_error as info
items.author: adenzhou1350
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main at `b8e337d939cde1b7aa65feb5287e5bdefa02154b`
- Python 3.12 and 3.14
- Reproduced on Linux and Windows
- CPU-only; no GPU or model is involved

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`ADLogger` defines AutoDeploy-specific severities and maps `verbose` to `logging.DEBUG` and `internal_error` to `logging.CRITICAL` in `log()`. The environment-variable path and `set_level()` instead use `getattr(logging, ...)`, so these same public severity names silently fall back to INFO.

```python
import logging
from tensorrt_llm._torch.auto_deploy.utils.logger import ADLogger

logger = ADLogger()
logger.set_level("verbose")
print(logger._logger.level)  # 20 (INFO), expected 10 (DEBUG)

logger.set_level("internal_error")
print(logger._logger.level)  # 20 (INFO), expected 50 (CRITICAL)
```

The same mismatch occurs when `AUTO_DEPLOY_LOG_LEVEL` is set before importing the module. Standard levels such as `warning` work as expected.

### Expected behavior

All public AutoDeploy severity names should resolve consistently in `log()`, `set_level()`, and `AUTO_DEPLOY_LOG_LEVEL`: `verbose` should select DEBUG and `internal_error` should select CRITICAL. Unknown strings can continue to fall back to INFO.

### actual behavior

Both AutoDeploy-specific names resolve to INFO in `set_level()` and the environment-variable initialization path, so verbose logs stay hidden and internal errors lose their intended severity.

### additional notes

I searched open and closed issues/PRs and did not find an exact duplicate. A minimal fix can reuse `_SEVERITY_TO_LEVEL` for all three paths and add a CPU-only regression test. I have reproduced the baseline/fix differential on current main and can submit the patch if this issue is approved, per the contribution policy. The behavior remains present even though AutoDeploy is being redirected toward the standalone backend.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [New Model]: Apertus (swiss-ai/Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509, swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B)
items.author: maxwbuckley
items.body_excerpt:
### The model to consider.

`swiss-ai/Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509` (`ApertusForCausalLM`) and the text path of `swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B` (`Apertus1p5ForConditionalGeneration`), from the Swiss AI initiative. Both are fully open models supporting more than 1,800 languages.

### The closest model TensorRT-LLM already supports.

Llama / Qwen3: a Llama-style dense decoder with per-head QK-norm (as in Qwen3) and llama3 RoPE scaling.

### What's your difficulty of supporting the model you want?

- A non-gated MLP with the xIELU activation ([arXiv 2411.13010](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13010)), which has two coefficients learned per layer.
- The existing fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel doesn't implement llama3 scaling.
- Apertus 1.5 ships as a multimodal checkpoint (decoder under `model.language_model.`). Its input embedding is larger than its output head, and its config type isn't in the pinned transformers.

An implementation is in #19735, with an optional CUDA xIELU op in #19737.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.author: Amineki6
items.body_excerpt:
### The model to consider.

aleph-alpha/kolibri-1 ( Kolibri1ForCausalLM ), from Aleph Alpha. 

It's an open, modern fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model.


### The closest model TensorRT-LLM already supports.

Qwen3MoeForCausalLM: shares per-head QK RMSNorm, fine-grained routed experts executed via TRT-LLM's fused MoE engine, and a shared expert (GatedMLP).


### What's your difficulty of supporting the model you want?

- **Alternating Attention Pattern**: 4 Sliding Window Attention (SWA, `sliding_window: 513`) layers alternating with 1 Full Attention layer with RNoPE (No Positional Encoding / skips RoPE).
- **Biased Sigmoid Routing**: Expert selection uses Top-k over $(\mathrm{logits} + \mathrm{expert\_bias})$, while expert weights are raw $\mathrm{sigmoid}(\mathrm{logits})$ without bias and without normalization (`norm_topk_prob: false`).
- **4-Norm Sandwich Structure**: Each decoder layer applies sandwich RMSNorms after attention (`post_attn_norm`) and after MoE (`post_ffn_norm`) before residual accumulation.
- **Fine-Grained MoE**: 384 routed experts (top-6 activated per token) + 1 shared expert, with intermediate size 512.

An implementation is prepared in a linked Draft PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: pycute left_inverse returns a different canonical layout than CuTe C++
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

pycute (`python/pycute`, the pure-Python reference implementation), not the CuTe DSL

### Describe the bug

`pycute.left_inverse` returns a different canonical layout than `cute::left_inverse` in `include/cute/layout.hpp` for non-contiguous and hierarchical inputs. Both results are valid left inverses on the image of the layout (applying them to `layout(i)` recovers `i`), so this is a fidelity gap between the Python reference and the C++ implementation rather than a broken inverse. Anyone using pycute to cross-check CuTe semantics gets different shapes/strides exactly in the interesting cases.

`python/pycute/layout.py` implements

```python
def left_inverse(layout):
  ...
  return right_inverse(make_layout(layout, complement(layout)))
```

while the C++ side uses a dedicated sort-by-stride algorithm (`left_inverse` at `include/cute/layout.hpp`, with a divisibility static assert and an explicit stride-0 skip).

### Steps to reproduce

Python (main):

```python
from pycute import *
print(left_inverse(Layout(4,2)))
print(left_inverse(Layout((4,2),(1,16))))
print(left_inverse(Layout(((2,2),(2,2)),((1,4),(8,32)))))
```

C++ (host-only, g++ against include/):

```cpp
#include <cute/tensor.hpp>
#include <iostream>
using namespace cute;
int main() {
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<_4>,        Stride<_2>>{}));        print("\n");
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<_4,_2>,     Stride<_1,_16>>{}));    print("\n");
  print(left_inverse(Layout<Shape<Shape<_2,_2>,Shape<_2,_2>>,
                        Stride<Stride<_1,_4>,Stride<_8,_32>>>{}));    print("\n");
}
```

Comparison gathered on main:

| input | C++ `left_inverse` | pycute `left_inverse` |
|---|---|---|
| `4:1` | `_4:_1` | `4:1` (agree) |
| `4:2` | `(_2,_4):(_0,_1)` | `(2,4):(4,1)` |
| `1:0` | `_1:_0` | `1:0` (agree) |
| `(8,4):(1,8)` | `_32:_1` | `32:1` (agree) |
| `(8,4):(4,1)` | `(_4,_8):(_8,_1)` | `(4,8):(8,1)` (agree) |
| `(2,4,6):(1,2,8)` | `_48:_1` | `48:1` (agree) |
| `(2,4,6):(4,1,8)` | `(_4,_2,_6):(_2,_1,_8)` | `(4,2,6):(2,1,8)` (agree) |
| `(4,2):(1,16)` | `(_16,_2):(_1,_4)` | `(4,4,2):(1,8,4)` |
| `(2,5):(5,1)` | `(_5,_2):(_2,_1)` | `(5,2):(2,1)` (agree) |
| `((2,2),(2,2)):((1,4),(8,32))` | `(_4,_8,_2):(_1,_2,_8)` | `(2,2,4,2,2):(1,16,2,32,8)` |

The C++ output for `4:2` contains an explicit leading stride-0 mode that the Python result lacks entirely, and the hierarchical case differs in both rank and strides.

### Expected behavior

`pycute.left_inverse` should return the same canonical layout as `cute::left_inverse`, matching shape and stride structure, so the Python reference can be used to verify CuTe behavior. Alternatively, if the two algorithms are intentionally allowed to differ, the divergence should be documented in the pycute sources.

### Environment details

- Bare metal Windows host; C++ side compiled host-only with g++ against `include/cute/layout.hpp` from current `main`
- Pure Python comparison needs no GPU

items.title: add_tile_offset cross-term is not scaled by the element size in most transform/threadblock access iterators
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++ - `include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_access_iterator.h` and siblings

### Describe the bug

`add_tile_offset(TensorCoord const &tile_offset)` moves the iterator by whole tiles along both ranks. When a caller passes a non-zero `contiguous()` component while advancing along the strided rank (or vice versa), that cross-term must be scaled by the element size because the iterators keep byte-based pointers. The residue-handling branch of the plain predicated tile access iterator does scale it, but every other path applies the raw tile count:

`include/cutlass/transform/threadblock/predicated_tile_access_iterator.h`, residue path (correct):

```cpp
pointer_ += Shape::kContiguous * tile_offset.contiguous() * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8;
...
pointer_ += Shape::kStrided * tile_offset.strided() * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8;
```

same function, steady-state path a few lines below (unscaled):

```cpp
pointer_ += Shape::kContiguous * tile_offset.contiguous();
...
pointer_ += Shape::kStrided * tile_offset.strided();
```

So the same call arguments take differently-scaled code paths depending on `is_residual_tile_`. The same unscaled pattern appears in:

- `predicated_tile_access_iterator_2dthreadtile.h` (both paths)
- `ell_predicated_tile_access_iterator.h` (both paths)
- `predicated_tile_access_iterator_triangular_matrix.h` (both paths)
- `predicated_tile_access_iterator.h`, `AffineRankN<2>` specialization, which additionally ignores `stride_[0]` for the contiguous rank

I believe no in-tree caller currently trips this: every `add_tile_offset` call site on these global-memory iterators passes exactly one non-zero component (`{1,0}` / `{0,1}` / `{0,-1}` style), so the cross term is always zero and the missing scaling is invisible. It is nevertheless a broken API contract for any external code moving tiles diagonally with `Element` wider than one byte, and the intra-file inconsistency shows at least one of the two paths must be wrong.

### Steps to reproduce

Static: diff the two branches of `PredicatedTileAccessIterator::add_tile_offset` in the file above. A host-side demonstration needs only instantiating the iterator with a two-component tile offset, which no current example does.

### Expected behavior

Both paths should apply the same, correctly scaled cross-term (element size, and for the `AffineRankN<2>` case the layout stride).

### Environment details

- Current main, header-only observation
- Found while auditing the transform/threadblock iterator family; no functional failure observed in any in-tree kernel

items.title: GEMM profiler verification compares only batch 0 when batch-count > 1
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The GEMM profiler's verification compares only the first batch when `--batch-count=N` with N > 1.

All gemm-family verify paths pass the per-batch stride as the element count:

```cpp
results_.back().verification_map[library::Provider::kCUBLAS] = compare_tensors(
  options,
  *gemm_workspace_.Computed,
  *gemm_workspace_.Reference,
  gemm_workspace_.Computed->batch_stride()      // <-- elements in ONE batch
);
```

(tools/profiler/src/gemm_operation_profiler.cu lines ~1369-1374 for cuBLAS and ~1542-1547 for the host reference; the same pattern appears in tools/profiler/src/block_scaled_gemm_operation_profiler.cu ~1357-1370 and blockwise_gemm_operation_profiler.cu ~1195-1200.)

`DeviceAllocation` allocates `capacity_ = batch_stride_ * batch_count_` (tools/profiler/src/device_allocation.cu ~350-356), so `Computed`/`Reference` hold all batches but `compare_tensors(..., count)` (tools/profiler/src/operation_profiler.cu ~630) only walks `batch_stride()` elements, i.e. batch 0. Batches 1..N-1 are never compared against either reference provider.

Consequence: a kernel bug that corrupts only later batches (wrong batch-stride advance in an epilogue or TMA descriptor) reports `Passed` under `--verification=true --batch-count=N`.

For contrast, the rank_k/rank_2k/symm/trmm/conv profilers compare with the full capacity, which is the conservative direction.

### Suggested fix

Either loop over batches comparing each `batch_stride()` slice at its offset, or compare the full capacity after ensuring padding regions are written deterministically. A one-line interim hardening is to compare `Computed->capacity()` instead of `batch_stride()` when `batch_count > 1`.

This is a static trace through allocation, stride computation, and the comparison call; I did not construct a deliberately-wrong kernel to demonstrate a false pass.

items.title: rank_2k_universal and symm_universal Arguments constructors discard batch_stride_B
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The `Arguments` constructors of two kernels discard their `batch_stride_B` parameter and store 0 instead:

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/rank_2k_universal.h:176
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),

// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/symm_universal.h:173
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),
```

`trmm_universal.h:158` stores its parameter (`batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B)`), which makes the intent clear; these are copy-paste typos. Confirmed by constructing `Arguments` for both kernels in a host program and printing the stored field: passing 200 stores 0.

Consequences:

1. `Params` construction copies `args.batch_stride_B`, so downstream code always sees stride 0.
2. Both kernels' `transposed_problem()` does `std::swap(args.batch_stride_A, args.batch_stride_B)` on an `Arguments` built by that constructor (`rank_2k_universal.h:189`), so after the swap the *stored* `batch_stride_A` becomes the dead 0 too: for the transposed path both batch strides are wrong, not just B's.

Additional observation while tracing this: neither kernel body ever reads `params.batch_stride_A` or `params.batch_stride_B` (unlike `gemm_universal.h`, which advances both pointers per batch), so batched operation through these kernels keeps A and B fixed across batches regardless of the arguments. The typo is provable on its own; the unused-stride observation may deserve separate attention.

### Suggested fix

Store the parameter in both places:

```cpp
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B),
```
